entries.title: 1CO 3:6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Man's work and God's. I. MAN'S WORK. It is: 1. Varied. Paul speaks of planting and watering; may extend to the multiform operations of agriculture. We cannot all do the same work. Let us seek to do that for which we are fitted. There is some spiritual work suited to each of us. In agriculture all find employment, from th~ boy with his clapper scaring away the birds, to the presiding mind which controls all operations. If Christians do nothing it is because they want to do nothing. 2. Impor- tant. As in husbandry, unless we sow and water we may not look for a harvest, so as a rule in things spiritual. Never think that what you can do is unimportant. You. may think too little of your work as well as too much. You will think too little if yon think that your work may safely be left undone. 3. Honourable. Christian work itself,-what can compare with it/or an instant? Further, in it we are "God'sfellow- worlcers" (ver. 9). The Christian worker is one of God's nobility. 4. Limited. We can only do so much. We may sow and water, but not give the increase. It belongs to, us to preach aud teach, not to convince; to invite and warn, not to convert. We cannot produce spiritual results. We are not responsible for them. 5. Not independent. We can1Jot do our own work apart from God; it is "as the Lord gave to every man" (ver. 5). The seed that we plant is God's; the soil and water are God's; our powers employed are not "ours" but "God's." 6. To be rewarded. Upon just principles; according to the" labour" (ver. 8); according to faithfulness in the labour (Matt. xxv. 14-30). Not according to success. We cannot command this, though success usuaily follows faithful labour, and lack of success often means lack of diligence, or lack of something which should not have been lacking. Many Christians have an unhappy facility in accounting for failure. II. Gov's WORK. 1. Wonderful. Deeply mysterious. How marvellous the develo1•- ment of the seed after it is planted! Before this expansion and multiplication of lifo science stands dumb and confounded. So with the seed of the Word in the human heart. What inexplicable working and result! Well may we bow in adoring awn ou. 111. 1-23.J THE FITIST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIA:NS. 11 l

beforo this mystery of Divine might. 2. All-important. The great need: without this, all nothing. If the increase comes not, of what service is it to plant and irrigate? If tl!e Divine blessing rests not on our preaching and teaching, of what possible service can Jt be? Alas/ how often we forget thi.~! No harvest becau-~e God i,gnored. 3. Independent. God is not in any way dependent upon us or others for the increase; neither is he for the sowing and watering. 'l'he storm-wind can be his seed-sower, the rainsano. the dews are his servants. Ill. REFLECTIONS. 1. God's work and man's are usually conjoined. God works generally by means. Let us, therefore, see that our part is done. 2. As our part is important, let us do it with the utmost possible efficiency. 3. Let us ever remember that we are working in God's field, and near to him, under his observation, etc. 4. Let us never attempt to do God's part or take any of the glory when it is done. 5. Let us ever oear in mind the relative importance of God's work and ours. Our work is nothing in comparison with his; we are nothing in comparison with him (ver. 7). 6. When we have <lone our part, let us look in faith to God to accomplish his. 7. Let us think little of man, much of God. 8. Let us never expect God's work from man. 9. As we work with and for the same God, let us cultivate unity.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 3:10
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-771e great Foundation. I. WHAT IT IS. It is Christ (ver. 11). He- is the Foundation of: 1. Christianity. Its basis is conveye<l. in its name. It rests upon Uhrist. If be be removed, it falls to the ground in ruins; if he be dimiuishe<l (as in the denial of bis divinity, for example), Christianity becomes weak and tottering. As Christianity is of Christ, so is it strong, abiding, glorious. 2. The Christian Church. Its doctrines and practice. How many other foundations have been laid for it from time to time! how often there bas been an attempted union of other foundations with the one Foundation, Jesus Christ I To tamper with this Foundation is perilous indeed ; to add to it is to deteriorate and to threaten the whole superstructure. The Christian Uhurch should look to her Foundation, and clear away all that is not of Christ. No hurricane or storm will move her if she is on the Rock; but if her dependence be upon the shifting sands of wealth, position, world-power, human learning, or other things of man, woe betide her! 3. Religious work. How Paul made Christ the Foundation of his work amongst the Corinthians when he determined to know nothing but Christ and him crucified (eh. ii. 2) ! When we teach we should teach Christ, when we prea~h we should preach Christ. Our work amongst men is not to be based upon our fancies or upon human theories, but upon Christ and his great redemptive work. We ma_v amuse men with the fireworks of rhetoric or startling supposition, but the blaze will soon be over, and the old darkness will seem more intense than ever. If we want to bring abiding light to men, we must not divert them with pyrotechnic displays, but we must bring them to the Sun-the Sun of Uighteousness. Much "religious work" is like a house built upon nothing. The marvel is, not that it should last so short a time, but that it should last at all. 4. Godly life. There is no sure foundation but this. Christ is the way to holiness. A life's labour after true excellence-will be thrown away unless Christ be the Starting-point. vVe shall not reach God without Cbri.,t: "No man cometh unto the Father but by me" (John xiv. 6); "\Vithout me ye can do nothing." From Christ we receive power to live aright. Many seek to be godly that they may come to Christ, instead of coming to Christ that they may be godly. We have heard of the man who resolved to rear the house first and put in the foundation afterwards, but he was not a successful builder. 5. National greatness. A 11ation is truly great only in so for as it is based upon Christ aud the principles which heexpounded. The nations have perished one after another; their greatness was spurious, and therefore they were ephemeral; they rested upon that which moved, not upon that which is immovable-" The same yesterday, to-day, an,\ ,vr ever." \Vhen the nation arises which shall be founded upon Christ and his truth, its glory and l!:reatne,s shall excel the palmiest days of Solomon, and it shall abide. Our duty as subjects is. to remove from the national foundations all that is not of Christ. Sacrifice may Leentailed, but never loss: it is never loss to cast away the bad. II. How IT IS LAID. 1. By human instrumentality. At Corinth b_v Paul: "wise" (ver. 10) was he as a master-builder to lay this foundation, as well as wise in his. maimer of laying it. Here is marvellous honour conferred upon human crerrn:rcs, that U2 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIANS. [cH. m. 1-23

uf laying tl1e great foundation. We may participate in this vast privilege; we may l,a\'c the high joy of laying the Fonndati,in, Jesus Christ, in some unsaved souls. If arclrnngels cnu!d envy, assuredly they would envy us this sublime, all-glorious work. How readily should we run to it! how gladly devote to it our every power! how unceasingly labour and pray until "Christ be formed in" those whoso salvation we desire! 2. Under Divine direction and by Divine help. What wisdom is here required I and of ourselns we arc but foolish; what power! and we are weaklings. ·• Our sufficiency is of God." Only are we "wise master-builders" when we constantly look up for guidance a1.d rely upon Omnipotence. If we do anythiug in this matter it can only -be "according to the grace of God" (ver. 10). This grace must be souuht. When recei,ed and made effective in our lives, all the glory of that which is a~complished must be ascribed to him from whom the grace has flowed.-H.

Yers. 10-15.-Christian work and its testing. I. CmusTIAN WORK: 1. Should be rightly based. Christ is the only Foundation for the spiritual buildinu. This Founda- tion may have been already laid for us by others where we are called to labour: if so, we must sec that we are building upon it; if it be not laid, by "the grace of God" (ver. 10) we must seek to lay it without delay. A.II our teaching must rest upon Christ. He is not only the Omega to be ended with, but the Alpha to be begun with. All our efforts will be fruitless unless identified with him. The well-constructed,house built upon the sand perishes; so the most earnest and devoted labour is thrown away M'bere Christ is ignored. The Christian builder should look carefully to his founda- 1 ion. Whilst others build upon all sorts of things, he should build only upon Christ. 2. Should be wisely ordered. It is not enough to work; we must work wisely and \\'ell. Some seem to think that if they engage in Christian service, it is no matter how .they engage in it; if the work be but done, it is no matter how it is done. Some of the moftt slipshod slatternly work under God's sun is done in God's Name and in connection with his kingdom. In other departments of life, care, watchfulness, anxiety, assiduity, are demanded; but in the religious sphere the thing is to get the work done somehow or other, and if it be but done somehow, all is likely to be well! Such careless builders sadly need the apostolic blast of warning: "Let every man take Leed how l,e buildeth" (ver. 10). Christian work should be conformed to Christ in c,ery particular. The superstructure should correspond to the Foundation. Epithets may go for little with us; in our teaching we should be just as "narrow" as Christ and just as "broad" as Christ. Our building will be of right dimensions if it is r,either wider nor less wide than the Rock-foundation upon which it rests. A.s to Leing "old-fasLioned," we need not greatly dread this if thereby we are more fully identified \\'itb our Lord; or "new-fangled," if thus we and our work are more truly after his mind. Christian work is planned work. A.s the architect has a plan for his work, so the great Architect has a plan for his work, and for that part of his worlc which he entrusts to us to perform. If we "take heed how we build," we shall take heed that we build only according to the Divine plan. Knowledge of this is to be sought in prayer and from the Divine Word. There is one way in which our life-work should Le done; that way has Leen conceived by the Divine mind; we should seek a revelation of it. The Christian must not be his own architect. 3. In Christian work right materials should be used. It is not enough that we teach; we must teach the truth, and we must teach the truth as it is in Jesus. Our doctrine must be of Christ, and it must be lj()und 'doctrine, the "sincere milk" of the Word; the revelation of God, iinedited by man. What rubbish has been and is taught by not a few! how much "wood, hay, stubble," placed in the great spiritual building I No wonder that tho Christian soldier is so often worsted when he fights with gingerbread weapons. Shame upon men that, when the right material for labour is provided, they go bunting about for the wrong. The Scriptures are the great quarry and mine in which costly £tones and gold and silver abound, and no zealous spiritual builder need lack who will i;earch these mines. II. CHRISTIA:?,; WORK WILL BE TESTED. A solemn thought. Ottr work will be tested I When Christian work is done, that is not the eud of it. It will be tried. Well may we ask: 1. When f On" the day," says.the apostle. Christian work is tested on many days. Much of it does not stand the test of these days. But on the day-the day of 011. 111. 1-23.] 'l'llE FIRST EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIANS. 113

<l11ys-the ju<lgment d11y-all shall be tested an<lfinally tested. "Each man's work shall be made manifest;" its true character will then be seen. "The day shall declare it" as it is, not as it has been thought to be. Now it may look well; but then 1 A veil now rests upon Christian work, then the veil shall be taken away; now the scaffolding obscures the building, then it shall fall, and then shall be seen "of what sort" the building is. The final test cannot beeNcaped from. 2. Jlow1 By" .fire." (Not by the fires of purgatory; the apostle speaks of fire applied to work, not to persons,-not remedial, but testing.) The test will be thorough, searching, perfectly efficient. The false work will stand this test when hay and wood and stubble can abide unchanged in the flame ; but not till then. Our work may look well now, but how will it bear the fire-test? 3. By whom 1 God. At the great day he will be Judge, and will try every man's work. He will apply thefire-test. He loves truth and hates lies, which we call shams. On that day he will manifest the truth concerning work done in his Name. Whatever it has seemed before, it will then seem as it really is. 'l'he careless and the false may well tremble. at the thought of this ordeal; but the sincere and faithful may have confidence; for a.s no work then will be ma.de to appear better than it is, none will be made to appear worse. III. 'l.'HE ISSUES OF THE TESTING OF CHRISTIAN WORK. 1. As to the work tested. Some will stand. The pessimists will then be ashamed; ra.ilers and mockers will then be silenced. '!'here is some work (and who shall say that it is little?) which will approve itself to God, and stand the final and most searching trial. 'l'his, doubtless, will be the work done in Divine strength, and, whilst the doers of it will rejoice with exceeding joy, they will.as assuredly cry," Not unto us." Some work will not stand the test. As hay and wood and stubble are speedily consumed in the fire, so this work will perish iu the last testing flames. To see a life-work destroyed in a day! A. life lived and uo fruit. No "Well done" because all bas been ill done. A.nd perhaps all through carelessness, sluggishness, self-reliance, inattention to the " mind of Christ." Sad, sad close of a "Christian course." 2. As to workers. Some shall "receive a reward;" their work has borne the test. Though they say truly that t bis reward is "unmerited," they shall have it. "Doth Job serve God for nought?" Certainly not; no man ever did or shall. We lose nothing by labouring for Christ; and note that we lose nothing by labouring thoroughly for him. We may lose by labouring halfheartedly-we may lose our reward. It is best every way to do our best in Christ's service. Some receive no reward. Their work perishes and they "suffer loss," but they themselves are saved, "yet so as by fire," i.e. barely, with difficulty. The reference is to those who bold fundamental truths (for they are supposed to build on the on~ l•'ouudation, ver. 12), but who mingle with their teaching the wood, hay, and stubble of human notions. Strikingly are we here taught that salvation is not of works; for the works perish, but the salvation abides. Doubtless we must suppose that in snch cases there is true Christian living and a real desire to do the Master's will ; for these are necessary evideuces of a saved, regenerate state; but the vital truth of salva- tion by faith is pointedly illustrated by the chief works of the lifo (upon which all would have been resting if salvation were of works) suffering ignominious rejectioll. Being saved "so as by fire" is in striking contrast to" the abundant entrance." May we have the ecstatic joy of the latter, and the holy gladness which comes from seeing that Wfl have not "lived in vain" 1-H.

Vers. 16, li.-God's temple. Declared to be the Church of Christ. Each community of Christians is a temple of God. The old temple has perished; this is the new and the imperishable. The Christian Church bas often been insignificant in number,, wealth, position, earthly learniug; men have despised her; judged by human standan\:; she has appeared contemptible; but the Divine thought h11s been this-the temple of God I I. RESEMBLANCES. 1. Erected under Divine direction. The olcl and new temples are of God; they express his thought and purpose. Believers who constitute the new templo become believers through him; for faith is the gift of God. 'l'hcy are gathered into the Church as spiritual stones, by his servants, unJer bis direction, and each has an appropriate place. God is the Author of the constitution of the Church. 2. Erected for the Divine glory. 'l'he supreme object. Everything in the Church to be wade I COlllNTHIANS. 114 TUE FIRST EPISTLE TO 'l'I.IE CORIN'l'HIANS. [cH. m. 1-23.

-.ikcrdent to this. To gl,,rify God should be the lire-object of the redeemed, And: ::. Erected .foi· the welfare of men. The temple of old was for God and also for man, The Church has a great mission to the world. There is no conflict between the twQ , ,l,jects. As the Church seeKs to save the lost, she is most truly seeking to brin"' gl,1ry to Go<l.. Her worship is likely to be a mockery unless her work is faithfully per~ Iormed. 4. Set apart for God. The Church should be separate, holy, peculiarly God's. "A peculiar people-a people for God's own possession" (1 Pet. ii. 9); "Ye are not ~·our own." 5. .AnobJectofbeauty. The beauty of holiness should clothe the Church. The world's adruirntion has often been commanded, in early days and since. And better ~till, God bas approved. 6. Of great variety in its parts. Vast diversity in gift and condition, but one spiritual building. In the Christian Church there cannot, perhaps, be too much variety as there certainly cannot be too much oneness. 7. The dwelling- place of God. Not only for God, but God's dwelling-place. This was the glory of the Jewish temple-the Shechinah-the Divine presence. 'l'he Church's joy and glory are that "God is in the midst of her." He dwells not now in temples made with hands, though he docs dwell in the temples made by the Divine hands. The ancient temple was unmeaning and useless without the presence of Jehovah. So is the Christian Church : "Ye also are builded together for a habitation of God through the Spirit" (Eph. ii. 22). 8. From it true worship should arise. Sanctuary worship, home worship, business worship, recreation worship, worship throughout all the life of those wh.:, constitute the temple. 9. In it should ever be the great sacrifice. Not the sacrifice of the Mass, but " Christ crucified " manifestly set forth. The temple of old would have been offensive to God without sacrifice, so we cannot be acceptable to him without the atonement. When the Church loses the cross she loses God. In every Christian com- munity there must be a Calvary. And the true Jerusalem has not its Calvary" without the gate;" Christ crucified is central, chief, ;sedominant. II. PUNISHMENT FOR INJURY. Aaronic priests who violated the ancient temple were doomed to death; injurers of the Church of Christ will meet a terrible fate. In ver. l'i the Greek verb, which means" to bring into a worse state," is repeated; what we do to the Church, God will do to us-if we injure it, he will injure us. At Corinth the dividers of the Church were likely to become destroyers, and so God will "destroy." 'l'bese are far more serious offenders than those named in Vtlrs. 12 and 15. God is jealous over bis temple, and men may not do evil to it with impunity. Those who sin against it sin directly against him. Note: We may injure the temple of God in many ways. For example, by (1) false doctrine; (2) unchristian spirit; (3) personal unholiness; (4) conniving at unholiness in others; (5) failing to do our part; (6) failing to take our place in the Church. III. How CAREFUL WE SHOULD DE m ALL THAT CONCERNS THIS TEMPLE. In Church life and Church work. How serious are these! in them there is no room for trifling. Alas! how many are living in the Church, and even labouring in it, who seem to feel little or no responsibility! Let us realize what this Church is, and then assuredly with more care than the Aaronic priests shall we comport ourselves. To avoid offence and injury and failure, we shall need the wisdom that cometh down from above (vcrs. 18-20).-H.

In Christian work right materials should be used. It is not enough that we teach; we must teach the truth, and we must teach the truth as it is in Jesus. What rubbish has been and is taught by not a few! how much "wood, hay, stubble," placed in the great spiritual building I No wonder that tho Christian soldier is so often worsted when he fights with gingerbread weapons. Shame upon men that, when the right material for labour is provided, they go bunting about for the wrong. The Scriptures are the great quarry and mine in which costly £tones and gold and silver abound, and no zealous spiritual builder need lack who will i;earch these mines. II. CHRISTIA:?,; WORK WILL BE TESTED. A solemn thought. Ottr work will be tested I When Christian work is done, that is not the eud of it. It will be tried. Well may we ask: 1. When f On" the day," says.the apostle. Christian work is tested on many days. Much of it does not stand the test of these days. But on the day-the day of 011. 111. 1-23.] 'l'llE FIRST EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIANS. 113

<l11ys-the ju<lgment d11y-all shall be tested an<lfinally tested. "Each man's work shall be made manifest;" its true character will then be seen. "The day shall declare it" as it is, not as it has been thought to be. Now it may look well; but then 1 A veil now rests upon Christian work, then the veil shall be taken away; now the scaffolding obscures the building, then it shall fall, and then shall be seen "of what sort" the building is. The final test cannot beeNcaped from. 2. Jlow1 By" .fire." (Not by the fires of purgatory; the apostle speaks of fire applied to work, not to persons,-not remedial, but testing.) The test will be thorough, searching, perfectly efficient. The false work will stand this test when hay and wood and stubble can abide unchanged in the flame ; but not till then. Our work may look well now, but how will it bear the fire-test? 3. By whom 1 God. At the great day he will be Judge, and will try every man's work. He will apply thefire-test. He loves truth and hates lies, which we call shams. On that day he will manifest the truth concerning work done in his Name. Whatever it has seemed before, it will then seem as it really is. 'l'he careless and the false may well tremble. at the thought of this ordeal; but the sincere and faithful may have confidence; for a.s no work then will be ma.de to appear better than it is, none will be made to appear worse. III. 'l.'HE ISSUES OF THE TESTING OF CHRISTIAN WORK. 1. As to the work tested. Some will stand. The pessimists will then be ashamed; ra.ilers and mockers will then be silenced. '!'here is some work (and who shall say that it is little?) which will approve itself to God, and stand the final and most searching trial. 'l'his, doubtless, will be the work done in Divine strength, and, whilst the doers of it will rejoice with exceeding joy, they will.as assuredly cry," Not unto us." Some work will not stand the test. As hay and wood and stubble are speedily consumed in the fire, so this work will perish iu the last testing flames. To see a life-work destroyed in a day! A. life lived and uo fruit. No "Well done" because all bas been ill done. A.nd perhaps all through carelessness, sluggishness, self-reliance, inattention to the " mind of Christ." Sad, sad close of a "Christian course." 2. As to workers. Some shall "receive a reward;" their work has borne the test. Though they say truly that t bis reward is "unmerited," they shall have it. "Doth Job serve God for nought?" Certainly not; no man ever did or shall. We lose nothing by labouring for Christ; and note that we lose nothing by labouring thoroughly for him. We may lose by labouring halfheartedly-we may lose our reward. It is best every way to do our best in Christ's service. Some receive no reward. Their work perishes and they "suffer loss," but they themselves are saved, "yet so as by fire," i.e. barely, with difficulty. The reference is to those who bold fundamental truths (for they are supposed to build on the on~ l•'ouudation, ver. 12), but who mingle with their teaching the wood, hay, and stubble of human notions. Strikingly are we here taught that salvation is not of works; for the works perish, but the salvation abides. Doubtless we must suppose that in snch cases there is true Christian living and a real desire to do the Master's will ; for these are necessary evideuces of a saved, regenerate state; but the vital truth of salva- tion by faith is pointedly illustrated by the chief works of the lifo (upon which all would have been resting if salvation were of works) suffering ignominious rejectioll. Being saved "so as by fire" is in striking contrast to" the abundant entrance." May we have the ecstatic joy of the latter, and the holy gladness which comes from seeing that Wfl have not "lived in vain" 1-H.

Vers. 16, li.-God's temple. Declared to be the Church of Christ. Each community of Christians is a temple of God. The old temple has perished; this is the new and the imperishable. The Christian Church bas often been insignificant in number,, wealth, position, earthly learniug; men have despised her; judged by human standan\:; she has appeared contemptible; but the Divine thought h11s been this-the temple of God I I. RESEMBLANCES. 1. Erected under Divine direction. The olcl and new temples are of God; they express his thought and purpose. Believers who constitute the new templo become believers through him; for faith is the gift of God. 'l'hcy are gathered into the Church as spiritual stones, by his servants, unJer bis direction, and each has an appropriate place. God is the Author of the constitution of the Church. 2. Erected for the Divine glory. 'l'he supreme object. Everything in the Church to be wade I COlllNTHIANS. 114 TUE FIRST EPISTLE TO 'l'I.IE CORIN'l'HIANS. [cH. m. 1-23.

-.ikcrdent to this. To gl,,rify God should be the lire-object of the redeemed, And: ::. Erected .foi· the welfare of men. The temple of old was for God and also for man, The Church has a great mission to the world. There is no conflict between the twQ , ,l,jects. As the Church seeKs to save the lost, she is most truly seeking to brin"' gl,1ry to Go<l.. Her worship is likely to be a mockery unless her work is faithfully per~ Iormed. 4. Set apart for God. The Church should be separate, holy, peculiarly God's. "A peculiar people-a people for God's own possession" (1 Pet. ii. 9); "Ye are not ~·our own." 5. .AnobJectofbeauty. The beauty of holiness should clothe the Church. The world's adruirntion has often been commanded, in early days and since. And better ~till, God bas approved. 6. Of great variety in its parts. Vast diversity in gift and condition, but one spiritual building. In the Christian Church there cannot, perhaps, be too much variety as there certainly cannot be too much oneness. 7. The dwelling- place of God. Not only for God, but God's dwelling-place. This was the glory of the Jewish temple-the Shechinah-the Divine presence. 'l'he Church's joy and glory are that "God is in the midst of her." He dwells not now in temples made with hands, though he docs dwell in the temples made by the Divine hands. The ancient temple was unmeaning and useless without the presence of Jehovah. So is the Christian Church : "Ye also are builded together for a habitation of God through the Spirit" (Eph. ii. 22). 8. From it true worship should arise. Sanctuary worship, home worship, business worship, recreation worship, worship throughout all the life of those wh.:, constitute the temple. 9. In it should ever be the great sacrifice. Not the sacrifice of the Mass, but " Christ crucified " manifestly set forth. The temple of old would have been offensive to God without sacrifice, so we cannot be acceptable to him without the atonement. When the Church loses the cross she loses God. In every Christian com- munity there must be a Calvary. And the true Jerusalem has not its Calvary" without the gate;" Christ crucified is central, chief, ;sedominant. II. PUNISHMENT FOR INJURY. Aaronic priests who violated the ancient temple were doomed to death; injurers of the Church of Christ will meet a terrible fate. In ver. l'i the Greek verb, which means" to bring into a worse state," is repeated; what we do to the Church, God will do to us-if we injure it, he will injure us. At Corinth the dividers of the Church were likely to become destroyers, and so God will "destroy." 'l'bese are far more serious offenders than those named in Vtlrs. 12 and 15. God is jealous over bis temple, and men may not do evil to it with impunity. Those who sin against it sin directly against him. Note: We may injure the temple of God in many ways. For example, by (1) false doctrine; (2) unchristian spirit; (3) personal unholiness; (4) conniving at unholiness in others; (5) failing to do our part; (6) failing to take our place in the Church. III. How CAREFUL WE SHOULD DE m ALL THAT CONCERNS THIS TEMPLE. In Church life and Church work. How serious are these! in them there is no room for trifling. Alas! how many are living in the Church, and even labouring in it, who seem to feel little or no responsibility! Let us realize what this Church is, and then assuredly with more care than the Aaronic priests shall we comport ourselves. To avoid offence and injury and failure, we shall need the wisdom that cometh down from above (vcrs. 18-20).-H.

entries.title: 1CO 3:21–23
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The 'believer'sposse.~sions. I. WHAT THESE ARE. 1. Ministers. Tbe Corinthians had made a strange mistake ; they had been regarding ministers as masters, and cl1oosing which foey preferred to serve. In a singular loss of dignity (singular because many of them were not a little afflicted with pride) they had become ambitious of belonging to ministers, forgetting that ministers, as such, belonged to them. Ministers are the servants of the Church, and thus among the believer's possessions ; instead of quarrelling over them, be should use and enjoy them. God has greatly enriched his people by sending to them many able and faithful ministers. Whilst these should be highly esteemed for their work's sake, their true relation to the Church should never be lost sight of. They ~hould bear it in mind, and thus check any tendencies towards lordsbip. 2. The world. It is generally thought that the world belongs to tlic Wicked One and his children, seeing that it appears to bo largely in their bands. This is a popular blunder. The world was made and is lcept for the people of Go~. Unbelievers have no right to the things which they grnsp. '!'he ung<)dly hold their CII. m. 1-23.] 'l'HE FIHS'f EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'I-IE COIUN'l'HIA~S. 115

possessions upon n prccnrious tenure. 'l'hey arc very short leaseholders, or rather they are tenants-at-will. Believers arc the freeholders, and at last" the meek shall inherit the earth." 'l'he child of God has not yet" come of age;" but his title is good, and now he enjoys as much of his inheritance as is good for him in his present state. But as believers look a.t the world they can say," It is ours-all of it, and all things in it work together for our good." Cowper says- "The Christian looks abroad into the varied field Of nature, and, though poor perhaps eompar'<l With those whose mansions glitter in his sight, Co.lie the delightful scenery all his own. His nre the mountains, and the valleys his, Ancl the resplendent rivers; his t' enjoy With e. propriety that none C'-an feel But who, with filial confidence inspir'd, Can lift to heaven an unpresumptuous eye, And smiling say, 'My Father me.de them all.'" 3. Life. Without Christ there is nothing worthy of the name of life. Life is emphatic- ally the believer's. What possibilities it has for him! how vast are his opportunities! Pity it is that some believers seem only half alive to this. 'l'he child of God has in life the experience most likely to benefit him: mercies, joys, trials, temptations, pains- all his, to do him good. The lives of others are also controlled for the welfare of the redeemed. 4. Death. Death, a precious possession. 'l'hc entrance to the life immortal. Death conquered has beco::ne the believer's servant. Death, the dire loss of the impenitent, the great gain of the saints. The death of those outside the Church is ordered for the well-being of those within. God strikes down the foes of his people when the right hour has come. 5. Things present. The present order and movement in the world; all governments and powers; the march of the ages ;-all these thin"S are made subse1·vieut to the great work of redemption. "God moves in a mysterious ~ay " but always moves/or his people. 6. Things to come. Not only the present order ~f the worid, but the future. Believers often tremble for what is coming; the Church quakes, for she dreads some future movement, glimmerings of which she can discern, perhaps, in the present. But God is in the future, giving that future to his people. All discoveries, all increase of knowledge, all progress, shall be for the weal of Zion : ·" The mouth of the Lord hath spoken it." And the believer reckons amongst thin"s to collle, the heavenly world, the life immortal, the higher service, the perfected natur~ the unsullied joy. All these are his. How rich, how blessed, is he! 7. .d.ll things'. Marvellous truth, that there is nothing of which he can say, "It is not mine." II. SECURED BY THE BELIEVER'S CONNECTION WITH CHRIST. Believers are Christ's. lHis servants? yes; his friends? yes; but his "brethren," and thus "heirs" with him - " joint-heirs with Christ" (Rom. viii. 17). Christ is God's. All that the Father bath ,is the Son's. All that the Son hath belongs to those that are his ; and this is "all things." What an amazing transformation, then, there is in conversion! The unsaved .has nothing; the saved, "all things." Are we unutterably poor or infinitely rich? The question is answered when another is: "Are we Christ's? "-H.

Vers. l-9.-0hristian teachers and their work. The apostle has still in view the -dissensions prevailing in the Corinthian Church. Throughout the first four chapters this subject is never absent from his mind, even when it is most in the background. The spirit of party, with the various phases of thought and life that found expressiun therein, suggests the several topics on which he enlarges. l. THE CHRISTIAN TEACHER ADAPTS HIS TEACllING TO THE CAPACITIES OF HIS HEARERS. (Vers. 1-4.) Paul has already said (eh.ii. 6) that he" spake wisdom among the perfect," and here he presents the other side. 1. At Corinth he had to deal with carnal Christians. In the last verses of the previous chapter he has contrasted the natural man and the spiritual man, the latter alone being able to discern the things of -she Spirit. Here the comparison is not between Christians and non-Christians, but between different classes of Christians, distiuguished according to spiritual attainment. Every bclieYer in Christ is a spiritual man as compared with those who do not believe ; 116 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO 'IHE CORINTHIANS. [cn.m. 1-W.

but one believer may be carnal in comparison with another believer. The new natme may be weak and sickly and all but overlaid by the old. 'l'his was the case with the Corinthians, whose fleshliness of mind appeared in the prevalence of" jealousy and strife" and of party spirit. These things spring from the flesh (Gal. v. 20), whcrnver they are found. When the Church is rent by faction, and men thick mainly of the aggrandizement of their favourite party, no further proof is needed of the reign of carnality-. "The fruit of the Spirit is love, peace." A fl~shly Christian I What opposites must we unite in describing real character l :.!. They were as yet "babes in Christ." Conversion is a new birth: young con'l'Crts are new-born babes (1 Pet. ii. 2), 'l'hey have in germ all that is to be fouud in the full-grown man; but they are weak, dependent, immature. Young Christians have the rudiments of the Christian character in more or less clear outlin'e, but only the rudiments. Infancy is be.\utiful in its season, and so is the young life of the new convert; but out of season, its beauty is gone. A child with the )·ears of a man is a monstrosity in nature; an old Christian with the crudeness of a young conrnrt should appear to us as great a monstrosity in grace. The "babe in Christ" is meant to develop into "a full-grown man, into the measure of the stature ot the fulness of Christ" (Eph. iv. 13). 3. As babes, they must be fed "with milk, not with meat." Infants and men must each have food suitable to their capacity. The doctrines of the faith may be presented in the form of milk or of solid foud, Milk bas- in it all the nourishing elements to be found in strong meat, though in more diluted form. The facts of the gospel history contain all the truths of the most elaborate theological system; a child can digest them in the one form, but not in the other. Every wise teacher will adapt his teaching to the capacity of his hearers. He will give to each only such food as he can receive and assimilate. He will not give solid food to infants, nor will he feed full-grown men merely with milk. The preacher should consider the wants of women and children, as well as of meo, and adapt some part of the public service to them (comp. Heh. v. 12-14). 11. MINISTERS ARE Gon's SERVANTS, NOT PARTY LEADERS, The childish condition of the Corinthians was ·6hown in their party divisions. They gloried more in the leadei: after whom their faction was called than in Jesus Christ. 'l'o correct this the apostle- presents the right view of spiritual teachers aud their work. 1. Ministers are but servants. They are not heads of sects or schools, whose object is to gather disciples for themselves. 'l'hey are servants of God, doing his work. Therefore they are not to be lifted above their position, as they are when they are regarded as masters in the Chureh ; nor are they to sink below it, as they do when they take the law from any other but God. 2. Each minister has his own peculia1· work. "I planted, Apollos watered." Paul began the work at Corinth; .A.polios continued it. One minister is sent to preach the gospel to sinners, another to edify believers, another to teach the ignorant, another to comfort the sorrowful; hut all are contributors to the Rame great interest .. The servant's work, bowever, is but a subordinate instrumentality. Plantiog and watering are the ordinary conditions of growth, but they do not of themselves cause growth. It is "God that giveth the increase." In the spiritual sphere, as in the natural, the life-giving power is Divine; but in both cases this power usually works through human ministries. It is only in connection with diligent planting and watering that we can expect the increase. 3. Each minister has llis own peculiar reward. .A 11 are one,, inasmuch as all are servants of one Lord and engaged about the same work. Hence they are not to be set against each other as rivals, 'l'heir work is one, yet diverse; and so is their reward. No faithful servant Rhall go without a recompense at his Master's band; but each shall receive his own, alike in kind and in degree. 'l'he principle that determines this is-" according to bis own labour." It is not according to the fruit or result of our labour, but simply according to the measure of our labour. What reversals of human opinion are in store for us I Men applaud success; God prai,es fidelity. Many an obscure but faithful worker shall receive a greater reward than be who basbeen less faithful but more prominent and successful. 4. Ministers are God'sfellowworkers. All God's servants are fellow-servants as workers for him; but here the fellowship is carried still higher. We are workers along with God, who is pleased to associate us with himself in the great work of his kingdom. What a thought is this! (1) What dignity it gives to tbe Christian ministry! It is to work with God. (2) Jlow inspiring to the Christian wurker ! Who would not labour when God is with

him? (3) How sure the reward I Will God leave his follow-workers without a due recompense? Ill. BELIEVEilB ARE Goo's FIELD. The same idea is elsewhere expressed under tha figure of a garden (Isa. lviii. 11) and a vineyard (Isa. v.). Consider: 1. The Proprietor of the field. 'fhe Church is God's field. It is not the Church of Paul, or A polios, or any other; but "the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood" (Acts xx. 28), It belongs to him; it exists for him; it is called by his Name. Hence the spirit 4lf faction, which ranges parties and sects under the names of rival leaders, robs God of his glory as the Church's Lord. 2. The labourers in the field, These are apostles, evangelists, pastors, teachers, etc. (see above). 3. The field itself. (1) Its original condition. Wild, untilled, full of merely natural ;growths. Believers are originally a part of the world, living in a state of sin, under no gracious culture. (2) The work bestowed upon it. Preparatory work : trenching, ploughing, ~athering out stones, fencing; and then the sowing of seed, planting, weeding, etc. Corresponding to this there is a preparation of heart for receiving the truth, an awakening to a sense of sin and need, a. quickening into spiritual life, a. culture of the cew life into fulness and streugth, etc. For these ends every true labonrer works, but always in dependence on the power of the Holy Spirit, who alone can make our labour fruitful. (3) Its produce. 'l.'he farmer looks for a. return from his field in the form of fruit in harvest; God expects his Church to yield fruit to his glory. Christian character, life, usefulness, productiveness,-these a.re some of the returns for which the Lord of the lield looks (comp. Luke xiii. 6-9; John xv. 1, etc.).-B.

entries.title: 1CO 3:10–15
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The Foundalion and the superstructure. Under the figure of a building, the apostle continues to speak of the work of Christ's ministers, and specially of his own labours at Corinth. As the first to preach the gospel there, he had laid the fouudatioa, upon which the teachers that succeeded him were -to build. 'l'he reference is primarily to doctrine, but the principles apply to work and life as well. I. THE FOUNDATION. This is Jesus Christ the Mediator (Isa. xxviii. 16; 1 Pet. ii. 6). He is tpe ~'oundation of truth: the system of Christian theology is built upon him. All Christian tea.cbiug and preaching must have him for their basis. 'l'he entire structure of knowledge rests upon him who is the Source of all wisdom. He is also the Foundation of life. The Church is built upon him, believers being " living stones" in the great spiritual temple. In bot.h these respects Josus Christ is: 1. A Divine Foundation. "Behold I lay." The Church requires a basis laid by God himself. 2. A sure Foundation. No work of God can fail. Jesus Christ is a Foundation, not of sand, but of solid rock (Matt. vii. 24.-27). It will bear any strain, even the weight of a ~vorld. 3. The only Foundat-ion. This is the point emphasized here. Men build on other foundations when they rest their systems of belief on humau opinion, or base their hope of heaven upon their own works, the merits of others, the general mercy of God, etc. But " other foundation can (3ovaTa,) no man lay; " there is but one. IL THE B"GPERSTRUCTUBE. Having found the true Foundation, we must " take heed how we builu thereon." The work of ministers or of believers in general is here viewed as the superstructure. Two kinds of materials may be employed : "gold, silver, ::ostly stones "-the beautiful and lasting materials, suited for a temple; or "wood, hay, stubble "-the baser and more perishable materials, fit only for a temporary house. Apply this to: 1. Doctrine. 'l'he "gold," etc., represents pure, scriptural teaching. Take Paul's Epistles, e.g., as a noble structurn of truth built on Jesus Christ. Such doctrine is precious and abiding, like its Foundation. The "wood," etc., represeuts human opinions and speculations put in the place of God's truth. In Paul's time, Jewish tradition, Gnosticism, etc. ; in ours, Popery, Rit.nalism, etc. Such doctrines aro not truly edifying. 2. Life. 'l'he "gold," etc., is a. Christian life of the noblest kind, built out of faith, hope, love. Pure, unselfish, Christ-like character. Variety may be indicated in the three materials. Gold may denote the most brilliant service rendered hy consecrated genius, heroic faith, patient suffering. Silver may indicate a. work less Lrilliant, but useful-the honest doing of tho Lord's will. Oo5tly stones-marble ot granite, e.g.-a life of solidity and strength, on which others may lean. Each of these classes has its own place and value. All are genuine. The "wood," etc., is a Christian life of the poorest kind. Dull as wood, with little spiritual insight. Swayed by 118 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [err. m. 1-23'.

public opinion, as the gmss b_~· .every b~ceze. 1:3arren as stubble, bringing forth littie to the glory of God. \Vhat d1f!erences m the lives of Christians I Gold or stubble~ which? III. THE FIERY TRIAL. The true nature of our life and work is not always seen here. \Ve judge wrongly of ?tJ:ters and of ourse.lves. Men praise the wood as if it were gold; depreciate the gold as 1f 1t were wood. But "the day shall declare it "-Dies irie, dies ii/a-the day of fire, when Christ comes to judge (Mai. iii. 2, 3; iv. 1; 2 Thess. i. 8). Time tests but par_tially; the thorough test is the judgment-fire. Shall our work stand that? 1. The edifice (!{ "gold," ttc., shall stand. Truth will come throuc,h the fire• so will a g~nuine, unselfish, Christly life: Work for time perishes; work 1·or eternity endures. 'lhe fie~y ordeal Wil~ onlY: brm~ out mor~ clearly its true quality. '!'he bmlder shall receive a reward m seemg lus work abide (Phil. ii. 16), in bein"' reco"'- nized as a good workman (Matt. xxv. 21), and in wearing the crown of lifi~• (Jas.i. 12). Obser\'e, the reward is not for being on the Foundation, but for what is bnilt thereon. Salvation is of free grace; the reward is "according as his work" (Rev. xxii. 12). 2. The structure of" wood," etc., shall be burned up. Error, falsehood unreality• a life animated by a worldly, selfish spirit ;-these shall be consumed. 'l'h~ builder i; glad to get away with his life, as one escapes from a house in flames saved "so as through fire." Picture the consternation o_f t~e poor builder as he_ see~ the fire doing. its awful work, and hears the crash of his life-structure I He himself is saved for· Christ's sake, but his labour is lost. LEssoKs. 1. See to the nature of your life and work as Christians. Apply specially to Christian workers. 2. Be not satisfied with bare salvation at last. Build with materials that will endure. Have an eye to the "full reward" (2 John 8). 3. If many on the true Foundation shall be saved only "so as through :fire," how shall they escape that are building on a false foundation? (1 Pet. iv.17, 18).-B.

entries.title: 1CO 3:16
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The temple of God. Paul again takes up the idea of a building and gives it a new direction. The noblest of all edifices is a temple in which architecture finds its highest and worthiest employment. Under this figure the apostle sets forth sometimes the collective Church of Christ, sometimes the individual believer (eh. vi. 19; Eph. ii. 21). Man was created to be a sanctuary of God, but this sanctuary was overturned by sin. It lay in ruins till the Lord Jesus came as the Restorer, whose work it is to rebuild the ruined walls; and now the temple is seen rising in its fair proportions in the hearts of the regenerated, and in the spiritual house built of these living stones (1 Pet. ii. 5). I. BELIEVERS ARE GoD's TEMPLE. 1. God dwells in them. The temple at Jerusalem was Jehovah's dwelling-place. There he had bis Shechinah in the cloud above the mercy-seat and between the cherubim, and there he was worshipped. Even so "the Spirit of God dwelleth in you." '!'he Father and the Son make their abode with the man who loves and obeys the Son (John xiv. 23), and this is effected by the Spirit. This indw11lling is the culmination of the work of grace within us. The heart must first be quickened, renewed, purified, ere the Holy Spirit can dwell in it. How wonderful a truth is this! God in me! It is not the dream of the pantheist, who calls me a spark from the eternal fire-Gou. dwelling in me because I am only a mode of the one universal existence. It is not the raving of the mystic, whose imagination has betrayed him into a hazy confusion of ideas regarding bis relation to God. It is the utterance of sober truth. In me the creature-the new creature-God the Creator makes his abode; not, indeed, in the infinity of his being, as if our tiny vessels could contain the ocean, yet really. The little flower-cup has the sun dwelling in it all the day, though he dwells in thousands besides; and his presence is made known by the colour and fragrance and growth of the flower. '!'he same Spirit of God who abides in the Church abides in every true member of it; and this abiding is revealed in the love shed abroad in the heart, in the odour that breathes through the life, and in the gracious bending of the nature to all that is righteous. 2. They are holy. As the place where Jehovah dwelt, the Jewish temple was holy--consecrated to him, and to him alone. None but an Israelite could tread the outer court; none but the priests could serve in the holy place; none bnt the high priest could enter the holy of holies. Believers are holy, set apart for God and his fervice. They are not a public street or common, which the ~H. m. 1-23.] 'l'.HE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 11'.l

world may use as it likes; they are a sacred enclosure, marked off and devoted to holy uscH. 'l'hey are God's temple-body, soul, and spirit corre8ponding to the three divisions of the ancient tabernacle. 'J.'his applies also to the Church, which is holy because dwelt in by God, II. Gon's TF.MPLE MUST NOT DE MAnRED, This follows from what has been said. If God dwells in believers, an injury done to them is done to his sanctuary. Consider: 1. How the temple may be marred. entries.title: 1CO 3:17
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The temple of God. Paul again takes up the idea of a building and gives it a new direction. The noblest of all edifices is a temple in which architecture finds its highest and worthiest employment. Under this figure the apostle sets forth sometimes the collective Church of Christ, sometimes the individual believer (eh. vi. 19; Eph. ii. 21). Man was created to be a sanctuary of God, but this sanctuary was overturned by sin. It lay in ruins till the Lord Jesus came as the Restorer, whose work it is to rebuild the ruined walls; and now the temple is seen rising in its fair proportions in the hearts of the regenerated, and in the spiritual house built of these living stones (1 Pet. ii. 5). I. BELIEVERS ARE GoD's TEMPLE. 1. God dwells in them. The temple at Jerusalem was Jehovah's dwelling-place. There he had bis Shechinah in the cloud above the mercy-seat and between the cherubim, and there he was worshipped. Even so "the Spirit of God dwelleth in you." '!'he Father and the Son make their abode with the man who loves and obeys the Son (John xiv. 23), and this is effected by the Spirit. This indw11lling is the culmination of the work of grace within us. The heart must first be quickened, renewed, purified, ere the Holy Spirit can dwell in it. How wonderful a truth is this! God in me! It is not the dream of the pantheist, who calls me a spark from the eternal fire-Gou. dwelling in me because I am only a mode of the one universal existence. It is not the raving of the mystic, whose imagination has betrayed him into a hazy confusion of ideas regarding bis relation to God. It is the utterance of sober truth. In me the creature-the new creature-God the Creator makes his abode; not, indeed, in the infinity of his being, as if our tiny vessels could contain the ocean, yet really. The little flower-cup has the sun dwelling in it all the day, though he dwells in thousands besides; and his presence is made known by the colour and fragrance and growth of the flower. '!'he same Spirit of God who abides in the Church abides in every true member of it; and this abiding is revealed in the love shed abroad in the heart, in the odour that breathes through the life, and in the gracious bending of the nature to all that is righteous. 2. They are holy. As the place where Jehovah dwelt, the Jewish temple was holy--consecrated to him, and to him alone. None but an Israelite could tread the outer court; none but the priests could serve in the holy place; none bnt the high priest could enter the holy of holies. Believers are holy, set apart for God and his fervice. They are not a public street or common, which the ~H. m. 1-23.] 'l'.HE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 11'.l
