HO:MILET1CS. V ers. 1-7.-.A true and a false estimate of genuine minister~ of the gospel. "Let •n man so account or us as of the ministers of Christ," etc. Here we have- I. A TRUE ESTIMA'l'E of genuine ministers of' the gospel. 1. They are servants of (Jhrist. " Let a man so ac~ount of us as of the ministers of Christ." There are some who regard ministers of the gospel as servants of their Church. The Churches guarantee their stipend, and they require that their dogmas shall be propounded and tli.eir law~ ·obeyed. The paymasters, whether deacons, or elders, or the state, naturally expect subordination in their ministers. He who yields in any measure to snch an expectation ,legrades his position, and is not in the truest sense a minister of Christ. He who is the truo servant of Christ will feel and act as the moral master of the people-the leader and commander. "Obey them that have the rule over you," etc. There is no -office on this earth so dignified and royal as that of the true servant of Christ. 2. As ~ervants of Christ, they are responsible. "Stewards of the mysteries of God." The "'mysteries of God" here mean the gospel, which in the second chapter is said to be "the hidden wisdom \vhich God ordained before the world." 'l'he gospel is a mystery, not in the sense of absolute incomprehensibility, but in ihe sense of progressive unfoldment, both in respect to communities and individuals. It is a mystery to the man who at firsts be;!ins its study, but as he gets on it becomes more and more clear. The true minister is entrusted with these "mysteries;" he is to bring them out, translate them into intelligible ideas, and dispense them to the people. As a steward of such things, his position is one of transcendent responsibility. 3. As servants of Christ, they are fait~ful. "Moreover, it is required in stewards, that a man be founrl faithful." Fidelity is an essential attribute of a true minister. He must be faithful to his trust, not abuse it, but use it according to the directions of its owner. Faithful to its owner, in all things regulated by his directious. He must be faithful to his hearers, seeking no man's applause, fearing no man's i'rown, "commending himse!r to every man's conscience in the sight of God." 4. As servants -0f Christ, they are independent. " But with me it is a. very small thing that I shouhl be judged of yon, or of man's judgment." Whilst no true minister will despise the flwour or court the contempt of men, he will not be concerned about their judgrnent so long as he is faithful to his God. Paul gives utterance to this sentiment in order, no doubt, to reprove those preachers in the Corinthian Church who were seeking the praise of men. Paul seems to indicate here three reasons for this feeling of indepeu- -dency. (1) His own consciousness of fidelity. "For I know nothing by myself; yet -am I not hereby justified." "The sense is," says a modern expositor, "I am not cunscic,us of evil or unfaithfulness to myself; that is, in my ministerial lire." It is well l'Cmarked by Calvin that " Paul does not here refer to the whole of his life, but only to his apostleship. And the sense is, 'I am conscious of integrity in this oflice. My ow1, rnind does not condemn me of ambition or unfa.ithfulness. Others may accuse me, but 1 am not conscious of that which should condemn me or render me unworthy of this office.'" (2) His confidence in the judgment of God. "But he that judgeth me is the Lord." I am content to abide by his judgment. If his jurlgmr.nt of me agrees not with my own judgment of myself, I will loyally submit. (3) His belief in a full revelation -of that judgment. "Therefore judge nothing beforo the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness," etc. Do not let us judge one another; ,lo nut let us even trust too much to our own judgment of ourselves. Let us await Heaven's judgment. (a) There is a period appointed for that judgmenr. "Judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come." There is a" day appointed in which he will judge the world in righteousness." Ah! that day. (b) At that period .there will be a full revelation of our characters. "·who both will bring to light the 11idden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts.'' (c) At that period, too, every man shall have his due. "And then shall every man have praise of God.'' "Praise" here does not mean approbation, but that every man shall receive .his just due. Such considerations as these may well make minist~rs independeut of tl1e \u1lgmcnts of men, and regardless aliko of their smiles and their frowns. 11. A l'ALSE ESTUIATE of genuine ministers of the gospel. "Aud these thiu:;s,. 139 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. 1v. 1-21.

brctbrcn, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos," etc. Paul here mc:rns to say that he spoke of himself nnd Apollos to show the impropriety of ono minister being pitted against another. The members of the Corinthian Church had c\·idently formed an incorrect estimate of the true gospel minister. 1. They seen1cd to estimnte ministers in proportion us they met their views and feelings. Every true. preacher preache~ the gospel as it has passed through his own mind, and as it passes throupJ1 his own mind it will, of course, be more interesting to the minds most in liarmony with his own experience, capacity, nnd sympathies. Hence, in the Corinthian Church, those who preferred Peter's preaching thought no one was like Peter; those who preferred Apollos' thought there were none like him; and so with Paul. It is sonow. "There is no minister like our minister; all others are grades below." This is Yery false, for inasmuch as the great bulk of the community are more or less uneducated, unreflecting, and sensuous, the preacher who approximates most to their type of mind will attract the largest crowd and get the loudest hosannas. But is he on that account superior to others? By no means. 'l'hus it is that some of the most inferior prcnchers are over-rated and the most elevated and devoted degraded; whereas all true mi11isters are" ser,ants of Christ," the "stewards of the mysteries of God," and as such should be honoured. 2. They seemed to estimate miuisters accordin" to the greatness of their natural endo•cments. "Who maketh thee to differ from a~other?" etc. Between the natural endowments of Paul, .Apollos, and Peter there was a great difference, and, indeed, bet\\·een all ministers of the gospel there is a difference in natural endowments, and a great difference in the quality and measure of mind. But what of that? There is notl,ing in those natural endowments for boa~ting; for they all came from God. The man of the most far-reachin_g intellect, the most brilliant imagination, and transcendent genius has nothing which he has not received from that Spirit \1·hich distributes to every man according to his own will. No man or angel deserves c!·edi t on account of natural abilities. Co~cLuSION. "Let .us strive," says F. W. Robertson, "as much as possible to be tranquil. Smile when men sneer; be humble when they praise; patient when they blame. Their judgment will not last; 'man's judgment,' literally,' man's day,' is only for a time, but God's is for eternity. So, would you be secnre alike when the world fro1vns its censure or its applause upon you? feel hourly that God will judge. That will be your safeguard under both. It will be a small thing to you to be judged of any man's judgment; for your cause will be pleaded before the Judge and the Discerner of all secrets."

entries.title: 1CO 4:8
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-.Apostolic treatment of vanity. "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us: and I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you." Vanity is a state of mind at once the most prevalent and detestable; it is a plant that springs from self-ignorance, and is disgusting to the spectator in all its forms and fruits. See how the apostle treats it here. I. \Vith WITHERING SARCASM. "Now ye are full, no,v ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us." The Bible furnishes us with many instances of irony (see 1 Kino-s xviii. 27; Job xii. 2), but nowhere have we it in language more full and forceful th;n here. "Now ye are full," or "already are ye filled.'' You have had enough, you \rant nothing; "ye are rich" or" already ye are become rich.'' You are affluent in all gifts and graces. "Ye have reigned as kings without us.'' "Here are three metaphors, tbe first taken from persons filled with food, the second from persons so rich that they require no more, the third from those who have reached the highest elevation--obtained a throne." Paul seems to say to these conceited teachers that they were FO great that they did not require such services as his. We scarcely know of a more eifective way of treating vanity than by sarcasm. 'l'reat the vain, swaggering man before you, not according to your judgment of liim, but accordin!! to his estimate of himself. Speak to him as one as stupendous as he believes himself to be, and yourirony will stab him to the quick. Sarcasm is often the instrument of a great manly soul when roused into indignation. II. With A NOBLE GENEROSITY. "I would to God ye did reign, that we also might rei"'n with you;" or," I would ye did reign." Here the north wind of sarcasm gives way to the south breezes of love. What he means is a wish that they were as truly

full, rich, and royal as they thought themselves to be. The irony of a Christly man,, however pungent, is not malign, but generous.

entries.title: 1CO 4:9
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Man an obfect of angelic observation. "For I think that God bath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men." The margin reads " theatre" for "spectacle," from the Greek word 6,11:rpov. 'l'he reference, in all probability, is to the ancient amphi- theatre, whose arena was surrounded by circular seats, capable of accommodating thousands of spectators. In this arena trained athletes struggled for prizes in the ancient games; on such an arena Paul speaks of himself and fellow-labourers as stru~- gling, the objects not only of human but of angelic spectators. The world is indeed a moral theatre, every man an actor, and disembodied spirits look on as spectators. "We are eucompassed about.," etc. Angels as spectators are intelligent, interested, numerous, constant. If the eyes of such intelligences are constantly upon us, what are the practical conclu8ions? I. THAT OUR CONDUCT HERE CONCERNS THE UNIVERSE. No man lives unto himself; each unit is a link in beiug's endless chain. His actions must tell banefully or beneficently on the creation ; hence all loving and loyal intelligences direct their attention to him with deep and unabating interest. Besides, men and angels are offsprings of the same Father, participators of the same nature, subjects of the san,e moral government. No wonder they are so concerued. II. 'l'HAT OUR PART SHOULD BE CAREFULLY PLAYED. How doubly careful are our actors on the stage, in the presence of spectators distinguished for the highest genius, erudition, and artistic culture! It behoves every man to be cautions how he acts in the presence of his fellow-creatures, whether they are children or adults, plebeians or princes; but how much more cautions should he be when he knows that angels, whoso pure natures loathe sin in all its forms, have their keenest gaze fastened ever on his life. III. THAT THERE IS NO CHANCE OF CO:::<'CEALI:S-G OUR BIN. The attempt to cloak or dissemble our sins is absurdly futile. ,vhilst there is One who reads the heart, there may be millions who mark all our overt acts, whether wrought in darknesJ or in li.~ht. IV. THAT WE MAY EXPECT HELP IN ALL HOLY ENDEAVOURS. Those celestial spirits are sent forth to minister to the heirs of salvation. They have received a lJi,·i:1ecommission to bear us up, lest we uash our feet against a stone. In all ages they have rendered assistance to the good, They hel;·ed Abraham on the plains of Manue, and Lot in his flight towards Zoar; they freed the apostle from the prison; they bore the spirit of Lazarus to the bosom of Abraham. CONCLUSION, "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which <loth so easily beset us" (Heb. xii. 1).

entries.title: 1CO 4:10–14
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Paul's treatment of self-conceited teachers. "We are fools foi· Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye arc strong; ye are houourable, but we are despised. Even unto this present hour we both hunger, aml thirst., and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwelling-place; and labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless ; being persecuted, we· suffer it; being defamed, we entreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day. I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you." Paul is still thinking of those teachers of the- Corinthian Church who were" puffed up," inflated with conceit. He treats them lll'l·c with- I. AN IRONIC APPEAL. "We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but yti are strong ; ye are honourable, but we are despised;" or, "ye have glory, but we have dishonour." "We are fools," we know nothing," but ye aro wise," you know everything; " we are weak," timid, and feeble, "but ye are strong" and fearless. "Ye are honourable," you have "glory," you arc thought a deal of, you are extolled, but" we are despised," the "offsconriug of all things." All this is sarcasm again, well deserved, and well directed. How would our little penny-a-liners feel if such a man as Thomas Carlyle were to stand before them and speak in this. 1 'O THE FIRST EPISTLE 'l'O Tim CORINTHIAKS. [err. 1v. 1-21.

"'~.,-? If tl1ey had any sense rem~ining, they ,,..ould quiver into nothinp;ness. How 11,11ch more woul,1 those small pretentious teachers in the Corinthian Ci1urch feel this stroke of satire dealt out to them by the gr~at apostle to the Gentiles! II. A rEHSONAL HISTORY. Here he refers to his privations: " Even unto this ]ircsent hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and aro buffeted, and have no certain d"·elling-place "-without nourishment, without clothing, without the shelter of a home. Here he refers to his labour.~: " And labour, workin,g with our own hands." lfrre he refers to his persecutions: "We are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things." Then he refers to the spirit in which he endured the sufferings: "Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it; being defamed, we entreat." Now, why did he state all this? Not for the sake of parading his great trials and toils, but for the sake of bringing these proud teachers to their senses. 'l'hey could not fail to acknowledge tbat he was an apostle-a pre-eminent mi11ister of -{;hrist; notwithstanding this, in the world he was treated with cruelty and contempt, ]1 c was poor and despised. \Vhat, then, had they to be proud of as ministera? Co~f'r.usrnx. From this subject it is natural to ask-Who in the preseat a"e e11ga, ed ia the Christian ministry are most likely to be of apostolic successiot 1 Those who are "full," and "rich," and royal, and "wise," and "strong," who pride themselves in all these things; whom the people favour and flatter? or those who, like the Apostle Paul, in the discharge of their ministry, endure privations, persecutions, aud all in the magnanimcus spirit of self-abnegation a:tid generous forgiveness of enemies? Call no man a successor of the apostle who has not the apostolic character. 'l'o call a rnan a successor of the apostle who bas not the apostolic character-manfully noble, {~bristly loyal, and withal self-sacrificing-is a mischievous imposture.

entries.title: 1CO 4:15
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Spiritual paternity. "For tho11gh ye have ten thousand instructors in -Cbrist, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Ghrist Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel." The suLject of these words is spiritual paternity, and three remarks are ~uggested. l. THAT O~E MAN MAY BECOME THE SPIRITUAL FATHER OF ANOTHER. \Vhat is it lo hecome the spiritual father of another? 1. Something more than to become the father -0f one's ideas. 'fhere are men in society gifted with that intellectual vitality and ,igour which enablPs them to generate the leading ideas in the minds of their con- temporaries. This they do by their conversation, their speeches, their writings. But these are not spiritual fathers, they are mere schoolmasters or teachers. Coleridge a.nd <":arlyle are examples of this. 2. Something more than the a11thor of a certain style of tl1inking. There are men in Rociety who not only generate leading thoughts in the minds of their contemporaries, but, what is perhaps something higher, a style of thinking-a style characterized by precision, freshness, and force. Aristotll', Bacon, etc., are examples. But a spiritual father is one who is the father of man's moral character, one who generates in another his own spirit, sympathies, and aims, one who tra □ storms the character of another into his own image. ] J. THAT THE NOBLEST SPIRITUAL FATHER IS HE WHO BEGETS IN ANOTHER 'l'HE CmasTLY CliARACTE!l. Many are the moral characters prevalent amongst men-the i;ensual, the sceptical, the selfi~h. 'l'he Christly character stands in sublime contrast to these; it is disinterested, spiritual, Divine. 1. The man who generates in others this character imparts the highest yood. ln tbe Christly character is harmony, kinghood, and paradise. To be like Chri~t is the highest end of being, it is the summum bonum of so1d,;, 2. The man who generates this chara"rer in others creates the highest mutual affection. Far deeper and profounder is the affection subsisring between the spiritual father and his offal'rin~ than that which exists bPtwi,en the physical. Christ recognize,l 1l1is when be said, "Whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and 1!1y sister, and my mother." Paul called Timothy his "beloved son;" and elsewhere J1e spe:::.h with inexpressible tenderness of his converts as his little children, with whom lie travailed i11 birth (Gal. iv. 10). ]JI. 'l'HA'I' THE CHRISTLY CHARACTER IS ONT,Y BEGO'l'TEN IN OTHERS DY THE G0SPF.L oF CrrllIST. "I have begotten you through the gospel." Natural rtligion cannot do it; Judaism cannot do it; Mohammedanism cannot do it; heathenism ca □ not do it; no speculative creeds, no moral codes, no ritualistic religions can do it. The gospel alone 011. 1v. 1--21.] 'IUE FIIlST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. lH

iR the power to f!Cnerate in man the true Christl_y character; it is that transformative i;lass into which as we look we get changed into the same image from "glory to glory." CoNOLUBioN. Learn from this : 1. The supreme interest of man. What is that ?· -learning, wealth, fame? No; Ohristl,;ness. He who has this has everything; all things are his. He who has not this has "nothing," says Paul. 2. The grandest distinctions amon.1Jst men. What are they ?-sages, soldiers, sovereigns? No; spiritual sires. '!'he man who generates in another the Christly character has don" a greater work than any ~age as sage, king as king, has ever done. Every man may and ought to become a spiritual father.

entries.title: 1CO 4:16–21
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Siz subjects worth reflection. "Whereiore I beseech you, be ye followers of me," etc. There are six noteworthy subjects ir. the9e verse9. I. A REMARKABLE BEQUEST. "Be ye followers of me." \Vere Paul an ordinary man, such an exhortation would resound with arrogance; but he was a man of preeminent excellence, Christly in spirit, deportment, and ministry. There were three reasons why they should imitate him. 1. He was a.follower of Christ. There was no living man who had followed his Master so closely. Elsewhere he says, "Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ." 2. He was their spiritual father. He had begotten them in the gospel ; they were his moral offspring. They had numeron9 instructors, but he was their father; they gave them ideas, he gave them character. 3. He was no partisan, Other teachers amongst them became the leaders of parties, these parties were contending one with another; but Pan! belonged to no party, he followed Christ, knew "nothing amongst men but Christ, and him crucified." Such a man was justified in calling on others to follow him. "Ministers," says an old writer, "should so live that their people may take pattern from them, and even after their copy; they 8hould guide them by their lives as well as bv their lips, go before them on the way to heaven, and not content themselves with pointing." II. A HIGH 'l'ESTIMONY. "For this cause have I sent unto you Timotheus, who is my hcloved son, an<l faithful in the Lord, who shall bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach everywhere in every Church." He is dear to me as a "son;" ho is "faithful in the Lord;'' he knows my "ways." High testimony this. And this is the man he promises to send to them. What for? '!'hat he might give them good reasons why they should be followers of him. I do not want you to follow me in the dark; I send him that he may throw light upon my ways everywhere, "in every Church.'' A man must have a high consciousness of rectitude who can trust the representation of his character to one who knows him a8 well as a son knows his father, and withal a mau of incorruptible honesty. III. A FOOLISH EXULTATION. "Now some are puffed up, as though I would not come to you.'' 'l'here were those in the Church at Curinth who were out of sympathy with Paul, and who had no desire that he should visit them, and as the "wish is father to the thought," when they heard he was coming they would not believe it. \Vhen the intelligence that he was sending Timothy to them reached them, they ,~ould be likely to say, "This proves the truth of our assertion; he is afraid to come himself, and so he sends Timothy." In this they seem to have rejoiced; they were" puffed up." Now, I rail this a.foolish exultation, because the visit of Paul to them was what they deeply 11ecdcd, and was intended to confer on them the highest blessing. How often do wu foolishly rejoice in deliverauce from visitations fraught with priceless blessings I " Ye fearful sC1inte, fresh courage take, The clouds yo so much dread Are big with mercy, an,l shall break In blessings 011 your head.'' (Cowper.) IV. AN EXEMPLARY DECISION. "But I will come to you shortly if the Lord will," clc. Paul believed that God had a will concerning him, and that will detenniued his destiny. Hence on this he basud all his calculations in life; all his pbrns and purposes were subject to that will. "If the Lord will." This is an exemplary decision. His will iM not only absolute and righteous, b1rt benevolent; thererorc to acquiesce in that will is not only right, but wise. "Go to now, ye that say, 'l'o-Jay or to-morrow we wtll 11'.l TUE Fll:Sl' EPISTLE '1'0 'l'HE COnIN'l'HIANS. [en. 1v. 1-21.

go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain; whereas •·e know not what will be 011 the morrow." • Y. A GLORIOUS SYSTEM. " For the kingdom of God is not in word, hut in power." 11y this be mc,ms, I presume, the gospel ministry. It is a divinely regal "kin,qdorn;" it is not a thicg of sentiments or ceremony; it is invested with Divine authority. It is not a thi11g of mere "word; " it transcends all lan'!uage, however logical in force or rhetorical in benuty; it is "power "-the" power of God unto salvation." YI. A SOLEMN PROPOSAL. "\Vhat will ye? shall I come unto yon with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness r" In any case I shall come as a father. Shall I come as a father to chastise you with a "rod," or with looks of "love" and words of -commendation and sympathy? God's minister is bound to deal with men according to their states of mind. His ministry to some must be as the severity of Sinai, with ot.hers as the tenderness of Calvary. Evermore is it true that the effects of Divine ,isitations depend on the spirit in which they are received, and what this spirit shall be is for man to determine. God says to every man, "What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or i11 love, and in the spirit of meekness?" This is the solemn proposal.

entries.title: 1CO 4:8–13
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-.A vivid contrast. Having shown that the Christian consciousness was a twofold realization of the worthlessness of whatever was its own, and the infinite worth of the "all things" in Christ, and having proceeded thence to the iclea of stewanlsbip and the urgent need of faithfulness, how can St. Paul withhold the stern application of such truths? Had it been a chil<lish self-complacency with which he was dealing, we know how he would have treated it. But it was an active jealousy, a pompous arrogance, a virulent self-conceit, a carnal temper in which the natural man survived, that he had to combat. Now, therefore, he would show them what they were. 'l'he weapons of his warfare were not carnal, but, nevertheless, they were weapons, and withal such weapons as Elijah bad employed, and even the Lord Jesus had not disdained to use. If, by means of contrast, we know everything external, and if thereby we know ourselves too and realize our identity by discriminating one mood of consciousness from another, it follows that irony bas its legitimate place and may be sanctified to the best purposes. Men are acutely sensitive to its caustic probe, an,l, ns they will not exercise it on themselves, its application is one of those olliccs, severe but humane, which must be performed on them. Is the conflict over and the victory won? Full and rich, lo I ye are reigning "as kings," and significantly enough, "without us," the apostles, the sent of God, iu this movement. And what dominion is that from which we are excluded? Where are your apostles in this hour of your coronation as kings? "God hath set us forth "-a terrible contrast to their sclf-.,dorification-at this instant are we so set forth, like criminals rloomecl to deaLh, and made a spectacle as in a vast theatre, "unto the world, a!ld to angels, and to men." Alas! the only use just then to which the great Apostle to the Ge1:tiles could put his knowledge of Greek games in the amphitheatre was in an outburst of indignation and sorrow. And then follows one of his characteristic sentences, in which impassioned feeling is quite as con- densed as strong thought: fools, weak, despised, are we the apostles, while ye arc wise aml strong and honourable. The formal contrast is dropped, and now, how \,kc U1e rnpid summation of his experience to the sulTtrings of hi~ Lord? Fidelity in sullcrn,g, 144 THE l<'IRST EPISTLE TO i'HE CORINTHIANS. [cR. 1v. 1-21.

fidelity to suffering, reconciliation to it, acceptance of its law as basic to his life, not an exceptional thing occurring at rare intervals as most of our sad experiences, but common and habitual, 'll'Ounds unhealed and yet deeper wounds, "even unto this present hour." Hunger and thirst, nakedness, buffctin~s, homeless, refusing all remuneration aud earning our own support, returning good for evil and blessing for cnrsina, objects of persecution, denied recognition as the friends of humanity and lovers of their kind, abused and vilified, ay, treated iu the centres of this world's intelligence and refinement as "the filth of the world and the offscouriog of all things," and no break or cessation, "unto this day." The sameness of these sufferings is twice mentioned, and the wondrous biography, first and last, is one chapter of woes. Over all stands a sinole motto, which came and could only come from Christianity: "For Christ's sake." At this juncture, call to mind a fact of some moment. Men are wonderfully individualized. by sufferings. Considering how suffering abounds, it is noticeable that few truly reg:trd themselves as provi,~ential sufferers, and realize in their experience the Divine discip)ine they are ~ppo!nted to undergo. Th~re. is much selfishness in our ways of endurmg the ills of hfe, m the uses made of affi1ct10n, and the habits of intellect arnl sensibility growing therefrom; and St.. Paul strikes the heart of the subjects when he connects his sufferings with "Christ's sake." This gives an instant pathos to the- r~cita) and an instant nobil!ty to _the ap?stle as. a sufferer. Furthermore, only for " Chnst's sake" docs he go mto this affectmg detail of the number, variety, and con- tinuation of his sorrows. A noble sufferer like St. Paul could find no selfish pleasure in such an enumeration; nay, in itself it would be painful. Vain men, ignoble men, gratify their littleness in recounting what they have endured, and these pensioners of pnhlic opinion-it may be the public opinion of a very diminutive world-find their account in the ill usury sense of sympathy. Far from this weakness-very far-was thi:, heroic man, to whom it was a new suffering to tell his sufferings, but who, in the courage of humility, the most courag~ous of the virtues in a true man, was even ready to uncover a bleeding heart for " Christ's sake." We shall no•;,, see that his love for these erring Corinthians prompted him to make the narration of his sufferings.-L.

entries.title: 1CO 4:14–21
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Warnin_qs rf tenderness. From mood to mood, yet in all, St. Pan! had the same dominant zeal and affection in behalf of his converts. Rebuke was nut with him a pleasure to which the natural man ministered, but a very painful duty that proceeded from conscience and kept sensibility unalloyed by animal passion. Herei;; he is distinguished from men who love authority because it is a signal of personal eminence and a means to make others feel their inferiority. A really superior miu,I ne~er likes to dwell on the infirmities of ignorance and littleness in those below him. The mountain points upward, and the higher the summit the more is it lost in tl1e heavens. "·who maketh thee to differ?" is always present as the interrogatory uf consciousness in such a nature, and the answer thereunto, whenever a true man has tu vindicate his authority and especially in rebuke, is as Divine as the question. The delicacy of the apostle and his depth of insight have not forsaken him in this try in~ hour, nor would he expose the vanity of such as made themselves leaders and assumed transcendent powers, save in a manifest spirit of self-abnegation. Manner is not a mere mode; it is a spirit; it is the very spirit of a man taking on a visib.e embodiment, a □ •l hence the rebuke administered by St. Paul is impregnated with the humility of his soul. There are men who co=it "Mischievous foul sin in chiding sin ; " but it would be a poor compliment to the apostle to say that he was not one of thi& class. What is most truly to his honour is his purpose to make the Corinthians sensible of the wrong to their better nature, and quicken from that side of their character the feelinc,- of repentance. This brings out the sentiment of his soul in the words, "I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you;" and again the master-thought of all his thinking recurs-Christ Jesns-in whom he had begotten them throtwh the gospel, urging them to be imitators of Christ in him. To be genuinely servic~able, imitation must not be mechanic.al aud servile, not be the liternl copyin~ ut' 11. pattern or model, but an education ir.. the art of discriminating, and particularl_r a i;eme of the ideal in those whom we follow. For this rea~on, that they may be remindcJ CII. lV. 1-21.] THE FrnS'r EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 115

of his "ways which be in Christ," he has sent Timotheus unto them. Prudence dictated this course. Circumstances were such as that absence would be his most effective presence-one of those occasions when a man's thoughts had better do their work unattended by the emphasis of eye and voice. But would they misinterpret this and attribute it to cowardice? "I will come to you shortly," leaving the time to the will of the Lord, for in executiag a grave purpose it is not enough that we havl! the Spirit in our motive and aim, but we must wait patiently on the providence of the Spirit, which is often our best discipline. St. Paul's expectations were rarely fol filled promptly,- instance his visit to Rome; hope grew morn reverent by delay; and in no aspect is his career more interesting than in that which shows how postponed gratification of desire ennobled the desire itself and secured a larger good to other;. Fruit must grow, ripen, mellow, especially inward fruits, and St. Paul prized the mellowing touch of time. Many a lesson he gives us unawares in psychology, many an insight into the philosophy of true feeling, many a revelation of the soul, which but for him would have been a "hidden mystery." But, while waiting for " time and place to cohere," he utters his opinions strongly as to those who are "puffed up." What an ever-recurring sens~ of cardinal principles! Great truths are never long out of sight, and hence the declaration, "The kingdom of God is not in word, but in power." Did he under-rate language? Nay; who ever spoke of language in a higher strain· than he who did not hesitate to allude to his own preaching as not in the "words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth "? But the idle and impotent word, the word of swelling vanity, the wonl that dishonoured the \Vord,-for this he had only rebuke and condemnation. Such use was stolen use, the gift turned against the Giver, a recleemeu. gift wrested from the Redeemer, a recognized organ of the Holy Ghost taken from its only Sanctifier. For this must be said of language, that it is not merely or chiefly a medium or acting on others, but that it reacts on the man himself. Apa.rt from its conventional functions, it is au instrument of communion with self, of stating self to self, of inspiring, while defining faculty to faculty in the mind's solitary cognizance of its own powers. Language is far mightier for introverted conception, for images that never escape the picturesque world in which they have their birth and life and death, for emotions and affections to which silence is the most precious of blessings-far mightier, ,ve say, is langu~ge in this respect than in its economic uses. From the lexicon we learn the language that gives us intercourse with men. From our own souls and by conversing with them we learn the langua:!e by means of which we compare "spiritual things with spiritLial." Even on the pbne of common life, the former is confined to communication. Expression is a very different thing from bald communication. Expression is due 'to the ability of the Spirit to vitalize words by imparting its own life to them. Something individual, something distinctly personal, imparts itself in expression. Hyperboles are matters of fact to the inmost consciousness, and all eloquence and poetry are but symbols of what the soul sees and can only intimate in this half-articulate way. "I will kuow wheu I come "-so St. Paul reasons-"whether your speech is empty words, the wisdom which man's wisdom teacheth and is foolishness to God, or the power of the Spirit." This is the test-God's power. Only through that power ca.n these Corinthians advance tho kingdom of God; for ouly through it can they have oneness with Christ anu. fellowship with his disciples. ComQ to them St. Paul will-come to them as a father-the acknowledgment of them as sons, beloved sons, precedes him, and he will not forget his relation to them; but how shall he come? With a father's rod or in love? Will they relieve him of the necessity of discipline? And the thought of love lingers in his miud, amplifies itself, seeks fuller utterance, and the father's heart throbs once more in the associ,ited clause-" the spirit of meekness.''-L.

entries.title: 1CO 4:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Spiritual steward$hip. In tho Corinthian Church two errors were prevalent with regard to the apostolic and other ministries-there was a tendency to exaggerate the importance of the agents by whom the truth was communicated, an,! there was a disposition to set one of these a.gents up as against another; so that r,artisanship and sectarianism violated the Christian unity. I. 'l'HE SUBORDINATE POSITION OF CHRISTIAN TEACHERS. None need deem it a degradation or an undue humiliation to stand where the apostle stood; indeed, P,rn! is an acknowledged and admired model to all who work for the king,lom. 1. They I. CORINTUIANS. • L 116 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIANS. [err. Iv. 1-21

are, in relation to Christ himself, ministers. They serve him, and count it an honour so to d0. For his sake, and in his Name, they act as servants to their follow-men. 2. They arc, in relation to the truth they promulgate, stewards. That is to say, the- trnth is not rernalcd by them, but to them; it is held not as their property, but as- their trnst; it is not appropriat~d to their own use, but dispensed by them for the- benefit of others; they are not at liberty to do as they like with it-they are accountable- to the Lord ofall for the way in which they deal with it. 3. This being so, faithfulness- is the ,irtue they are bound to culti,ate and display. 'Whilst those who are indepen- dent am not especially bound to this duty, all who have derived from another, and are accountable to that other, are emphatically called to be faithful. Such is the position of all the ministers of Christ. - 11. TrrE TRUE DIGNITY OF SPIRITUAL SERVA~'TS ARISES FROM THEIR RELATION TO• THEIR LoRD AND TO BIS '\VoRD. 'l'here is a contrast between the service and the Master, between the stewardship and the mystery. The minister cannot think too lowlily of himself or too loftily of his theme and trust. 1. If they are ministers, they are ministers of Christ. An ambassador may be a person cf lowly birth and feeble- powers, but if be is an ambassador, his relation to his sovereign and the credentials- and commission be has received entitle his message to peculiar consideration. And. however the pastor, teacl~e•, or_ evangelist may in himself be lacking in claims uponthe respect of the superficial society called "the world," however he may be destitute of the shining gifts which command the admiration of the Church, still neither he nor those whose welfare he seeks are ever at liberty to foriret that he is an ambassador from hea,en, that he is commissioned and authorized by the King of kings. 2. If they arc stewards, they are stewards of the mysteries of God. By mysteries the apostle meant truths which had in the past been hidden but were now revealed. Revealed in Christ, the Divine purposes of grace, salvation and life to all mankind, were published by the apostles aud their fellow-labourers. And the declaration of the mind and. heart of God was well worthy of being regarded as the impartation of a mystery compared ,Yith which' all the wonde1s of Eleusis sank into insignificance. Of this Paul was conscious, and it would be well if every preacher of the gospel were ever to have this before bis mind. '\Ve have this treasure, though "in earthen vessels." 'l'be solemnity of publishing Divine truth and the responsibility of hearing it are alike by these considerations brought very vividly before the mind. 'l'hus are ministers unto some a savour of life unto life, unto others a savour of death unto death.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 4:3–5
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Judgment, human and Divine. No man can work· entirely with reference to his own labours and his own opinion of them. We all need to live under the sense that others are taking some notice of what we do; and with most there is danrrer of attachinu exao-gerated importance to human criticism. But it is well for us to cherish the feelin(}'O of the nearness and the supervision of the omniscient Searcher of hearts. In this passage St. Paul represents the effect which both human and Di,·ine judgment should have upon the Christian's life. I. THE JuDGMENT WHICH IS DEPRECATED. This is the judgment: 1. Of our fallibl~ fellow-men. For they have not the necessary material or the due knowledge and opportunity for forming a just judgment. Men are influenced in the opinions they form of one another by their prejudices and prepossessions. We judge our friends toofavourabiy, and are too severe in our censure of our opponents. Hence our Lord haswarned us, "Judge not!" 2. That which is passed at this present time. This is the time for work, not the time for judging and for recompense. No man's work can be fairly judged until it is completed. And beside this, we cannot see life in its trueproportions when we look at it from a point of view so near. To judge now is to judge - " before the time." II. TnE JUDGMENT WHICH 1s ANTICIPATED. 1. This is God's judgment. He will, brinrr every work into judgment. His acquaintance with all who shall appear before his bar is perfect. His material for forming a judgment is complete. His mind isunclouded by human prejudices. He is infinitely just. 2. This shall take place upon. our Lord's return. His parousia is what the Church looks forward to with affectionate interest and hope. Her children offer the frequent prayer : "That at thy,

second coming to judge the world we may be found an accept(<ble people in thy sight." For whilst the judgment shall be Divine; it shall be accomplished by "that Man whom God hath appointed to judge the quick and the dead." 3. This shall be accompanied by revelation. There are bidden things of darkness which must be brought to light; virtues and vices of which the world has taken little or no note, but which must be brought forward and taken into account, in order to a just decision and award. There are counsels of the heart to be made manifest; for whilst men necessarily judge by the conduct, God will take into account the secret intentions and motives of those who have laboured for him, both good and evil. 4. This will be by a perfect discrimination. The hypocrite shall be distinguished from the sincere, the diligent from the idle, the time-server and men-pleaser from the true servant of God. 5. 'l.'his will be the occasion of recompense. The case of the utterly unfaithful is left out of view as irrelevant in this connection. But among the faithrul it is presumed that there are degrees of fidelity; and every man shall have his praise from God. This implies that each has a special meed for special service; anrl it also implies that praise shall be accompanied by a substantial and everlasting recompense. It is well, therefore, to work "as ever in the great Taskmaster's eye,'' to avoid judging one's ~elf, tu be indifferent to the partial judgment of men, and to wait for the revelation and the awards of eternity.-'!'.

entries.title: 1CO 4:7
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -.A.ll is of grace. Paul's quick, impulsive mind here flashes out into indignation at the spectacle of partisanship and schism in the Corinthian Church. They who lay great stress upon individual human teachers and ministers are in danger of forgetting, perhaps already have forgotten, two things, viz. (1) that every minister and teacher has a special blessing for the Church; and (2) that all such agents are but messengers from the court of heaven, and distributors of the blessings of God. l. \VE MAY TAKE CREDIT TO OURSELVES ONLY FOR OUR WANTS AND FOR OUR CAPACITY. \Vhy should any man be proud, when he remembers that he was born a helpless babe; that he was dependent upon the kind services of others for the preservatiou of life; that he has learned nothing which he was not taught; that. he enjoys nothing except through the good offices of his fellow-men? And why should auy Christian be "puffed up" with spiritual conceit, when he remembers that all be brought to the Scriptures, to the Church, to the Lord, was just his necessities and his capacity tu receive spiritual blessings? II. WE ARE INDEBTED FOR ALL THINGS TO HUMAN MINISTRATIONS. When we reganl our circumstances, our worldly possessions, our education, our position in life, our family, our friends, this fact is obvious enough. But the same is true of our religiol1s advantages, our spiritual blessings. The Bible was secured to us by human efforts and labours; the gospel was preached to us by human lips; the Church bas been to us the fellowship of our human teachers and brethren; our religious knowledge has been conveyed to us by human interpreters; our piety has been inspired by human examples, Ill. DIVINE MERCY HAS MADE HUMAN MINISTRIBS SUBSERVIENT TO OUR SPIRITUAL WANTS. It is not wise or just to d1scriminnte too nicely between human gilts and Divine. The human gifts are Divine gifts bestowed by humau hands. It is the privilege of the devout and enlightened mind to look through the seen to the unseen; to recognize in every Christian helper and friend the messenger of God, the minister of Christ. 'l'he form, the voice, may be earthly, but there 1s behind a spiritual presence and a Divine power. It is the Giver of every good gift e.nd every perfect gift who is so near.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 4:9
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-.A spectacle. In the midst of his irony and sarcasm, Paul here reverts to the more natural habit of his mind. The self-exaltation and self-importance of the Corinthians were mingled with depreciation of the apostle, at least on the part of some. But alas! if his own converts, so deeply indebted to his labours and his care, could think slightingly of him, what earthly compensation could he expect for all the paiu, hardship, contempt, and danger he cheerfully endured? Wero not be and his fellowapostles like gladiators doomed to be flung to the wild beasts-" a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men "? THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cH. 1v. 1-21.

J. THE GRAl\DEUR Al\D SUBLIMITY OF THEIR POSITION DEMANDS OUR ADMIRATION. They were not r.s slaves cast to tlie lions. They were men who might have led a quiet and peaceful, and some of them an honourable and distinguished, life. Dut they gave their hearts to Christ, and having done so gave up all for him. Thero was no exacrcrera- tion in the apostle's language. On the contrary, he spoke tl,e plain truth wh;~ he 1 eprcsented himself as standing before the universe as a witness to the Lord Christ, The position was one of dignity and moral impressiveness; the an()'els felt it then and the world of humanity has come to feel it now. '

II. THE PATHOS OF THEIR POSITION DEMANDS OUR SYMPATHY. We observe the bodily prirntions, the homelessness, the physical toil, the ignominy, the persecutions the general contempt, which the apostles passed through; and we cannot observe ali this unmoved. Doubtless it touched the heart of that Divine Saviour who was made perfect through sufferings; doubtless there were those who wept with their leaders when these were constrained to weep. Nothing in all human history is more profoundly aITccting. Ill. THE MORAL PURPOSE OF THEIR POSITION DEMANDS OUR APPRECIATION. The mofr,es that induced Paul and his colleagues voluntarily to submit to such experience as they relate were two-fidelity to Christ and pity for men. Christ the Master had c<>ndescended himself to be upon the cross a spectacle to the world; and those who llC'ncfited by hi~ redemption and shared his Spirit were ready to follow h~ example. They were the true followers of him who" endured the cross, despising the shame." And th, ir aim and hope was to b1in; 1he world to the foot. of the Saviour's cross. For this e11<! they "counted not their life dear unto them." It was for the sake of their fellow- 1uen tbnt they consented to brave the scorn of the philosopher and the jeer of the rnnltitude. IV. 'l'HE MORAL LESSONS OF THEIR POSITION DEMAND OUR STUDY. 1. It is a rebuke 10 self-indulgence and ease. Shall we be satisfied and eujoy our ease in the midst of the world's errors and sins, when we call to mind the heroic and pathetic sufferings of our Lord's first followers? 2. It is a consolation under any contumely and discredit we may endure in 1he Christian profession and vocation for Christ's .sake. "The like Mffiictions have befallen our brethren who are in the world." 3. It points on to the !.'lory which shall be revealed. "Through much tribulation ye must enter into the kingdom of heaven." The apostles have ended their struggles, and now enjoy their victory; the Church militant will soon become the Church triumphant.-T.

-Ver. 15.-Children, tutors, and fathers. Our religion makes use of all the many and various relationshlps that obtain among men to set forth ail<l to assist us in understanding spiritual realities. I. GENERALLY SPEAKING, CIIRISTIANS MAY BE DESCRIBED AS CHILDREN. 1. Like the Corillthians, most members or the Church of Christ need constant and watchful care. Provideucc has appointen that children should be born more dependent than the offspring of the inferior animals upon parental attention a?d devotio?, From iu fancy until the approach of manhood acd womanhood, human bemgs stand m need of the supervision and assistance of their parents. So _is it with the r_nembers ~f Christ's Church. They are in need of pastoral care and kmdness, a!ld without this are not likely either to grow in Christian character or to escape the assaults of their foes. 2. In addition to care, they need wise and fatherly counsel. It would be well if spiritual pastors bore in mind the inexperience of a large proportion of the flock. Paul Wll.8 n. faithful counseUor, and in writing to these Christians at Corinth he warned them very faithfullv ao-ainst the faults and errors they were in clanger of falling into. Not with severity," but with directness and earnestness, he admonished his spiritual children, and entreated them to render obedience to his advice and directions. Even sincere <lisciple8 ul Christ are often in peril by reason of their own want of knowledge and experience, and by reason of the temptations which beset them in this world. Hence the importance of such pastoral admonitions as those of which Paul here gives an example. II. THERE ARK IN THE Cm;RCH OF CHRIST 1.'H0SE WHO MAY DE DESIGNATED SPIRITUAL FATHERS. At Corinth the apostle occupied a pre-eminently honourable and influential position. He claims in this passa;::e to have been, what the hist_o~y of the Acts shows 1.hat lie was, tlie 1,Ianter of the vrneyarcl, the founder of the edifice, the father of tho CJJ. IV, 1-21.] THE Frns·r EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. lrn

fami\y. It was by bis labours, bis bravery, his perseverance, that the Christian commumty came into existence. In the highest sense, of course, the Father was God himself, who gives the Spirit of adoption to all his people. But instrumentally, the apostle was blessed by God, through the preaching of the gospel, to the begetting and birth, so to speak, of this congregation, this spiritual household. This relationship involved the ubligalion on their part to reverence, hon,,ur, obey, and p-atefully to love and rejoice in, one to whom they were, under God, so immcasnrably indebted. For hi~ was a unique position with regard to them. No other could claim to stand in the same relation, and Paul was bold to tell them so. Still are there those who are honoured by the calling of God to this spiritual fatherhood; and such should meet with that respectful and grateful recognition which is the due of benefactors so signally favoured by God himself. III. To·roRS AND INSTRUCTORS IN C11msT OCCUPY IS TIIF. CIIURCII A POSITIO~ O:S-LY INFERIOR TO THA'l.' OF SPlltITUAL FATHERS. At Corinth the chariswL of teacbing seems to have been imparted and exercised in a measure almost embarrassing in its abundance. Paul speaks hyperbolically of the "myriads" of tutors who followed up hi~ apostolic labours. 'l'hc same Spirit bestows gifts in multiplicity and variety. Let Christians 1" grateful for all the "means of grace," and especially for the holy and devout ministrations of the learned, the wise, the sympathetic, and the strong. For thus is it appointed that the Church should grow in grace.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 4:20
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The power of the kingdom. The Corinthians were given to words; they delighted in eloquence; they were addicted to disputations. The Apostle Paul, who fulfilled his ministry by language, written and spoken, was not the man to disparage words. But no man was more impatient of mere words--of words with no reality, no force, no conviction. He bad reason to complain of his converts at Corinth, and was resolved to bring matters to an issue with them; and it should be a contest, not of barren ver bia.ge, bu~ of spiritual force. I. THE NATURE OF Goo's KINGDOM PROVES THAT IT CAXNOT BE MERELY IN WOI\D. 1. A kingdom implies authority exercised, obedience rendered. Although a kin~dom uot of this worid, not maintained and supported by human means, by laws an,\ arms, still God's empire is a reality. Christ is the King nnd Head ; his laws are binding an,l stringent, although the motives that inspire obedience are gratitude and love-hiH subjects are willing and submissive. 2. Such a kingdom is incompatible with the reign of words. 'l'o be a subject of Christ is not (1) to be merely by verbal assent, as by confirmation or any other form of admission to Church privile~es, associated with the society of Christians; nor is it (2) to make any kind of profession ; nor (3) to recite and maintain the great Christian creeds; nor (4) to utter words expressive ot devotio11. Men may make use of many and sacred WGrds, and be none the nearer the kingdom L•f heaven. A nominal and verbal kingdom is weak and despicable; such is not the spiritual kingdom of our Lord. ll. THE ORIOIN AND NATURE OF THE POWER OF TIIE KI:s"GDOM. 1. ·words may be only from man; power is from God. All natural and physical power origin,1tes in him. But moral power is either good or evil; and the good only but always is from Go,\. Christ is "the Power of God." 2. When we contemplate this spiritual power which pervades the new kingdom, what do we find it to be? The power of truth, the power of good- ness, the power of pity and of love. Ill. WHERE AND HOW THIS POWEil DISPLAYS ITSELF. 1. Its seat is the soul; there it first enthrones itself, and thence it spreads until it pervades the whole nature, changing the beliefs, the feelings, the principles, and the habits. For "the kingdom or God is righteousness, peactJ, and joy in tl1t, Holy Ghost." :.!. The power of this king- dom manifests itself through the whole realm of human nature and life; both by the forces, obstacles, and oppositions it overcomes, and by the results it produces. "\V c observe these effects especially in (1) the newness of life which is characteristic of the kingdom, as emphatically in the case of the first disciples, brought out of Judaism and paganism into the marvellous light of the gospel; (2) in the social results, which were exhibited in the cities where the gospel took root, and where the sent1men~ of brother- hood proved a new power in humanity, sanctifying society within and attracting elements from without. (3) We have a proof of this-power in the case of those martyrs who for 150 THE FIRST EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'HE CORIN'l'HIANS. [cu. rv. 1-21.

Christ's sake were content to lay down their life; for here we have evidently a new spiritual force, capable of inspiring with a fortitude in the cause of an unseen Lord which surpassed the heroic devot.iou of a Roman to his country's aood. (4).The pro"ress O and perpetuity of this power stamps _it as Divine, as the on; great prevalent and successful force working iu human society for its purification, its elevation its lasting and highest welfare.-T. '

entries.title: 1CO 4:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -" ~Ministers qf Christ." I. ,VHAT THEY ARE, 1. .Yinisters, Not masters; servants, not lnrds. The word means literally "under-rower," or common sailor, alld is generally used of the lower class of servants. Ministers are the mere servants of Christ; they have no authority save that which they may receive from him. "Be not ye called Rabbi" (Matt. xxiii. 8). A domineering despotic spirit is altogether out of place. If any will be chief, he must be servant of all. Many ministers have trouble with their Churches because of their own masterful spirit. Like Rehoboam, they do not heed the sage counsel, "If thou wilt be a servant unto this people this day, and wilt serve them, and answer them, aud speak good words to them, then they will be thy servants for ever" (1 Kings xii. 7). Some of the Corinthians had unduly exalted their teachers ( eh. L 12); others, perhaps, had regarded them as utterly insignificant (" I of Christ"); Paul defines the legitimate position. Ministerial activitv is hinted at• ministers are to be workers, not idlers, 2. Ministers of Christ. This makes thei; calling: most honourable. They are servants of the Church, servants of their fellows, but not primarily. They serve the Church and their fellow-men because they desire to serve Christ. They are (1) appointed by Christ; (2) responsible to him; (3) to be judged by him; (4) to be devoted to him; (5) to speak in his Name; (6) to preach him and his redemption; (7) to rely npon his help; (8) to take orders from him; (9) not to originate, but to ascertain his mind. 3. Stewards. A position (1) of trust and con- fidence; (~) of influence; (3) of responsibility; ( 4) of some peril; (5) of much honour. 4. Stewards of the mysteries of God. "Mystery " in the New Testament dces not mean something: iLco01prehensible, but something beyond the reach of unaided human intel- ligence. The "mysteries of God" are thus "hidden" (eh. ii. 7) until revealed by hi01. They are the truths of the gospel-" the truth as it is in Jesus." Ministers have special charge concerning these truths-(1) to preserve them; (2) to dispense the1n. As stewards, they should be deeply impressed with (1) the vast importance of the "riches" entrusted to them; (2) the need of utmost care in discharging the duties uf their office; (3) the awful issues to themselves and others if they are remiss. Many are satisfied if self-approved or if praised by others; but Paul looked to the judgment of Christ (ver. 4). We are not to be despondent if we are" unpopular" with men, so that we are approved by our Lord. Though "unpopularity" with men is very far from being an argument that we please ou~ Master : "The common people heard him gladly," and probably would so hear us if we were more like him. II. A NECESSARY QCJALIFICATION. Faithfulness. This is a first requisite in those who are "stewards of the mysteries of God." Stewards must not use their lord's goods for their own advantage. What evils result from unfaithfulness in an earthly stewardship! who can estimate the evils flowing from an unfaithful ministry! A minister sbould be faithf'ul: 1. To Christ, in (1) obedience, (2) love, (3) zeal, (4) devotion, (5) holiness. 2. To his fioclc. (l) Preaching unadulterated doctrine. Not corrupting the Word of God. Not substituting something else for it. (2) Rightly dividing the word of truth. (3) Reproving, rebuking, exhorting with all long-suffering and teaching (2 Tim. iv. 2). (4) Striving "to present every man perfect in Christ Jesus" (Col. i. ~ti).-H.
