entries.title: 1CO 6:1–8
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-7Jie ideal Ohurch a tribunal. "De.re any of you, having a matter against ,anothet,'' etc.? In our sketch on the preceding verses we looked on the true Church as a/east. Here we have to look on it as a tribunal, a court of judicature, where disputes are to be settled and grievances redressed. It would appenr that questions arose among the Corinthian Christians that required settlement-questions of wrong done to persons or to property, and that too the litigious spirit was so rife in their midst that they took their grievances to the heathen courts. For this the apostle reproves them. "Dare .any of you, having a matter ago.inst another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?" Three remarks about the ideal Church as a tribunal. L IT IS SUPERIOR TO OTHER TRIBUNALS ON THE EARTH. 1. It is a court formecl of .morally righteous men. 'l'his is implied in the words, "Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints 1" So.ints, -or just men, form the tribunal. In worldly courts of judicature men are judged by 'legislative enactments or judicial decisions. Not so in this court. It is a court of equity, a court that tries cases not by statutory precepts, nor by ecclesiastical laws, but by ,scriptural principles, and these principles as they are embodied in the teaching of him who delivered the Sermon on the mount. The true Church is his representative and .administrator. 2. It is a court whose jurisdiction is universal. "Do ye not know that the saints shall judge the world?" In many ways men of Christly lives are judging the world now. Their ideas of right and wrong, between man and man, am! mo.n ancl God, form that standard of character to which the consciences of men me constantly appealing, and to which they are forced to bow. All men at last will be judged by the character of Christ, and the Church is the representative of that character. "'l'lw words I say unto you, they she.II judge you in the last day." Not only docs this Ch~irch- tribunal judge the world, but judges angels also. "Know ye not that we shall JU<l,!e angels?" Hedeemed humanity is in some respects higher than angelic natures. lt has pnss~d through greater changes and is brought into closer connection with tbo Divine. They who have in them the spirit of absolute justice in the highest measure are the best juclges of character. In modern courts this spirit is often very feeble, and .in some caseH extinct. Hence the sad bluuderings about the intcrpr~tation of statutes 196 'l'IlE FIHST EPISTLE TO THE COUTNTHIAKS. [cu. vI. 1-20.

11ncl the decisions of judges. Dnt tbe spirit of absolute justice reigns in the truo Church. II. IT IS A TRIDUNAL FOR THE SETTLEMENT OF ALL DISPUTES, Paul intimates that it is to judge disputes on the "smallest matters," and of "things pertaining to this life.'' These expressions seem to comp_rehend all ~ispntes-not merely religions, but secular; not only disputes on great sub.1ects, but disputes on minor subjects 11s well. The instinct of Cbristly justice which inspires it peers into the heart of all moral conduct. It has an "anointing from the Holy One, by which it knows all thincrs." The more· spiritually pure a man is the more readily will he detect the wrou!!. o7ily a few years· ago some of our judges occupied twelve months or more, at an enormous expense to the nation, in order to fincl out whether a man was an impostor or not. 'l'o a mind full o( moral justice an impostor is detectecl instinctively and at once. No locric can read the ~idden pri_nciµ~es of_ 8: man's heart. Christ !mew". what was in man," a~d those highly unbued with his Spmt are to some extent gifted with the same insiirht. III. DISPUTANTS WHO WILL NOT HA VE THEIR CASES SETTLED IN THIS COURT ARE: JUSTLY LIABLE TO REPROACH. 1. Reference to another court is unwise. "If then ye· have judgments of things pertaining to this life, set them to judcre who are least esteemed, in the Church." The meaning is that any other court to whi;h the case is t11.ken· is of no account in the estimation of the Church-it is a morally inferior institntion. The trib~m~l of man in comparison to Ch~ist's ~ribunal is a truly contemptible thing. You Chnst1ans degrade yourselves by taking disputes to such tribunals. "I speak to your shame. Is it so, that there is not a wise man among you?" It is a shame to you to ha,e your disputes carried to such tribunals, a shame that yon cannot settle your· disputes among yonrselves, that "brother should go to law with brother, before the unbelievers." 2. Reference to another court is wrong. "Now therefore, there is utterly a fault [a defect] among you, because ye go to law one with another." Better than to do this, better than to go to a worldly tribunal to settle your disputes, better you should suffer wrong than take your grievance into the worldly courts. "The Church bas principles," says Robertson, "according to which all such matters may be set at rest. And the difference between the worldly court of justice and the Christian court of arbitration is a difference of diametrical opposition. Law says, 'You shall haveyour rights;' the spirit of the true Church says, 'Defraud not your neighbour of hi&,. rights.' Law says, 'You must not be wronged;' the Church says,' It is better to suffer wrong than to do wrong.' "

entries.title: 1CO 6:9–11
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Genuine reformation. "Know ye not that the unrighteous shaU not inherit the kingdom of God? Be not deceived: neither fornicatorR, nor idolaters,. nor adulterers, nor effeminate, nor abusers of themselves with mankind, nor thieves, nor covetous nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God. And ~uch were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye. are justified in the Name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of o~ir God." Reformation. of some kind or other is an object most earnestly pursued by all m every land who are alive to the woes and wrongs of life. Some of the reformations sought are of a ques-• tionable utility; none will prove of any essential and permanent service but that presenteu in the text. The reformation is- I. A REFORMATION OF THE MORAL CHARACTER OF MANKIND. "Know ye not that the unrighteous shall not inherit the kingdom. of God? Be not deceived: neit~er fornicators nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effemrnate, nor nbusers of themselves with mankind/ etc. Sin, which may be defined as self-gratification, is here presented in a. variety of forms-" fornication," idolatry, avarice, intemperance, etc. All these manifestations are hideous developments of the same ungodly principle, self-gra~ific~tion. 'l'he principle of sin, like holiness, is one and simple, but the forms are multifarious. N1Jw, these morally corrupt classes we are here told were changed; they were " washed," and, "sanctified," and "justified," which, stripped of figure, means, they were changed in th~ very root and fountain of their character. They were, to use Scripture phraseology, converted, regenerated, created anew in Christ Jesus to good workH. The reformatwn was not doctrinal, ecclesiastical, or institutional, but ntoi-al. II. A REFORMATION INDISPENSADLE TO A HAPPY DESTINY, What is the only happy destiny for man? 'l'o "inherit the kingdom of Goel.'' What is the "kiogdom Of

Go,!"? Tiighteonsness, peace, joy in the Holy Ghost. It is the reign of truth, pnrity, light, bariuouy, aud Llessedness. To" inherit" that empire, to bt in it, not as occasion,11 visitors, but as permanent citizens, holding fellowship with its Sovereign, and minglincr with the great and the good of all worlds,-tl,is is our high destin,v. For this we wer"'e made, and for nothing lower. Hence Christ urges us to "seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness," which means-come under the Divine reign of truth and right. Now, there is no getting into this kingdom without this moral reformatioa. .Al' who have not undergone this reformation are excluded. Ill. A REFOilMA'l'ION EFFECTED BY THE REDEMPTIVE AGENCY OF CHRIST. " And such were some of you: but ye are [were] washe<l, but ye are [were] sanctified, but yr, are [were] justified in the Name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God." This means that they had been cleansed from all moral foulne~s, " washe,l ; " that they had been consecrated to holiness, "sanctified;" that they had been made right in their being and relatio11ships, "justified." And all this, how 't "In the Name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God." 'l'his is the reformative measure, the gospel; nothing on this earth will effect this moral change but this. Not the enactments of legislations, not the creations of genius, not scientific systems. I disparnge none of these, but they cannot effect this reformation of soul, the reformation which humanity wants, a reformation without which all other reformations are bbt reformations on parchment, a change in mere outward forms of lire. "Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again." "Without holiness no man shall see the Lord."

entries.title: 1CO 6:12–20
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Chi·istianity in relation to the body. "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient," etc. It would seem that there were those in the Church at Corinth who regarded Christianity as giving them a kind of liberty to do whatsoever they wished. Some of them having left Judaism with its various restraiuts, and others pag~nism, which also had restrictions, they were too ready to push the doctrine of religious liberty, as proclaimed by Paul, far beyon<l. its limits. The apostle here states, pi!rhaps in answer to a question on the subject, that there is a limitation to Christian liberty. He says, "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient." As the liberty which they seemed to covet was a liberty in relation to the gratifications of bodily appetites, he takes occasion to state certain things in relation to the body. His remarks suggest to us the relation of Christianity to the huma11 body. '\Ve observe- !. 'l'IIA'l' IT RECOG::SIZES A'l''l'EN'l'ION TO THE NATURAL NEEDS OF THE BODY AS PROPER. "Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats." This means the bo<ly has appetites, and there are provisions intended and fitted to satisfy them. Christianity allows man to partake or those provisions in nature necessary to satisfy and strengthen his physical nature. To act thus is to act in harmony with the constitution of nature. entries.content:
-Civil relations and Church membership; litigation before heathen courts. The chapter opens abruptly. "Dare any of you "-a strong expression of dis- appro'l'al-" having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust?" Judaism. had taught the Jews not to go before Gentile judges with a lawsuit against their brethren; the Romans bad accorded to the Jews the right to settle their disputes among themselves, and Christians at that time might avail themselves of this rule (Lange). But St. Paul, true to his ruling method, views the matter froni Christian ground and treats it solely on the principles of the gospel. The argument in the preceding chapter concerned social relations, the present argument applies to civil relations, and yet they are sympathetic in his mind. Emotion is an associative force, and often establishes or rather discloses connections of ideas not perceptible in the "dry light" of intellect. In both these arguments the underlying sentiment is the same, viz. the dignity of Christian character and the supremacy of its obligations over interest, custom, usage, and every form of self not compatible with the generous spirit of sacrifice "for Christ's sake." Bear in mind, then, in reading St. Paul's Epistles, that if at times you lose the compactness of logic and its tenacious unity, you are always sure to find that more interior tie which binds thought to sentiment and displaces order for the gain of a higher method. Method, rather than order, marks the thinker whose vocation is tl) instruct the mass of mankind. Saints, as saints exist in the ideal of Christianity, "shall judge the world." They are to rule with Christ, to share his glory, a11d be- acknO\dedged by the universe as participants in the final triumph of his mediatoria1 authority. If so, the mediatorial honour in fature prospect bas a certain scope of present activity, since it could not be then unless it were now. Of the character ot' these functions and the circumstances incident to their display, what know we? They fall under that law of reserve which the Lord Jesus spoke of when he said, "Of the time!lor the seasons, which the Father bath put in his own power,'' we are kept ignorant, and are the better for the ignornnce. Details of great facts may intensify the intellect of sense, and work damage to the higher mind. If Christ was the Son of man, and as such filled the sphere of humanily, while admitting as such the limitation of his knowledge· in one direction, viz. "of that day and hour knoweth no man," surely we need not perplex ourselves as to specific theories bearing on this subject. Christianity bys the stress on intelligence rather than on information, and, in fact, assures us that restraint. is essential in our condition to equable development. 8t. Paul argues from the future to the present; thus," shall judge the world, ... shall judge angels;" and the conclusion is emphasized,-" how much more things that pertain to this life!" On this grounw CJrr. v1. 1-20.] THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. Hl9

of the spiritual superiority of the saint.~ in Christ, he claims that the judgment of believers may now be most advantageously exercised. It is a training in tl,e school of Christ, and the discipline, while varied, is adapted to the highe,;t ~ood. Does St. Paul mean to put earthly tribunals under the ban? By no means. Again and agaitt he sought their protection against Jews and Gentiles, and, if Homan law had not befriended him, his apostleship-as men reason would have had a speedy tnrnination. Who was more explicit and earnest than he in urging the doctrine that human government was a Divine ordinance, and as such to be obeyed and honoured? And who among statesmen and philosophers ever saw as deeply into the nature and functions of sovereignty as au essential element of the idea of man in the scheme of the universe? In law, in its administration of justice, in its protection of persons and property, in its power to verify and conserve the multitudinous interests of society, he recognized the right arm of Providence. The sense of providence must be social no less than individual, must transcend geographical bounds, and embrace the human family as a family of "one blood," or it failed of its office. So, then, he bas no issue with la\\· and its adjudications as such. But the uses of the law by Christians; the common and facile resort to it in order to gratify covetousness, pride, ambition, revenge, and any and every form of seifishness ;-that is the grave matter before his mind. "There is utterly a fault among you," a weakness, a repudiation of noble sentiment, a departure from the idea of the true self in Christ, "because ye go to law one with another" before unbelievers; brother arrayed against brother; and this exposure of a mutilated unity, with its accompanying ~vils, made in the presence of men whose criticisms would be only too eager to detect and magnify your imperfections. This is one aspect of the matter. But you gain your rights. Ay, and rights may be purchased too dearly. Go to law and get your rights; and then, as yon retire from the seat of judgmcnt, think of what yon leave Lehind you-what losses of sentiment, trust in others, hope of humanity, brotherliness of heart, perchance even integrity and honour. Right and rights, how often they part company, and the one is the burlesque, the shame, the bitter contempt of the at.her! "Rather take wrong;" it is altogether a manlier thiug, if done for Christ's 8ake. Lonl Erskine, when at the bar, once said to Dr. Parr," Accommorlate the difference amicably . . . . I can scarcely figure to myself a situation in which a lawsuit is not, if possible, to be avoided." This is another aspect of the matter. Alas! there is an aspect yet sadder. Law is used as a means to inflict a wroug. "Ye do wrong, and defraud, and that your brcthre!l." What gigantic wrongs have been perpetrated under the name of law, we all know; but who can tell bow far this spirit, which uses justice to accomplish injustice, has gone forth into all the relationships of men, and vitiated life among the. sacred retreats of home and the Church? The depravity of man's lower nature is fearful, not because it is cruel and brutal, but because it is continually re-enforced and invigorated by the depravity of his higher nature. What is true of the iudividual in this respect is true also of society. History and our own observation warrant the statement that the :rrossest perverters of law and justice have been found among those who were wealthy, or in high office, or otherwise influential. Their ·example, in very many instances, has worked downward, just as certain poisonous gases, too heavy to ascend, have infected the air on a level with us. Then follows a question cont,iining its own answer: "Know ye not that the unjust shall not inherit the kingdom of God?" His impassioned formula," Be not deceived," introduces a catalogue of i=ornlities that slrnt out men frorn God's kingdom, in which we have a startling revelation, common wilh St. Pan!, of bO(lily sins. "Such were some of you." But how different now !-washed, sanctified, justified, in the Name of Christ, and by the Spirit. W ouhl they fall back into their heatheniRh practices? Within the compass of a few vcn;es, St. Paul gives us principles t.hat permeate civil society no less than religious. 1f carried ont, \\'e should have much less law and much more equity, and both law and equity would be immense gainers by the change. '!'he tendency of the argument is the thing to notice. 'l'hat tendency is to give _men a true spiritual conception of themselves, ai1d to develop their thought of self in nccordanco with God's thon~ht of them. The sense of pt:blic justice may compel us to resort to law, but this will not confiict with St. Paul's idea. On the other hand, any abuse of an institution, whether ~ovcrnmcntal or domestic, whether ecclesiastical ot· earthly, i.s an abuse of manhood, and on this truth he expc_nds the force of his reasoning. In these verses, as in the previous chapters, argu1 u:;, :.!00 THE I<'IRS1' EPISTLE 1'0 THE COHl~THlANS. [ou. v1. 1-20.

denouncing, exborting, pleading,-it is the voice of a grand doctrine and a lofty trust and a sublime hope that we hear. And we hear it in the midst of strife and turbu- lence, out of the depths of a lienrt most sorrowful and yet" always rejoicing," and able to command itself and its faculties and resources whenever and wherever needed.-L.

Vers .. 12-20.-The human ~ody and its rela~ion to Christ. Among the objects about him proper for use and enJoyment-those obJects which accorded with his nature and position as a redeemed man-was there anything from which he was excludecl? "All things are lawful unto me," and, in this sense, libe1ty and law are identical, the measure of the one berng the meam1e of the other. If law is of God so is freedom • if the former is the expression of the Divine will and character, so is 'the latter· and if man is the image of Christ in law, so is he in freedom. Observe then that i't is not law and liberty a,, existing in a perfect world that the apostle i; considerina but as found in this mixed and disordered world, in which probation is going on to it.~ eternal !ssues. Idea_lly "all things _are lawful," and yet~ because life is a discipline, how could 1t be otherwise tl~a~ t~at hbcrtf should be abnd~ed? One of the main purposes of probJt10n 1s to d1s':1J:l~n_e the will, to ch?ose for itself_ among a multitude of objects addressmg our sens1b1ht1es. Scores of thmgs appeal daily to our senses, and if all our sensat;ons are converted into desires, thence into motives, thence accepted by volition, and made a part of ourselves, then certainly this is not freedom for the ends of moral discipline, but. freedom for simple and universal gratifieation. Freedom in St. Paul's Yiew is not a final cause, it is a means; and he would have the Corinthian remember that one of their greatest obligations was to restrain this freedum. The freedom itself 1iad a large range as to the objects allowed its use and enjoyment. Should it cover the whole area of activity? Kay, says the apostle, this would be bondage in another form. •· I will not be brought under the power of any," for "all things are lawful unto me," which is to ~ay, "all things are in my power," and I will exercise my puwer by imposing limitations cm self-indulgence. Of course, then, this restraint put on ind1- Yidual freedom is our own volm,tary act. Such is the stress laid on personality that a man's Christian virtue must be specifically bis own, and recognized by infallible signs as hi~ own. Development is a common duty, self-development segregates a man from his fellows that he may grow in a given way. Self-denial is a common duty, but under this law of individuality in using our freedom, self-denial assumes a variety of shapes, and becomes wonderfully potential in human affairs by the diversity it presents. In this view the self-denial of A is no guide for B. '!'lie special form of your sell~ denial may not commend itself to me, nay, it may be hurtful to me; and, assuredly, it will lose its virtue if I adopt it merely because it is yours. And hence the value of example in this respect is not to create a slavish imitation on the part of others, but to set forth the worth inherent in the spirit of self-denial. If this principle, so boldly urged by St. Paul, bad been faithfully adhered to, it would have saved the ()hurch from many inconsistencies. Private opinion, while it is content to be such, may be over-stringent, and yet do no great harm. But in many cases it exceeds the limits or individuality and takes sl1ape as the tyranny of public opinion. Morbidness is rarely satisfied ti21 it acquires notoriety l1efore the eyes of men, and so it comes to pass that we ha\'e ecclesiastical agitation and legislation about many things-for instance, amuse- ments-conceroin" wbich no ~xact standard cau be set up for everybody. If we could have an exact sta;dard, it would not compensate for the loss of personal freedom, fince this is precisely one of those matters in which self-denial owes all its excellence to the restrictions that it imposes upon itself. St. Paul's emphatic "I" in this connection is the "I" of every redeemed man, and accordingly, as a universal prerogative, this exalted characteristic of individuality is most carefully guarded. And how is it guarded? To say nothing of what Christian freedom is in itself as delegated by God in Christ, and conditioned widely different from Adam's sovereignty in Eden; to say nothin" of its ofr•inal limitations by the Divine Law, and the fixed barriers over which it may"not pass, ~nd, if true to itself, cannot pass; what is this liberty but a gloriun; priYile"e to be made still more olorious by our own self-enacted laws of restraint? It is a n~w limitation peculiar to<> man. It is a limitation which each man under the "race of the Spirit ori"inates ancl executes in attestation of his own endowments as God's redeemed serl'at;t. It is sonship in its most beautiful and tender funn-tiJ.o or. v1. 1-20.J '!'HE FlHST EPISTLE TO THE CORI.\THIANS. 20l

"Abba, Father," which is not heard in the rrsponses of the Church, nor in hymns of tmcial worship, but is an utterance that rises to God in those hours when loneliness is 11, supreme joy. I have the power; I will not use it; I will deny myself its exercise, and I will do it because "all things are not expedient." \Vhat other eye save his own could penetrate those mysteries, from which he draws reasons and motives for particular acts of self-denial? Mysteries, we say ; for many an advanced believer yields in this phase or experience to half-awakened instincts and undefined impulses. How can ministers of the gospel, how can Churches in their official capacity, get at the lmowledge of what is wisest and best in those matters that belong to the very highest -attributes of personality as the ground of individuality? "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind." "Fully persuaded " he can never be unless he use ihis liberty untrammelled. If you dogmatize and legislate, the full persuasion cannot be the outcome of "his own mind." If God can trust him, why not you? The safeguard has been provided-it is expediency. And this sense of expediency or of fitness and propriety is a conservative and prudential force, which operates to check all excesses, and binds about the man the golden cestus of moderation. Expediency is never self-willed and arbitrary. It presides over tastes and the minor moralities no 'iess than over the more prominent virtues; nor does it trifle with trifles nor disdain the helps of look and tone and manner, but is cardinal to whatsoever reflects the man upon his associates. Keenly alive to discriminations, it educates us to know the best from the merely good, and, by its fine tact and subtle sagacity, goes on swift wing to the noblest objects. It considers, as though it were a part ot itself, the welfare of others, and thus becomes a guarantee that a man's liberty shall not invade the rights of his fellow-man. And remembering that "all things" are his only so far as he is •Christ's, he realizes that it is "no more I that live, but Christ liveth in me." Then :St. Paul proceeds to dwell on the sanctity of the human body-a favourite topic, on whicl1 he expends much thought. In the third chapter he had discussed it, and in subsequent passages, every one of them singularly clear and vivid, he recurs to this great topic. Here the leading idea is that our bodies "are the members" of Christ's body. "The body is for the Lord, and the Lord for the body." And hence St. Paul, in his concrete method of thinking, refuses to separate, even in thought, body and soul, as they are -connected with redemption. Matter and mind are perfectly unlike; they are known to us only by their infinite contrariety; and yet matter and mind meet and unite as \iody and soul, and the union is humnn nature. These two substances grow each in its own way, the natural union at birth becoming closer and yet closer as years progress, and the body subordinating itself more and more to the mind's service. Jn the mature mnu-the mechanic, the accountant, the artist, the poet, the philosophera vast advance has occurred in the nearness and adaptability of ihe corporcity to the wants, demands, and aspirations of the spirit. If the providential idea in education and culture be fulfilled, the co-operative activity constantly increases, each forward -step a step for both, and the law of development taking effect in mutuality of ndvantage. Still more fully is this fact brought out in Christian experience. St. Paul's figures on this subject stand for facts. Bodily appetites cease to be mere anima: instincts. '!'hey are elevated and purified. If Christ was raised from the dead, so too our bodies shall be raised, for the companionship of mind and matter as soul and bo<ly is not a transient but nn eternal fact. One may speak of being "here in the body pent" and of the "body of humiliation" (vile bndy), but the idea of body as an investiture of spirit and an auxiliary to its functions is a part of the original scheme of humanity, and will ha1•e its complete development in the future life. Little do we realize that the resurrection-man is now in a process of training as to his corporeal form. This training is double-mental and material-and hence, while it is true that certain physical functions will expire and be known no more, yet the effects of their experience will survive in the soul itself. "A spiritual body" is assnred us by Christianity and confirmed to us by Christ's resurrection; and, agreeably to this doctrine, the present growth of body into the mind's service, the tuition of the senses, the reduction of the nerves to the will, the command which is ncquired over the lower organs, all indicate that the resurrection-man of body and spirit is now in process of formation. If this i3 true; if the resurrection is not only a prospective_ glor_y but a realization now going on by means of the present ennoblement and sanct1ficat1ou of TUE FmST EPISTLE TO '1'1-IE CORINTHIANS. [en. v1. 1-~C>.

the human body; and, furthermore, if Christ's edncation of his own body to tbo offices he fille<l as Teacher, Miracle-Worker, Philanthropist, Uedeemer, etc., as to the· spirit actuating him, an example to his followers ;-then surely we have the weightiest of reasons for rcgar<ling the body as the "temple of the Holy Ghost." Greek philosophy' had abused the truth that all creatures are for man, and that he is the measure of all things. Professing Christians had followed a carnal philosophy in .the application, of this truth. And now that St. Paul has rescued it from its perversions and set it in its proper light, he may well urge the conclusion," Ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's." Could anything more timely, more momentous, more si1snificant of the aim of Christianity ns it respected the social regeneration of mankind, have been said by St. Paul? The sin of the body; that one sin which surrenders the body to another and de()'rades it ns nothing else can degrn,le; that sin of sins, which debauches the body where it ought to be purest, and sinks lowest that which should be highest ;-could it~ wickedness be set forth in stronger language than when he speaks of the body as the tabernacle, in wl1ich not only tbe soul but the Holy Ghost dwells? "Which ye have of God," and therefore "not your own," but " bought with a price." And yet this redeemed possession, the purchase of Christ's blood, a member of his mystical bo<ly, a. tabernacle of the Spirit, alienated, abused, prostituted to the most shameful and the most fatal of all vices. Of nothing is it so true as of this vice, that we become like that with which we associate. Association is assimilation, and, in this case, nssimilation is the most dreadful form of desecration. 'l'hese verses (18-20) contain, as bas been suggested (Alford), the germ of the three weighty sections of the Epistle about to follow. And we do well to enter into their meaning and implore the grace of God to assist us, lest we fail to receive the profound impression sought to be made. It iN useless to blink the fact that among Christian nations and in the nineteenth century this colossal vice of a desecrated human body is the Satanic citadel of iniquity. Take- all the vices and sins on earth, aggregate them in one huge bulk, and the misfortunes, evils, catastrophes, tragic disasters, put together, would not outweigh the consequences morally and socially viewed of this enormity. Half of th.e man goes straight and quick into the hands of the devil, and the other half, unless God interpose, follows on in a fascination of blindness exceptional among illusions. God help us! For verily "vain," in this instance, "is the help of roan." ·we need a much larger and bolder discussion of the religion of the human body; and if writers and preachers would study the art of doing this work, the Church and the world would be vast gainers. Any way, this is open to us all, viz. to lay a much greater stress than is commonly clone on the dignity, worth, and glory of the human body as seen in the light of Christ's. teaching. Full justice is not done this subject, not even approximative justice, and, therefore, no wonder the body is disparaged, vilified, tolerated by many as a nuisance, and immolated by thousands as a creature of appetite and Inst. "Bought with a price," the blood of the Lord Jesus paid for it-a glorious thing to be bought and not too precious a ransom pain, and now sprinkled by that blood and hallowed by the indwelling Spirit. Oh what intenseness of soul should go into the pleading, "Glorify God in your body"! -L.

-Litigation; or, How shall Christians settle their differences and diryutes 1 Remarkable is the insi"ht which this Epistle affords us into the interior life of a Church of the first age. We s~em to be brought into the presence of remarkable virtues and of remarkabl~ faults, and are impressed with the incongruity of the picture. One thing is certain, that human nature was then what it is now, and that Christianity offersthe one Divine remedy for individual and for social ills. I, JT IS TO BE EXPECTED THAT DIFFERENCES AND DISPUTES WILL ARISE WITHIN THE llOUNDAHIES OF CHRISTIAN COl1MUNl'l'IEB. 'l'he occasions are manifold; the conflict of interests and of opinions and of tastes will account for not a few. It i8 irrational tosuppose that human nature can be at once transformed from the condition of the selfindul()'ent pagan, for example, to the position of a mature and holy servant of Goel. 'JhPr; are to be found in the Church on earth persons occupying every point intermediate between these extremes; and among such "offences will come." ll. lT IS SCANDALOUS THAT SUCH DISPUTES SHOULD llll BROUGHT BEFORE ·A BEATHE!\ oH, VI. 1-20.) 'l'HE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE COr.I:N"THIAXS. 203-

-rmnuNAL, Thll Greek~ were an especially disputatious and liti:dons race. It was natural enough that those who in the days of their heathenism had been accustomed, to refer their disputes to the judges of the city should still carry any differences that might arise into the same courts. But reflection, as the apostle nrges, must have made manifest the unwi~dom or such a proceeding. Christianity proclaim€d itself a religion of peace and love; and its adherents spoke of one another as broth~rs; whilst it wag known that the great_Lord had enjoined tbe forgiveness of injuries, and had himself set an example or such forgiveness. 1t is clear that for Christians to go to law with one another before the tribunals of the heathen was to create a scandal, and to bring both the religion and its profossors into contempt. The same reasonings apply wherever, in our own day, the powers that be are unchristian, and the followers of Jesus are but as leaven in the mass or heathenism. IJI. EVERY CHRISTIAN SOCIETY CONTAINS WITHIN ITSELF ELEllENTS CAPABLE OF DEALit-G WITH SUCH EMERGENCIES. .According to the apostle's teaching, the "saints" shall be assessors with the Lord Christ- in th_e jndgment or the world anrl of angels; and those destined to fulfil functions so majestic may surely be entrusted with the settlement of trivial disputes. It is best if the two persons between whom a misunderstanding has arisen can compose their differences with no outside assistance; if this cannot be donr, it is well to call in the aid of a Christian of calm, impartial character and of large experience, with a common agreement to accept his award without murmuring. There is surely a large opportunity for the exercise of the virtues of wisdom and justice in such directions as these. Much bickering and heart-burninl!: might be avoided were· there a sincere and general desire to act upon the counsels of the apostle. The courts of justice, even in Christian countries, might thus be relieved or much of their business, to the advantage of the whole community. IV. 'l'HE BEST PREVENTIVE OF QUARRELLING IS A DISPOSITION TO SUFFER I:S-JURIES RATHER THAN TO RESENT OR EVEN TO REDRESS WRONG, '!'here is something very startling and very grand in the apostle's sudden, unexpected questions, ""Why not rather take wrong? why not rather be derraut.led?" These arc "counsels of perfection." 'l'he alternative already sugl!:ested is good; but this is better far, however it be opposed to the inclinations of" the natural man." Christ has given us an example of sullcring ,1-ro11~. From the world we are bound, if it be so ordered, to accept with patience language or con- tumely or treatment of injustice. And it is suggested that, even amongst those who n.rc fellow-members of the same body, there may be mutual forbearance, there may be a patience amounting to magnanimity, a renunciation of rights which shall make it clear or how little importance are all those matters upon which it is possible for good men to- ditfer. "Learn how sublime a thing it is To suffer, nncl be strong I" T.
