entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Aspects of responsibility. "As concerning therefore the eating of those things that are offered in sacrifice unto idols," etc. This paragraph suggests thr<e general remarks. I. 'l'I.IAT THE MOllAL ODLIGATIO:SS OF ALL MEN ARE DETERMINED DY THEIR RELATION -ro 'l'JIE ONE Goo AND ms SoN. "As concerning therefore the eating of those things that nrc offered in sacrifice unto idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world,. and that there is none other God but one." There arc many objects in the world that. men call gods, and treat as gods, but they are really nothing, their existence imposes on them no moral obligatipn. There is One, however, and only One, from your relation, to wh.:>IT. there grows up all moral obligations. "One God." ;,!onotheism is demon- cu. vm. 1-W.J THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 261

strnted by all nature, by all consciences, as well as by the Bible. 1. He is a Father .. "'!'he Father, of whom," etc. The Creator of the universe, but the Father of spirits; .spirits arc his offspring. 2. He is the Source of all things. "Of whom are all thing,s." The mighty universe and all it contains are but streams from him, the Fountain of life. 3. He is mir End. "\V c in him," or "unto him," more properly. The supreme End of our existence and Object of our love. In connection with him there is another," one Lord Jesus Christ." This one Lord Jesus Christ was not only bis creative Agent," by whom are all things," but bis redemptive Agent, the Mediator between God and men. And we by him," or "through him." As Christians, we are what we are through him. Now, the will of this one God, as coming through Christ to us, we are morally bound to folfil. An obligation this which not only can never be abrogated, but never modified by any circumstances, age, or revolution. I!. THAT WHAT MIGHT BE WRONG FOR ONE MAN TO DO MIGHT NOT BE SO FOR ANOTHER. The apostle teaches that those in the Corinthian Church who bad reached the conviction that an idol was nothing in the world, and that consequently there was no harm to them personally in eating of the sacrifices that were offered to idols, would commit no wrong in doing so. 'l'be meat itself bad not been corrupted because it had been offered to idols, it was as good as any other meat, and as their consciences were not against i~ there would be no wrong in them participating in it as food. On the other band, those who had a superstitions idea that they ought not to touch the meat they sa,v the priests feeding upon in heathen temples, would commit wrong in using it as food. " Meat commendctb us not to. God: for neither, if we eat are we the better; neither, if we eat not, arc we the worse." The right or the wrong depended on each man's conscience. That which is against a man's conscience may not be a~ainst the eternal law of right, but is against bis own sense of right, and therefore should be avoided; and that which is in accord with a man's conscience, though it may not be in accord with the principles or absolute rectitude, would not be wrong to him. Though sincerity is not a virtue, it is always relatively binding; insincerity is always an absolute sin. Thns what is relatively wrong to one man is not so to another. Here is the principle, "\Vhatsoever is not of faith is sin." "To him that knoweth to do good and doetb it not, to him it is sin." Therefore, "let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind." Ill. THAT TO OFFEND TIIE CONSCIENCE OF A GOOD MAN, HOWEVER WEAK, IS A WRONG IN ALL. "Take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumbling- block to them that are weak." Respect for the weak consciences of good men: 1. l\Iay require self-denial on ow· part. A truly enlightened and healthy minded Christian may feel at perfect liberty to do that from which a weak-minded disciple would recoil with horror. The apostle, for example, might have felt at perfect liberty to sit down in heathen temples, and feast on meat that had been offered to idols, for his great soul had risen up out of the letter and form of religion, concerning meats, and drinks, aud cere- monies, and statutory laws, and exulted in that "liberty wherewith Christ makes his people free." Therefore any restriction in such matters would involve more or less self- deuial, and this Paul willingly accepted, rather than" offend" a" weak brother." On this principle it becomes all to act. Men who have reached the higher stages of Christly lifo may feel at liberty to do many things; but if they are surrounded by good people whose consciences are in the strongest antagonism to all such things, it is their duty to deny themselves of such liberty. 2. Is urged on the strongest considerations. (1) The lack of it me.y inflict serious injuries on the weak. (a) It may" become a stumbling-block to them that are weak." This means, I presume, an occasion of sin. '!'heir faith may be shaken, and they may become apostates; and, more, (b) they may be" emboldened," encouraged to do the wrong. Without your moral streu~th, imitation or you will be pernicious. (c) It may ruin them. "And through thy knowlctlgc shall the· weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?'' Christ died for all, tasted death for every man; yet his death, it seems, does not necessarily ensurt' the salvation of any. What a Rolemn thought, that the conduct even of an advanced Christian may lead to the spiritual rnin of others! (2) The lack of it is a sin both against the weak brethren and against Christ. "When ye sin so aaainst the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ." 3. Is ex~mplified in the sublime resolve of the apostle: "If meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standcth, lest I m~kc my brother to offend." Here is benevolent expediency, the strongest grouud on which the -268 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [en. vnL 1-13.

temperance reformation can b 7 ''.'iscly and effectively advocated. In this sublime utterance you hav~ tbe self-s,,cnficmg and magnanimous spirit of the gospel. Give up all rather than rum souls. Such an utterance as this is characteristic of Paul. "But I could wish that I myself were accursed for my brcthrcn's sake mv kinsmen accorilino-0 to the flesh." ' • CoxcLUSI?N· _\:VherP, in. the s_tate or in the Church, can you find a man who approaches m spmt the sublime philanthropy of Paul'! Jn the state we have men who call themselves reformers, who grow eloquent in proclaimincr the ricrhts of man and the glorie_s of liberty; but.can you find ~ith~r in their speeches ir deeds° the matchless spirit of plnlanthropy, heammg and booming m these words of the apostle?-" \Vherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth." Are not our reformers, alas! more or less traders and hirelin"'s? Where even in our Churches ~o ~e _fin~ prea_ch~rs aglow with this unconquerable "'love for man? And yet this is Chnshamty:,t'~1s 1s what t?e ,;'orld w:ints: what it must have ere it can be morally rndeemed. 'I here never did, says Sir \V alte1· Scott, "and never will exist anythino- permanently noble and excellent in a character which was a strano-er 'to the exercis~ of resolute sclf-,lenial. Te~ch self-denial! and make its practice pl~asurable, and you -create for the world a destmy more sublune than ever issued from the brain of the wildest dreamer."

entries.title: 1CO 8:1–13
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Strength and weakness; lcnowled.r,e and love. The discussions contained in this chapter relate to" things offered unto idols.'' Bear in mind that idolatry was not then simply a religious ~ystem, but a system immensely extended and covering -a corresponding surface of political, social, and business interests. At all points it touched individuals and families, and was connected with feasts, entertainments, and etiquette. "Most public entertainments and many private meals were more or less Temotely the accompaniments of sacrifice" (Stanley). How far might knowledge assert itself and put on independency? What was the true use of expediency? Ancl what the offices of conscience? And to what extent must the strong be tender and considerate towards the weak? Two parties existed on this subject in Corinth: the one that rested on Christian liberty, and, believing that "an idol is nothing in the world," demonstrated its adhesion to this belief by buying and eating meats sacrificed t-0 idol~, and even went to the excess of attending the feasts" in the idol's temple;" the other party looked upon such conduct with abhorrence. If, now, Christianity had been a mere scheme of human thou)!ht, an elaborate philosophy, a poetic inspiration, it is obvious that no such earnest dispute could have arisen. If, again, St. Paul had contemplated the subject on the ground only of abstract and the-:,retical principles, following out the logic that "an idol is nothing," and claiming the full freedom -guaranteed by the assumption, a very different chapter from this would have been written. But see how he approaches the matter. His first step is to check the liberalists, and he docs it efficaciously, for he convicts them of pride and recklessness <Jn the side of intellect. Intellect he docs not condemn, but its wrong use. His condemnation is founded on the fact that the intellect arrogantly claims to be the mi □ d, to be the equivalent of the man himse)F, and, consequently, shuts off the Tecognition of anything except knowledge. St. Paul's po5ition at tho outset is, "Enowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth." It is vigorously stated and is accompanied by evident impulse. The" knowledge" referred to is knowledge isolated from its rightful and essential associations, the knowledge of a truth, and yet without its checks and balances-an engine lacking safety-valve and governor. No matter how valuable the knowledge may be in itself; call it insight, call it what you please; if it abuse itself in its use, it loses its worth. Selfishness vitiates its excellence, and makes it doubly harmful, pernicious to the possessor, and obstructive of benefit to him on whom it acts object:vely. Men arc prone to exaggerate knowledge as knowlcdg:. 'l'hey say, "Knowledge is power." So it is, but whether the power be for good or evil depends on the man behind the knowledge. 'l'hink of tl,e intimate connection between the intellect and the body, :md how much more it is affected thereby than other on. VIlL 1-13.J 'l'HE FIRS'!' EPISTLE TO THE CORIN'l'HIANS. 2C9-

portions of the mind; think how tangled it often is in the nerves, 9.nd imprisoned in the cells of the brain,-and can you wonder at the distrust that wise men have of its functions, unless controlled, and that ~ternly, by principle and sentiment? What ~ubtle poisons creep into the blood and thence into thought! A slight imprudence in eating, a bad dream last night, a household worry or a business vexation, distnrbed \Jreathing or accelerated heart-action, and the intellect is warped and enfeebled. Do what we may to curtail tbo evils, infirmities cling to all its activities. Yet much may be done, and it is done in no other way than that suggested by the apostle. "Charity [love] edifieth [bnilrlcth up]." By this he means that the heart must be under the influence of grace, and thus inspire the intellect so that it may be delivered from its selfishness and especially its self-conceit. And so fully bas Christianity indoctrinated all our best thinkers with this idea, that they have come to believe that wisdom is the conjoint product of right thought and true feeling. "If tny man love God, the same is known of him," and the knowledge here predicated of God has a reflex agency on the man's kno,vledge. Instead of being "puffed up," instead of an immodemte and unjustifiable use of bis Christian freedom, instead of a vauntiug display of his superiority to prejudice and ignorance, be is rcgardful of the scruples of others, and, while aware of the difference between them and himself, turns the difference to the account of humility and forbearance. 'l'he idol is nothing, but its nothingness is no reason for insensibility to the claims of weak brethren on his manly sympathies. For the great doctrine of "one God, the Father, of whom are all thing~, and we in him," is so profoundly realized, that human brotherhood is itscomplement in his character and conduct. "One Lord Jesus Christ, by whom arc all things, and we by him," the Mediator of the natural universe, in whose sovereignty ,~II laws aud institutions and objects have their reason and end; the Mediator of the spiritual universe, who has consummated the manifestation of humanity in the person and work of the Holy Ghost ;-this Jesus of Nazareth, who is tl,c Christ of God and Lord over all, has so embodied the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of humanity in his own incarnation and office, that henceforth the grandeur of the one is the strength and joy and glory of the other. St. Paul loses no opportunity to enforcethis supreme truth. Does he argue in behalf of Christian liberty"? Here is his basis. Docs he plead for expediency? Here is his warrant. Does he harmonize them a,; coexisting and co-operating sentiments? '!'hey are mutually supporting because their possessor has the knowledgo which comes from God in Christ. From thi,; sublime height he is never long absent. 'l'hitherward is he always tending, nor \\"iii he decide any question, whatever its bearings, with I\ judgment detached from the great truth Uhrist taught: "I in them, and thou in me, that they may be mado perfect in one." All, howeHr, have not this knowledge. 'l'be insight of some is partial and confused, "whose Christian faith is not yet so emancipated from the religious convict.ions of their old heathen state, and who are still in the bonds of their former conscience, moulded by heathen ideas" (Dr. Kling). Having this "conscience of the idol," looking upon the idol as a r(•ality, and forbidden by his conscience to cat the flesh offered to an idol, the "weak brother" is offended. 'l'hc meat itself is a matter of indifference, nor are you the "better" or the "worse" for the mere act of eating. A gmve question, howc\'Cr, lies at the back of the action. It concerns "this liberty of yours," and the spirit actu,1ting your mind in doing this thing. " Take heed;" this liberty may de;;eneratc into a haughty self-valuation, may become a "stnmbling-hlock," and may induce the "weak brother" to imitate your example, and thus sacrifice his conscience under your influence. 'l'hough the conscience be weak, it is conscience; it is his; its authority ove1· him is sacred; obey it ho must. "\Vorse than all, your conduct, taking effect upon him, may i"mperil the salvation of a man, "for whoru Christ died." Enlighten his conscience all yon can; help to make it truthful as well ns sincere; but, meantime, "talce heed" lest sympathy and conventionality embolden him to err. "·weak" now, you will only weaken him tho more if your liberty mislead him. 'l'he only element in him out of which strength r.an grow is the conscience. Use your freedom so as to liberate, not to eusla1·e, this highest authority in our nature. Use your knowledge to illuminato, not to darken, this divinest of all the organs personal to tho soul, through which truth reaches the man. Uso your Church relation to build up and not pull down your brother, that 270 THE FIRST El'IS'l'LE TO THE CORINTHlANS. [ea:. vm. 1-13.

you nrny be a co-worker with God and .with his conscience in makinO' him a "templlJ of the Holy Ghost." Then comes the utterance of great-heartcduess~the declaration that be will cat no such meat for ever if it make his brother to offend. This \\'(1.s no sudden effervescence of sentimentality. It was genuine sentiment. It was orgnnic to the man's nature. Impulse was strong because conscience was stron"er. 'l'he current ?f fce)ing was no catara?t leap!ng from a rocky bed into rocky depths, and dashing itself mto foam, but a nnghty nYcr that could not become too full for its banks.-L. Ver. !.-Knowledge and love. In the Divine DeinO' himself both knowled"'e and love are perfect; he is lif!;ht; he is love. Man, made "'in God's image, is C(l.p~ble of both; but h:s knowledge 1s and must be very limited (1.nd partial, whilst he has vast capacities for love. Not only so; as the apostle here teaches love is better than knowledge, for whilst this puffs up, that edifies. We recogniz~ this superiority in several particulars. I. Ix ITS INFLuENCE UPON THE INDIVIDUAL'S OWN CHARACTER. Paul's observation convinced hitn that this was the case. There were at Corinth those who boasted of their knowledge, of their iutellectual powers of discrimination, of their superiority to the ignorant vulgar. Dut these very persons, although Christians in name, were very far from displaying the character of Christ himself, evincing little of consideration and forbearance towards their fellow-believers. In fact, they were "puffed up,'' their knowledge inflatmg them, but imparting to them no real stability or vigour of character. On the other hand, such as were animated by the purifying and elevating principle of love were, by the action of that principle, delivered from selfishness and self-seeking. They were "edified," i.e. built up, as a temple in stately proportions, upon a secure and ample foundation. This is a generalization, the justice of which is borne out by the experience of the Church of Christ. A show of knowledge is often unlovely when compared with the reality of love, which imparts a beauty and a radiance to the. character beyond what human effort and culture can possibly bestow. II. l!> ITS I!-FQ::;E:;:cE UPON HUMAN SOCIETY. It has ,been maintained in our own <lay (by Mr. Buckle) that moral beliefs have no influence in the development of society, which is due to the adrnnce of scientific knowledge. But facts are in contradiction to this theory. Ltarning, science, art, are all good in themselves; but they give no guarantee that they shall be wisely and beneficially used, and they may be far from a blessing to society. Dut where compassion and benevolence are prevalent and ruling principles, there society feels the benefit of their operation. The Church is maintained in peace and harmony; the world around is profited by the self-denying efforts made for the amelioration of its condition. We have only to compare the condition of ancient Rome with that of modern England to be assured of this. III. IN ITS ACCEPTABLENESS TO Goo. We are not to understand that our Divine Ruler is indifferent to the progress of knowledge. "That the soul be without knowledge is not 0"Ood." And there is a kind of knowledge which is near akin to love: to know God is life eternal. But mere intellectual activity, mern speculative acquaintance with truth are vain and worthless in his sight to whom all things are known from the begiu'ning. But love, as it is the highest expression ~f the Divine nature and character, is peculiarly congenial and acceptable ~o God. With the lovele_ss soul ~od has no sympathy; but tlie soul that is on fire with Joye to God and man 1s preparmg to dwell in the everlasting radiance which makes and blesses heavcn.-1'.

entries.title: 1CO 8:3
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Intimacy between God and man. As the passage treats of man's knowledge._ professed, supposed, and real, we should expect in this verse to find a statement regarding man's knowled"e of God. And by some the second clause of this verse has been interpreted in this sense. If this somewhat strains the language, and if it is necessary to understand that we have here an assertion that the lover of God is known by God, all the same the apostle must be acknowledµ:cd hero to affirm a spiritual intimacy between the human spirit and the Father of s1,irits. I. THE co:s-DITIO!> m' THIS IXTllIACY. 1. lt is a condition which could sc(l.rcely cccur to man apart from revelation. Men fear Go<l, reverence God, worship God, seek to avert the wrath of God; but to love God is uot an exercise of mind which seems congruous to the relat;on between the Creator and his creatures. 2. It is a condition -cH. vm. 1-13.] THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 2il

which Christianity renders possible and natural. By revealing God as love, by brincrincr that love home to the heart in the incarnation and the sacrifice of the Son of God~ Christianity makes a claim upon human love. The manifestation of affectionate interest and benevolence in a way so remarkable, so unique, is sufficient to account for a new relationship, and for new emotions corresponding therewith. 3. It is a condition capable of universal fulfilment. "If any man love God." There are many whose natural powers of body m.J of mind are very limited. But there is none who Las not the capacity for love. There may be a moral unpreparedness, but this may be overcome. The Gentile .as well as the Jew, the illiterate as well as the learned, are capable of loving the Authol' ,of salvation. 11. THE .CHARACTER OF THIS INTIMACY. Love is represented as leading to, as involving, knowledge. 1. On the side of God himself. This is the explicit statement of the text : "The same," i.e. the man who loves, "is known by him," i.e. by God. Knowledge is, in Scripture, according to a Hebrew idiom, often used as equivalent to favour; even as we say we know a person intimately, meaning in the knowledge of friendship. Of course, the Omniscient knows all his creatures; but he has a friendly, fatherly, affectionate, intimate knowledge of those who love him. He reads the language of their hearts. "'!'he Lord knoweth them that are his." He knows them to wat-:h over and keep, to guide and govern, to strengthen and to save them. 2. On the side ,of man. This is the implicit stateme11t of the text; for he who in the sense affirmed is known by God also knows God. How true it is that he who loves God knows him too! There are many respects in which we cannot know our earthly, human associates, unless we are drawn to them by the cords of love. Love opens the doors of knowledge. It creates that sympathy which gives intensity to the intuitive gaze of the soul. Thus it is that, whilst many learned and philosophic minds arc ignorant of the Deity, there are to be found, among the lowly, the ignorant, and the feeble, those who, with hearts quickened and softened with grateful love, live in a hallowed iutimacy with him who is the Father of their spirits and the God of their salvation.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 8:5
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The unity of God. The Apostle Paul had been trained in the monotheis1:1 which bad from tho first been the belief of the Hebrew race, and from which they hacl .not for centuries previous to his time ever swerved. Ilut as a preacher of Christianity, a religion which aspired to world-wide empire, be was constantly brought, especially as the apostle of the Gentiles, iuto contact with the worshippers of idols, both philosophic and popular. And he was often called to be the counsellor of those - who, although called out of heathenism, still lived in a heathen atmosphere and wern e11tangled iu consequence in not a few practical difficulties. In discussing for the benefit of these Corinthian questions of conduct arising out of their necessary association with those who practised heathen customs, Paul took his stand boldly and uncom- promisingly upon the great religious doctrine of the unity of God. I. TIJE UNITY OF GOD IS CONTRASTED WITH POLYTHEISTIC DELIF.F AND WORSHIP. 1. 1'he deities of the heathen are called gods. They are called, but they arc not; it is .a delusion. "Au idol is nothing in the world." The grand denunciation of the Hebrew psalm occurs to the mind: "Eyes have they, but they see not," etc. 2. 'l'hcse deities are deemed "gods" and "lords." 'l'hey were and still are, in hcatbe11 lands, deemed superhuman, supernatural, and arc invested by the imagination with some claims to the homage,. reverence, and service of intelligent me □. 3. 'l'hcy arc i11 number many, every river and grove having its deity. It is well known that the heathen hail evcu their household gods, e.g. the Romans their lares et pe1wtes. 4. They have their several localities and ranks and realms of dominion. '!'hey arc "in heaven," as tho superior Olympian deities; or "on earth," as those inferior nttmina which haunt this lower world, nymphs and fauns and dryads, etc. Such was the system which ·Christianity found, with which Christianity came into conflict. II. TnE UNITY OF GoD FURNISHES A CENTRE AND AN AIM FOR TllE NEW RELIGIOUS LIFE OF MEN. 1. In himself ho is "the one God, the Father." In itself this was a glurious revelation; and in Jesus Christ provision was made for its wide promul~ation and acceptance. 2. He is the Creator and Upholder of all; "Of whom are all things." 3. And especially he is the great Object of our faith, love, and devotion. W c arc" for, • , . unto him." It is at this point that the great revclatiou of the new theology becomes 272 THE FIRST EPISTLE 'l'O 'l'l:IE COHlNTIIIANS. [cH. vm. 1-13.

the great motive of the new religion. Polytheism distracted the minds of tho- worshippcrs, and made it impossible that faith in God should become the inspiration of a new and better life; for it was a qncstion-\Vhat measure of reverence and of service shall be offered to this deity, and what to that? But Christianity revealed one God in whom arc all perfections, and who is not only the Creator but the moral Governo1~ and Saviom of mankind. They who live to serve this God have an elevatina0 purifying, powerful aim in the conduct of their life. '

Ill. 'l'HE UNITY OF GOD FURNISHES 'l'HE NODLEST MOTIVE TO THE NEW RELIGIOUS J.IFE. l. The one God is made known by the one Lord Jesus Christ. It is a mis- understanding of the Scripture doctrine to conceive of this view of the Redeemer as. conflicting with the monotheism which is the glory of the Bible revelation. '!'he ono Lord reveals the one God, as the \Vord reveals the Utterer, as the Son reveals tho- Father. 2. Christ is the universal Mediator, "by whom are all things." 'l'his is the doctrine of John as well as of Paul. And we may well understand the moral as we![. as the physical creation to be included. For all the biessinas 0 which the Father destines fer huµ1anity be has resolved to co:.fer by Jesus Christ. 3. We as Christians are what we are "through him." As in the former clause we recoanized the areat aim, so here we recognize the great mean.~ and motive of the ',new, the distinctively Christian life. The Divine nature and mediation of Immanuel, so far from obscuring our belief in the unity of God, is the best and strongest and most effectual support of. that doctrine. Even as Jesus himself said, "He that bath seen me hath seen the Father;" and "No man cometh unto the Father but by me."-'l'.

entries.title: 1CO 8:8
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Christian liberty. No doubt Paul was regarded as the great champion of liberty. The apostles at Jerusalem were more under the influence of the old JuJaism; Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles, gained a larger spirit of tolerance through bis association with men of various races and habits. 'l'he t:ipirit of God set him free from restraints by which many good men were fettered. To him the party of know- ledge, of emancipation, of liberalism, would naturally look for countenance and encouragement, when scruples about trifling matters of outward observance perplexed the conscience and threatened to divide the Church. And, so far as his views ol' religion were concerned, Paul was with this party; yet, as this passag~ reminds us, in- his view, religion had one side turned towards God, and another side turned towards men, and be would not have this second side overlooked. l. THE INDIFFERE:S-CE, AS A MATTER OF PnINCIPLE, OF OUTWARD ODSERVANCES. 1. The general doctrine. It is not what we eat or abstain from eating that God regards, that God will judge us by. 'l'he reasons for this doctrine are obvious. (1) The nature of God, who is a Spirit, and in whose view what is spiritual is of overmastering and supreme interest. Priests in their pettiness may think matters ali-important whichin God's sight are trifles light as air. (2) 'l'be nature of man, who is a reasonable and spiritual being, and whose highest welfare cannot consist in what food enters into his body and what food he refrains from partaking. (3) 'l'he nature of Christianity, which is a sr•iritual religion, and seeks to take possession of human nature and so· to influence bnman life. It is not a religion of feasts and fasts, but a religion of faith, hope, and love. 2. The special applicati011. qf the doctrine. 'l'he query propounded by the Corinthians is fairly answered. It is as though Paul bad sai<l, "So far as God is concerned it makes no difference at all whether y·,u belong to the scrupulous party, and refrain from eatin"0 meat which may possibly have been offered in idol F.acrifice and worship, or to the Ji beral party, and, despising such distinctions, eat whatever is· purchased in the market or placed upon the table. These habits of yours cannot make you either better or worse, cannot commeud you to God or involve you in 'his displeasure; he looks at something very different from such things." So with p:1rallel cases; matters may have importance as regards the Church, as regards human society, which are utterly unimportant as regards our relation to God. II. 'l'HE DA:S-GER OF CARRYING CmuSTIAN LIDEllTY so FAR AS TO INJURE OUR FELLOW- MEN. A .Christian in these early days might be himself quite superior to the small scrnplcs by which hio neighbours were influencecl. Ilut, at the same time, he might be justly calkd t1pon to consider his weak brethren, and not to put an occasion of offence in the path of any. 'l'he best things may be abiiscd, and it is often so with, cu. vrn. 1-13.J 'l'HE FIIlST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 273

liberty. Pnul cared not a whit for idol fen.sts and sacrifices, and, had he consi<lered only himself, he would have eaten meat that had been presented i11 an idol-temple; but he cared for his brethren, and he cared for them all the more if their knowled"'e was slight, their faith feeble, their apprehen~ions of spiritual realities obscure. He would not break the bruised reed; he would rather abstain than injure a brother's conscience, It was a grand view of Christian duty tliis which Paul took; ?. noble resolution this which Paul formed. A lesson to the whole Church of God in all the various phases of experience and trial through which it is called to pass. Let Christians think first, indeed, of their own position in the sight or the heart-searching God. But let them not omit to think of their relation to their brethren in Christ, and let them so act that none may be troubleJ in conscience or caused to. fall by reason of any want of consideration and sympathy, by reason of any disposition to push liberty to too great an extreme. God is our Lord; yet his people, however feeble, are our brethren. Their interests are dear to our hearts, and our intercourse with them is to be guided not only by wisdom but by charity.-'!'.
