entries.title: 1CO 8:11
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -The brother's claim. It seems as though Paul treated of this case of conscience at inordinate length. Perhaps this would be so were it not that, in disposing of this difficulty, the apostle was really disposing of many other dilfaulties which should emerge in the course of the centuries. Principles are laid down in this "casuistical" portion of the Epistle which arc applicable to Christian conduct in varying states of society and throughout all time. l. 'l'HE DANGER TO CHRISTIAN BRETHREN OF THE UNRESTRAL.~D INDULGENCE OF LIBERTY. Let a Christian man consider only what will commend him to God, what is in accordance with his right and liberty; and what will be the result? This passage makes this very evident, showing that for an enli);htened Christian to partake of food offered to idols may prove prejudicial to weak brethren, who take such conduct as a sanction of idol-worship and of idolatrous practices generally. No doubt this is a misconceptioa, but it is a misconception which is likely, which is certaia, to happen. Thus the mau of weak conscience, of little enlightenment, has his nature defiled aad hardened, and, according to the very strong expression of this verse, is in danger of perishing. An awful, unforeseen, consequence to follow upon the indulgeace in Christian liberty. 'l'he possibility of such a consequence is in itself sufficient to mah a liberal Christian pause lest he should carry his liberty too far. II. 'l'HE GREAT CHRISTIAN MOTIVE WHICH RESTRAINS THE EXERCISF. OF LIDERTY. The apostle calls upon the ealightened Corinthians to consider who lie is whose welfare and salvation are endangered by the course si1pposeu. 1. He is a brother. ·who will say, "Am I my brother's keeper?" On the contrary, the spiritual bond thnt unites the people of Christ one to another is so closo and precious that auything that threatens its permanence should be regarded with suspicion and drea,1. 2. Nut only so; he is one for whom Ghrist died. Observe the contrast which is so powerfully presented in this languago. 'l'he Lord of glory died to ransom and to save e:i.ch disciple and friend of his; submitted for his sake, not to inconvenieuco and reslraiat, but to sufferings, to the cross, to the grave. Aad shall any follower of the Lord Jesus treat with contempt even the weakness and prejudice of one whom the Lord of glory so pitied that he g:we up his own life to save? Who are we th:i.t we should act .in a mauner so contrary to the action of our Divine Lord nnd Leader? Let him be our Example, as in other things, so in this; let his self-sacrifice be our mo,lel and motive, that with a sympathizing and alfoctil,nate dispositiuu we hold dear the security and well-being of every Christian brother, however ignorant and howevct· feeble. So far from assisting in the ruin, be it ours to promote the salvation of every member of the spiritual family, every sheep, every weak and helpless lamb, of the vast flock of that good Shephenl who laid down his life for his shecp.-'l'.

entries.title: 1CO 8:12
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-" Sin against Ghrist." It is a proof of the personal and intimate character or the relation between Christ and his people, as that relation was conceived in tho primitive Churches, that it should be the very climax of reproach against any professed Christians because of any course of action they followed, to charge them with sin against Christ. It is surely obvious that language like this could not be used of any l, COnINTITIA NS, T 2,1 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cH. vm.1-13.

merel., human teacher or leader. One who was on the one hand so closely united to, the Di,:ine Father and on the other hand so truly a Son of man, as Jesns, Immanuel, could atone be spoken of thus. It was not possible to go further in expostulation than by the use of such language as this, addressed to those who considered too little the conscience of a weak brother," Ye sin against Christ." To act without due sympathy, ?o~sideration, and charity towards a brother Christian is to sin against Christ, because It I S - I. To OFFEND AGAI:,;"ST CHRIST'S COMMANDMENT. Our Lord's great commandment, his new commandment, his oft-repeated comruandmeut, was a commandment to his disciples to love one another. He even went so far as to make obedience to this law of charity a test and note of discipleship: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." A disregard for the feelings, the conscience, the spiritual health, of a Christian brother was an evident and flagrant violation of the Lord's great precept, and was therefore "sin against Christ." II. To CONTRADICT CrrnisT's EXAMPLE. Our Lord did not enjoin a spirit or conduct which he did not exemplify in his own life. Whoever reads the record of that life must observe that his spirit in dealing with his disciples was one of forbearance, consideration, pity, and benevolence. He washed his disciples' feet; he bore with their infirmities. and their slowness to understand him; he pitied and instructed their ignorance; he overlooked and forgave their cowardice and desertion; in a word, he laid himself out in e,ery way for their spiritual good. How then could any Corinthian, how can any other professing Christian, be a follower of the blessed Lord, if he display an inconsiderate, contemptuous, unforgiving spirit towards a brother in Christ? In so doing he sins against the Master. III. To INJURE CHRIST IN THE PERSON OF ONE OF HIS LITTLE ONES. Jesus laid down this principle with great clearness when he identified himself with his own, assuring us that what was done-good or ill-to his little ones he should, in the· judgrnent, regard as_ done unto himself.. The Head is insulted when the member is injured; the King is aggrieved when his subject is attacked; the Shepherd is smitten when his sheep are scattered. Whosoever is indifferent to the welfare of the Lord's servant sins against that Lord himself, and shall not ·be held guiltless. Christ expects all his people to act as if he were present in the person of every one whom he loves and. for whom he died.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 8:1–11
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-T/ie two guides-knowledge and love. I. TrrEY ARE BOTH EXCELLENT- This requires no proof. 'l'he apostle who sat at the feet of Gamaliel, would have been the last to speak slightingly of real knowledge. We are made capable of ~n. eve_r- increasincr knowledO'e. How much knowled(J'e has been the means of accomphshmg m this world! IO'nora nce is but a "fool's paradise;" "Knowledge is power." .And how excellent is lov e. How dull and sad this world would be without it! How much more, prolific in crime and evil even than it now is! One's o_nly regret about love is that there is so little of it. It is the world's great want. Herem heaven and earth contrast, seeing that there is much love there and little here. The triumphs of knowle,!ge are great, but greater are the victories of love. II. THEY ARE COMPLEMENTARY. One is not without the other. 1. Knowledge without love leads to (1) pride; (2) intolerance; (3) selfishness; (~) injury to others; (5) manv blunders in thou(J'ht, feelin", and action. Knowledge 1s not enough for a people. ·we may have abundance of k;owledge, and yet be very unwise, very injuriou~, and very unlovable. 2. Love without knowledge leads to moral_ catastrophe. It )B impossible to predict what conduct may result fro!'n mere affectwn. Knowled~e. 1s necessary to determine within what limits we may rightly act. Knowledge can <lec1de for us what is "lawful." Love determines what, within the circle of the lawful, we shuuld choose. Knowled(J'e and love united lead to that more perfect, that penetrating, that true practical knowledge, the opposite of whicl~ P~ul d?scribes in ver. 2. Truo Jove controllin" sound knowled(J'e leads to a deeper insight-In other words, to a truer knowled;:!:e. for example, a ma~ may know God as God; may have somo conception of the Divine attributes, etc. But when he loves God his knowled~e makes incalculable strides· he now knows God so much more fully and truly that his former knowledge· lll littl~ better real[.)•. al.Id no better practically, than crass ignorance. Knowledge- ou. vm. 1-13.J THE FIRS'l' EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 275

"puffeth up;" by itself it is sometimes worse than ignorance. Love, not actin" with- out knowledge, but on the lines of knowledge, "bnildeth up." III. A SPECIAL CABE IN ILLUSTRATION. The Corinthians had written to the apostle respecting their liberty to eat meats which had been offered to idols. The portion of victims not consumed upon the idol-altars belonged partly to the priests and partly to the offerers. Much of this meat found its way to the public markets, or was consumed in private houses, at social gatherings, or at feasts in the temples. Christians would be often tempted to partake of these idol-meats. I. The apostle shows that knowledge alone would be a very unsafe guide in such a matter. An enlightened rnintl -:vould perceive that meats were in themselves the same, whether offered or not offered. to idols; and knowing also that "meat eomrnendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse;" would consider the matter as purely indifferent, and to be determined solely by inclination. But here mere knowletlgc would lead to error. Love, which concerns itself about others, steps in and says, "T2.ke heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumbling-block to them that are weak." All do not realize the nothingness of the idol, or the fact that idol-meats are unchanged by idol-contact. Their immature and weak condition leads them to conclude that the idol is something, and to them the eating of idol-meats is an act which identifies them with idol-worship. Thus the partaking by the more enlightened may prove both a sc_andal and a temptation to the unenlightened. Knowledge says, "Do all that you have a right to do ; " Love says," Consider others, especially the weak." Knowledge alone leads to contempt of the weak and ignorant, and to indifference as to how they are affected; but Love champions the cause of those who specially need consideration and help. Knowledge does not take into account the weak brother, but Love yearns over his welfare, and forgets not that Christ died for him. Love kindled at the cross flames forth in Christ-like self-sacrifice. Love, directing its glance arouncl, sees that the highest interests of those for whom Christ died may be imperilled if the claims of liberty be too rigidly enforced; and so she leads men to the choice of that "better part," self-sacrifice for the welfare of others. This is the "shining way" once trodden by the reet of the Son of God. This is the path of the truest knowledge; for here we learn not only what we may do, but what iu the highest sense we ought to do. 2. 'l'he apostle has here no occasion to show that love without knowledge would prove a faulty guide. But it evidently might. Love might lead the weak and ignorant to eat the idol-meats, so as to please those more enlightened, and so as not to be a check upon their desires. We need, for safe guidance, the twin guides, knowledge and love.-Il.

entries.title: 1CO 8:6
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-"0ne God .. . 01l6 Lord." I. THE ONE Go». The oneness of Deity is here emphasized. It is insisted upon throughout the Scriptures. 'l'he true Israel, ancient and modern,• has been monotheistic. The conflict, contradiction, confusion, and absurdity, conspicuous enough in the polytheistic systems, find no place in Judaism or Christianity. The oneness of Deity is confirmed by (1) nature, (2) providence, (3) tho moral sense. The one God is : 1. The Source of all things. "Of whom are all things." Ho is the great Originator; all things sprang from bis creative touch. We know not how-the manner is not revealed to us, the fact is. God may have left much to man's scientific instinct to discover; he may have intended not a little to remain enshrouded in mystery. We may travel reverently along the lines of true knowledgo until tboy cease for us; then the great truth remains still for our enlightenment and comfort. 'l'lie march backward of science is towards unity; revelation began with it. 2. The End of all things. "We unto [not 'in'] him." What is bore asserted of some of God's works ("we") applies to all (see Col. i. 16). All things were created "unto" God ; the object of their existence terminates in God, they show forth his glory, they subservo his purposes. The whole universe looks God-wards. So far as intelligent creatures do not find the end of their existence in God, so far as they do not seek the Di vine glory, so far they fall out of harmony with the rest of creation and bring failure into their lives. We are not created for ourselves, but for God; we should therefore "glorify God in our bodies, and in our spirits, which are his" and/01· him. Il. THE ONE Lono. This is Jesus Christ-the•• Son of man" ancl the" Son of God." We are here taught that the Head of the Christian Church was the active Power in creation. Of the Deity, as such, were all things; through the one Lord, the second 276 THE FIRST EPISTLE 'l'O THE CORINTHIANS. [rn, vm. 1-13.

person ir. the Deity, were all things. Some have been led by this verse to question the divinity of Christ: it appears to teach it in a very impressive and convincincr manner. The administrntiYe, mcdiatinl): position occupied by Christ is indeed reco"~izecl but the assertion that "through" him all things were seems scarcely susc~tible' of a fair interpretation if his divinity be excluded. Moreover, this very expression," through him," is applied elsewhere to God as such (see Rom. xi. 36; Heb. ii. 10). And the expression which we have here applied to God, "unto him," is in Col. i. 16 applied to Christ. '!'he apostle is speaking to the Corinthians about idols as "gods and lords." These were all regarded as deities. In carrying over the same terms to the realm of Christianity, there is nothing in the statements made which should lead us to reo-ard "Lore!" as less Divine than "God." "' Ill. TUE SPECIAL RELATIONS SUBSISTING BETWEEN BELIEVERS AND THE ONE LORD AND oi-.-E Goo. 1. Believers are " through" Jesus Christ. As creatures, they are amoncrst the "all things" which are said to be "through" him. Eut the additional stateme~t, " we throngh him," indicates a very special relationship. Believers are such through Christ; they believe on him. Through Christ they are separated from the "aH thin<>s" and made a" JJeculiar people." All that distinguishes them from others in condition ~nd prospect is "through" him. He is their" Alpha and Omega." He created all thincrs, and they are bis new creation-a creation of a higher order and with sublimer ends. Apart from Christ believers are nothing; through him they become "heirs of God." As through Christ in the realm of nature the chaos became order and beauty, so through Christ men pnss from the disorders of a lost state into the excellences and glories of a redeemed and consecrated existence. 2. Believers are "unto" God. All things arc, but belic\'ers arc in a very special sense. 'fhis is "through" Jesus Christ,, As all the creation under the administration of Jesus Christ is" unto God," so in a peculiar and lofty sense are believers. They show forth the Divine glories as none other of the human race can. Thev reflect the Divine love mr.nifested in the transcendent work of redemption. They-are· presented to God as the fruits of the Divine grace. Their" lire is hid with Christ in God." 'Ibey are" not their own." 'l'heir lives are devoted to the Divine service. They are" servants of God." Once rebellious, they are now obedient; once defiled, now purified; once lost, now saved " unto God." Here is pre-eminently the believer's condition ; he is emphatically "unto God." Is this so with us? If we are saved by Christ, for what, to what, are we saved? Some seem to be saved for nothing in particular! Many are satisfied with being "saved," and never ask," Saved for what?" 0. God is the Father to 'believers. In a certain restricted sense he is the Fath<::r of all. We are all his offspring. But in a spiritual sense God is not the Father •Jf all. Of certain unbelievers Christ sairl, "Ye are of your father the devil." Gad cannot be our Father unless we are his children. There must be the double relationship or none. Some are willing enough for God to be their Father, but not willing at all to be his children! But the true believer has received the adoption and cries, "Abba, I?ather." High privilege indeed! How it speaks of care, and support, and protection, and guidance, and teaching, and love! How near to God we are brought when he hecomcs our Father! Our origination is in the mysterious Deity; we arc fashioned by the hauds of Christ; amid the infinities of creation receiving existence for the Divine glory, we seek our own, and become blots on the universe otherwise so fair; "through" Jesus Christ we become changed, redecme.d ; by him we are led back to God, and see as Jife's supreme object the glory of God, now brought so much nearer to our grasp; and as we reach the dread presence of the Eternal, whence all things come, we lift up our eyes and behold "our Fatber." 'l'his also is •; through Christ." God is the Father of J esns Christ, and Jesus Christ has become our Brother. If Christ be our Brother, his Father is our Father.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 8:13
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The great argument for abstinence. I. ARGUMENTS IN FAVOUR OF ADSTI- NENCE OF'.l'EN RUN UPON SUCH LINES AS THE FOLLOWING :-1. 'l'hat from which we are enjoined to abstain is asserted to be dangerous to ourselves, since we may be led to indulge to excess. Or: 2. ls injurious to oursell'es, physically, morally, or spiritually. Or: 3. Is pure \l'aste, bringing with it no real benefit. Or: 4. Is intrinsically wrong. II. SucH AHGUMENTS FllEQUEN'l'LY LACK coGEl\CY. 1. The fourth will have no applic[\tion to tht large class of Lhings indifferent in thcruselvc8, and it is generally in oH. VIIL 1-13.] 'l'HE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 277

respect o_f such ~hat ~be war is waged .. 2. The second and third will generally be open to question. 'Ibe difficulty of proof 1s great. Facts, apparently conflicting, will be adduced, and where knowledge is limited and imperfect, the contest is likely to continue the advantage now seemingly being on one side and then on the other. 3. The firs;, seldom carries conviction, since every man deems it an impossibility for him to fall. Every one else may be weak, but ,ve are certainly strong. The argument a.~ainst often acts a.s a temptation, for when human nature is warned of peril it often deli<Thts to show how brave and steadfast it can be. "' III. THE APOSTOLIO ARGUMENT. 1. The apostle enlarges the view so that others ar~ included as well as ourselves. Abstinence is not for ourselves alone, sometimes not for ourselves at all, but for our fellows. "Look not every man on his own things, but also on the thin)!s of others." Whether we realize it or not, we always decide for moro than one. ,ve are units, but united units. We cannot legislate merely for that little area which we ourselves occupy. 2. The apostle recognizes the influence or example. Mentally, we instantly assent to this; practically, we generally deny it. Our words are a spider's web; our acts are a cable. Men do what we show them, not what we tell them. And we cannot persuade men that we are strong and that they are weak ; they will believe the opposite with ve~y little persuasion. Men are like sheep: though the shepherd calls and the dog barks, 1f one sheep leads the way the others will follow, though it be over a precipice. 3. 'l'he apostle assorts the obligation of self-sacrifice for the welfare of others. That which is "indifferent" becomes anything rnther than indifferent if our indulgence in it is likely to cause injury to ou-r fellows. \Ve arc not only to think of others, but to deny ourselves for others. Our sacrifice will often seem very small indeed compared with their possible loss. Here is an argument which will stand where many others fall. It has special force for Christians. (1) They have a great example of self-sacrifice in their Master. They are to imitate him. "He saved others; himself he cannot save." He "gave himself for us." 'l'he apostle seems to suggest a comparison of Christ's sacrifice with the sacrifice which be desire<l the Corinthians to make. Christ died to save men : you are called npon to ~acrifice what that men may not fall away from salvation: how little compared with how much! And to those not making the required sacrifice : Christ died to save the weak brother; you, to gratify your appetite, are causing him to perish. (2) They havo a more impressive view of the issues involved in the fall of a fellow-creature. (3) 'l'heir non-nbstineuce may be a sin against a fellow-Christian (ver. 11). The fall may be, not of an unbeliever, but of a brother, associated in Christi:l.n fellowship and service. And thus be (4) a sin against the brethren (vcr. 12); against the Church, bringing scandal and disgrace through a brother's fall. And also (5) a sin against Christ (vcr. 1:}). For Christ an<l Christians a.re one-he the Head and they the members. (6) They have in their ears certain suggestive utterances of their Master's; such as, "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me" (M:ltt. xxv. 40); and, "Whoso shall offend [' cause to stumble,' as in text] one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea" (Matt. xviii. 6).-H.

Vcrs. 1-13.-0n the eating of sac1·ifices offered to idols; liberty and expediency. Another of those questions which troubled the Christian community at Corinth comes up hero for consideration. 'l'o understand the difficulties connected with it we must bear in mind that the religious worship of the pagans entcreJ. largely into their social life. 'l'he victims offered in sacrifice to the gods were not entirely consumed on tho altar. A portion went to the priests, and tho remainder was either given to tho poor or sent to tho public market. 'l'hus not only the feasts in the temples, hut also privato meals, were brought into cl0se connection with idolatrous worship; and tho Christians could never be sure that the meat they purchased had not fonncJ. part of a sacrifice. It is easy to sec how this interweaving of religious with social lifo would occasion complications and perplexities as to practical duty. To the Jewish converts the eating of things sacrificed to idols would be an abomination. Among the Gonlilo converts two classes may be discerned. 1. There wero those who had been completely emancipated from their old ideas regarding the heathen divinities. 'l'o their view these divinities were more creatures of the imagination, having no real existence; and accortlingly 2,8 THE FlRST EPISTLE TO THE COlUNTHIANS. [01.1. vm. 1-13.

\liry felt tbemseh-es quite free to partake of the sacrificial flesh when set before them. :l. There were those who could not get rid of the idea that au idol was a reality, and that consequently everything connected with the system they had abandoned was 1•olluted. Thus the question became an important one, and the decision of it hau an interest, not only for the Church at Corinth, but also for other Churches where the same difficulties had arisen (comp. Rom. xiv.). But it may be asked-Had this matter not been already settled by the council at Jerusalem (Acts xv.)? The apostle himself was present on that occasion, and we naturally ask why he does not simply refer to the Jerusalem decree, instead of proceeding to give a judgment of his own in some respects opposed to it. 'l'he answer is to be found in a ricrht view of the o-rounds on which that decree proceeded, which were grounds of expediency. The "'Gentile converts were enjoined to abstain from things sacrificed to idols, out of regard to the feelings of the Jewish converts among whom they were located. But this reason did not hold good in a Gentile community like Corinth; and consequently the whole subject had to be considered on its merits and in view of the altered circumstances. The question in itself is no longer a living question for the Church, but there emer"e in connection with it great abiding principles which never lose their value. "' I. KNOWLEDGE AND LOVE. The apostle prefaces his treatment of the question- " concerning things sacrificed to idols,'' by a statement regarding the relative value of knowledge and love. 1. Knowledge by itself puffeth up. Knowledge without love inflates the mind with conceit. Take the knowledge of God. You may read what is written on the pages of nature and of Holy Scripture, so as to know a good deal about him; but if there be no out.going of heart towards him, you do not really know him. "\'i'hat you have learned of God will lead to a false exaltation, inasmuch as you rest iu it as sufficient instead of advancing to a personal acquaintance with him. Or take the case in hand. 'l'he knowledge of the nullity of idols led many of the Corinthians to think themselves superior to their brethren, who could not shake themselves clear of the notion that an idol had a real existence. They were filled with conceit, which, being unternpered by love to others, led them to please only themselves. 2. Love leads to true lcnowledge and true tdification. The way to knowledge is through love. This is true of the knowledge of God. "If any man loveth God, the sarne is known ot him" (ver. 3). "Every one that loveth is begotten of God and knoweth God. He that loveth not k.noweth not God; for God is love" (1 John iv. 7, 8). Love gives itself away to the object beloved, opens out the nature to receive impressions, and puts all it has at the service of the loved one. Love to God brings us near to him, and gives us experience of bis gracious dealing, while he in turn opens himself to us. It is only where mutual love exists that there is a mutual revelation of heart to heart; and this holds good, with necessary limitations, of our relation to Goel.. \Ve know hint only in proportion as we love him, and even his knowledge of us turns upon love. "The Lord knowetb them that are his" (2 Tim. ii. 19), in a way that be knows _no others. Our knowledge of God is more correctly bis knowledge of us; for all we can know of him here is but the alphabet of that more perfect knowledge which comes with perfect love (comp. eh. xiii. 12). Now, the knowledge tha~ co~1es ~hrough love is not an empty thing, puffing up the soul as a bubble, but a sol1u thmg, imparting strength and stability.. It builds up the spiritual temple within with the stones of truth. The lesson is-You can know God only by loving him, and the measure of your love will be the measure of your knowledge. 3. Conceit of one's knowledge is a sure evidence of ignorance. The man who is proud of what he knows has no adequate view of the greatness of the object. The more we real_ly know !h~ more humble do we become. This is true of secular knowledge, but especially of D1vme knowledge. The glimpses we get of God lay us in the dust. He who is puffed up because he has gathered a few pebbles on the shore has never looked out on the great ocean of truth. II. Tim LIBERTY THAT COMES THROUGH KNOWLEDGE. (Vers. 4-6.) Heturning now to the question in hand, the apostle shows how the faith of the enlightened Christian suggests a ready answer. 1. Tl1e idols which the heathen worship are mere noueneities. Their so-called gods, with which they have filled the heaven and the. earth, havo no real existence. There is no Jupiter no Mars, no Venus. They ure simply creatures of the imagination, having nothing ~orresponding to them in the unive_rs_e. This view of the pagan divinities finds frequent expression in the prophets, who ridicule them as <:H. vm. 1-13.] THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE COltINTHIANS. 279

mere vanities (comp. Isa. xliv. 9; Jer. x. 3; Ps. cxv. 4). How melancholy a picture -does this present of the condition of those who know not the true God! Men must worship, and so strong is this impulse that they first create the objects of worship and then bow down before them. It is the blind groping of the human mind after the Most High-a creature, ,vith dreamy recollections of a lost glory, stretching out suppliant hands towards a silent heaven. 2. There is but one living and true God. This is the Christian's simple creed. (1) Instead of "gods many," "to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we unto him." 'l'h!s Supreme Being is the Creator and Primal Source of all things, our Father in heaven, for whose glory we exist. This is the fundamental doctrine on which all true religion rests, and which at once takes the ground from pagan polytheism. It also strikes against all modern idolatries which are practised in Christian lands: hero-worship, mammon-worship, etc. (2) Instead of "lords many," there is" one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, aud we through him." There is but one Governor of the universe, into whose hands all power has been committed, Jesus the Messiah, by whose agency all things were created, and in whom we are made new creatures. This is the second article of our holy faith. Instead of the endless series c,f p:ods and demigods, who were supposed to hold sway over different parts of the universe, "there is one God, one Mediator also between God and men, himself man, Christ Jesus" (1 Tim. ii. 5). 3. From this the inference is plain that eating or not eating of t!tings offered to idols is a matter of indifference. If au idol has 110 real existence, it cannot defile that which is presented to the image in the temple. The flesh which formed part of a sacrifice is neither better nor worse on this account, and may be used without scruple. Thus the enlightened Christian is freed from the entanglement of such petty questions, which belong to the bondage of legalism rather than the liberty that is in Christ. How important is a full acquaintance with Divine truth! How good it is to be free from prejudice, and to receive the whole truth as to our standing in Jesas Christ! But such knowledge is dangerous if it stands alone. III. LIMITATIONS TO LIDERTY ARISING FROM C1mISTIAN LOVE. (Vers. 7-13.) An enlightened view of the nature of heathen divinities delivers the Christian from questions as to the lawfulness of eating what had first done duty as a sacrifice; but all Christians are not thus enlightened. '!'here were at Corinth believers, converts from heathenism, who could not get rid of the idea that the idols they had formerly worshipped had a real existence, and who consequently regarded the flesh used in sacrifice as polluted. A due regard to the case of these weaker brethren will modify the use of their Christian liberty by the stronger. 1. Consider their case. '!'heir conscience was weak, inasmuch as it could not rise to the conviction that an idol is nothing, and was therefore troubled with scruples ll.'l to the lawfulness of partaking of a thing sacrificed to an idol. Hence such persons could not eat without defiling their conscience, i.e. without the feeling that they had done wrong. This carries with it principles that have an important bearing upon Christian ethics. It is wrong for a man to do what his conscience tells him is wrong, or what it does not clearly approve. 'l'he thing in itself may be good, but if you are in doubt about it you are thereby debarred from doing it. The dictates of conscience are al ways imperative, but with this there goes the duty of seeing that conscience is instructed. Comp. Rom. xiv. 23, where Paul is treating of the same subject: "He that doubteth is condemnecl if he eat, because he eateth not of faith ; and whatsoever is not of faith is sin." Apply this to some forms of amusement, doubtful practices in trade, extravagant living, etc. It is not enough to plead the example of others, if you are in doubt regarding Lheir rightness. "Let each man be fully assured in his own mind." Do not disregard the faithful voice within your bosom, even when it speaks in whispers. 2. The eating of such things has no religious significance. Neither the use nor the abstinence from use commends us to God or affects our standing before him. To abstain from eating for the sake of weak brethren is not tc summder any spiritual benefit. It is a matter of ludilfercnce. "The king,lom of God is not eating and drinking" (Rom. xiv. 17). Observe the class of matters to which alone the apostle's reasoning is meant to apply. They must be such !lS involve no religious principle-cases where accommodation to the weakness of others does not imply the sacrifice of truth or duty. In such cases we are free to consider the condition of our brethren, and to regulate our conduct by a regard to them. 3. Tlic strong must not use their libei·ty so as to put a stumbling-block in the path of the weak. 280 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORIN'l'HIANS. [cH. vm. 1-13.

If a weak brother, who had doubts about. the eating of sacrificial flesh, should by the example of another be emboldened to ent also, in that case he would siu and his conscience be defiled. The more enlightened Christian would thus be the occasior, -of stumbling to his brother, bringing him into danger of perishing altogether, and would thereby sin against Christ who died for him. Rather than do anythin" that might lead to this result, the apostle declares, "If meat maketh my brotl~er to stumble," etc. This is the principle of Ch1·istian expediency, of which Paul is the great exponent, and which enters so largely into the believer's practical life. It has its root in loYe, which leads us to" bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal. vi. 2). It is an outcome of that spirit of self-denial which dwelt in him. "Nmv we that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselve~. Let each one of us please his neighbour for that which is good unto ed!fy(ng. For Christ also !:'leased not hi_mscl~" (Rom. xv. 1-3). In applyiu'g this prmc1plc, note: (1) It applies only to thmgs m themselves inditferent. Where true Christian libert) was i~ danger, ~auJ re~nsed to yield (Gal. ii. 3-5). (2) It is not to be confounded with mere tnne-servmg or man-pleasing. (3) Each Christian must judge for himself how this principle requires him to act in special circumstances. Total abstinence from strong drink for the sake of others is a good example of its application.-B.

entries.title: 1CO 8:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-K71owledqe and love. There is a great difference between being" puffed up" and being" built up." The one implies something pretentious and plausible, but hollow and unreal. It means show without substance, size without solidity, inflation withou\ real enlargement. The other implies the gradual accumulation of substantial materials, on a firm basis, to some useful and enduring result. Now, the apostle would have the Corint.bian Christians determine the question of personal duty concerning attendance at feasts in honour of idols, or eating of meat offered in sacrifice, on far other ground than any supposed sagacity of their own. All, no <loubt, had" knowledge." But there is a higher criterion of judgrnent than this. Love is a better guide in such matters than knowledge. In all these things let it be that delicate regard for the feelings and interests of others which love implies, rather than any :ibstrnct ideas about their own liberty, that determines their conduct. Hence the broad principle," Knowledge puffeth up, love edifieth." Uonsider- 1. THE KKOWLEDGE THAT PUFFETH UP. The case contemplated is one in which the purely intellectual element in the determination of moral questions is divorced from right feeling. It is a knowledge ideal and speculative, not vital and spiritual. The knowledge of the theologian, the logician, the casuist; not that of the man whose reason and conscience and heart are alike alive unto God. The characteristic of this knowledge is that it makes men vain, conceited, self-asserting, "thinking more highly of themselves than they ought to think." A true knowledge of the things of God has no such tendency as this. "lf a man thinketh that he kuoweth anything," etc. (ver. 2). Real knowledcre in the spiritual sphere is beyond the reach of one who is destitute of humility and Jove. Even in the realm of purely secular science, true knowledge does not make men vain. The lives of such men as Newton, Herschel, Faraday, etc., illustrate the truth of this. They were men of lowly, childlike spirit. They stood reverently, as with bared head and unsandalled feet, before the infinite mystery of the unive~se. It is the novice, the mere tyro in learning, the mnn of shallow thougct and narrow view, who is proud of his attainments, dogmatic and self-asserting. How much more will it be so in matters purely spiritual, belonging to a region into which our science cannot climb! Take Sr. Paul himself as an example. While he moved within the narrow circle of Jewish traditio11 and prejudice, he was probnbly the very type of personal vanity. His Pharisnic pride was not only that of logal blamelessness, but of theological culture. Had he not sat at the feet of Gamaliel? Who could teach Lim what he did not know? It is a porlrait of himself that he paints in those halfsarcastic words: "If thou bearest the name of a Jew, and restcst upon the Law," etc. (Ilom. ii. 17-20). But when the light from hea\·en shone upon him, how was the loftiness of his pride laid low I He "became a fool that he might be wise." Moreover, thi~ mere theoretic knowledge is as profitless in its effect on others as it is to one's self. It becomes disputatious, "gen<lering strifes about words," etc. '!'here is no "edifying,.

quality in it. It docs not make men one whit the nobler, purer, more gracious in heart and lifo. It in no way promotes the reign of those Divine principles ot· "righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost," in which the kingdom of GoJ consists. II. 'rHE LOVE THAT BUILDETH UP. Take love here in the highest and broadest sense, as including love to God and love to man. These are but two sirles and aspects of the same affection. It is an essentially religious affection. There are tender sensibilities and generous sentiments which give a natural grace to human character quite apart from all religious thought and feeling. They may prepare the way for the awakening of this Divine affection, but are not to be confounded with it. Only by personal fellowship with Christ can we rise into the atmosphere of a pure, unselfish, all-embracing love like his. Love builds up the temple of God. The separate personality of every Christian, and the complex, many-membered personality of the whole redeemed Church, are the dwellingplace of God, prepared by gradual enlargement and adornment to be the fitting shrine of his glory; and it is.the office of love to promote this process. It is the effective power in the development and perfecting of personal Christian character and social Christian life. In confirmation of this, think of it: 1. As the essential spirit of all other graces. It gives them their highest, richest quality. It is the life, the beauty, the strength, the very soul, of them all. Consider the position love occupies in the circle of the Divine attributes. Truth, justice, purity, goodness, etc., are attributes of the Divine character; but "God is love." A similar position does love occupy in the ideal character of his true children. \Ve are such poor, fragmentary, distorted reflections of the Divine beauty that even in the best of us this truth is too often obscured. Personal Christianity assumes many forms-the gentle and the severe, the reserved and the demonstrative, the meditative and the practical, the punctilious and the free; but this is the essential spirit of all its forms. It is true to the Divine ideal only so far as this spirit breathc3 through all its moods. 2. As the bond of Christian unity. Keenness of spirit11CLl insight, zeal for truth, fidelity to conscience, may of themselves have a separatin:-:; effect; but love draws and cements men together in a real fellowship of life. Differcncc,i in opiuion, modes of thought, ecclesiastical usage, etc., become of comparatively small account, "so love at heart prevail." 3. As an incentive to all real Christian activity. It is the distinction of Christiauitv as a Divine method of moral culture that it bases practical and social virtue on this foundation, casts it freely on the prompting anrl sustaining power of love. "Love is the end of the commandment, the fulfilling of the Law." Get your soul filled with love, and you will never want for an effectual motive to all noble living. .As the materials of the building arrange themselves and rbe into their finished form in obedience to the thought and will of the nrchite~t; as the notes fall, as if by an instinct of their own, into their dne place according to the inspiration of the musician; as the words flow in rhythmic cadence in answer to the mood of the poet's genius; as the grass anrl the flowers and the corn grow by the spontaneous energy of the creative and formative mind that animates them all ;-so will you rear for yourself the structure of a beautiful and useful Christian life, if your heart is filled with love. 4. As the mightiest of all instruments of ble.1si11g to others. By the sweet constraint of his love Christ wins the hearts of those for whom he died. Dy the almightiness of his love he will ultimately conquer tho workl ano. build up that glorious temple to his praise-a re,leemc<l humanity, a creation ransomed from the curse. Let his love be the inspiration of our life, and we wield a moral force akin to his; we share his work, his triumph, and his joy.-W.

Ver. !.-Knowledge and love. Revised Version, "Knowledge puffeth up, but lovu cdifieth ; " Greek, "buildeth up." This remark is made at the outset of the consideration of a new topic. It embodies a principle upon which Christians may safely act in any of the practical difficulties that may arise. The precise matter which engaged the apostle's attention only concerns us historically. It hardly represents any kiml of difficulty that is likely to arise in modern society. "In Corinth and other cities me11t was offered for sale which had been used for sacrificial purposes in the heathen temples, having been sold to the dealers by the priests, who received a large sharo of the sacrifices fur themselves, or by the individuals who offered them, anti had more remaining of their own share than they could use themselves. Thus a Christian ·282 TIIE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE COIUNTHIANS. [cH, vm. 1-13.

might unconsciously cat of meat, either a.t the house of a. friend or by purchasing it himself in the public shambles, which ha.d been previously brought in contact by sacrificial use with an idol." Exactly how to trea.t such a matter it wa.s not easy to say. Some had no compunctions in partaking of such food. Others had very troublesome scruples; and only too readily contentions might arise over such a. sornll and insignificant question. Some would say strongly," We know that an idol is !.!stl,i1,g, and so he cannot defile the meat." Such persons would be likely to laugii. to scorn the feebleness and superstitions (as they would call them) of the weaker brethren. Their knowledge would "puff them up," and make them positive and inconsiderate; whereas the " charity " l':hich "endnreth all things, and thinketh no evil," would make them gentle and ,ar.sidcrate, ready to put their own ideas aside if pressing them unduly seemed to offend the weaker brethren. This is the point to which ◊\!! attention is -directed. I. KxowLEDGE TEXDS TO PUFF UP. This is a fact, attested by the experienc_e of all ages, and well within our own observation at the present time. There is often a positi,·eness, a dogmatism, and a contempt of others about persons who have a little knowlc<lge, which may properly call for an apostle's reproof. W~ must, however, remember that fulness of knowledge is almost always attended with humility, considerateness, and cheerful readiness to serve. It is a little knowledge that has the injurious influence. A man may pride himself on the limited pond in his own grounds, but he must feel humbled when be stands before the boundless ocean, and knows that powers are too small and life too short for him to exhaust the infinite stores. But the point which St. Paul helps us to impress is that knowledge puffs up because it keeps a man thinking about himself. It is always what I have read, what I know; and the egotistic sphere is the most dangerous for any of us to dwell in. "Look not every man on bis own things, but every mau also on the things of others." II. LovE TENDS TO BUILD UP. This may be applied both to the man and to the Church. Seli-seeking and self-worship so engross a man's attentions that the interest of others cannot be served, little things are easily magnified into difficulties, and dissension and dispute are fostered. But "love," "charity," cares more for others than for self; concerns itself about the general well-being; asks about everything-what influence it will have for good or for evil; and puts strong restraints upon personal feelings and preferences, if pressing them against the opinions of others would cause contention. Love is set upon "edifying," upon "culturing," upon "up-builu.ing," upon preserving that "peace" in which alone souls can thrive and grow. So St. Paul earnestly urges that loue ought to rule and decide in all our Church relations and practical diflicu1L1es.-R. ~'-

entries.title: 1CO 8:3
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-E11owing God, and being known of God. The construction of this sentence jg peculiar. We expect the apostle to say that the man who loves God is alone the man who can be f&id to know God. There is, however, in his words the under-thought -of the identity between knowing God and being known of him. Olshausen says, "'l'hc knowiedge of God presupposes the being known of him: the soul will not vivify wii,n life from above until God has drawn nigh." It may be noticed that St. Paul, in "deal:ncr with inqwsitive and argumentative people like the Corinthians and Galatians, takes ca~e to invert the phrase, so as to exciude all glorifying on the part of man." 'J'be statements of the Apostle John, in 1 Epist. iv. 7, 8, should he compared with this. Fixing attention on the two terms, "knowing God;" "being known. of God," observe- !. How THESE ADE RELATED. Are they two parallel things, or does the one follow after and result from the other? If we take this latter view, which of the two comes first? Show that the lcnowledge of God is an impossibility for unaided man. This impossibility is shown (1) from the facts of man's depmvcd and distorted nature; (2) from the statements of Holy Scripture, "No man, by searching, can find out God," etc.; and (3) from the actual experiences of men, as individuals or ns nations. Four tho~sand years of experiment lefc God still virtually the "unknown God." God must graciously come near to us, re,€al himself to us, manifestly concern himself for us, and show that he knows us, or we can never get to apprehend him. And this he has done in Uie manffes~a,ion of his Son. And this he does still in a gracious inrlividual rc~pouse to oH. vm. 1-13.J 'rI:lE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 283

the open and trusting soul. If we arc known of God, taken into his special regard, and favour; if he "lilts upon us the light of his countenance,"-then we can be said to know him. But the knowledge comes alwaya by Divine condescension to us, not by the unaided efforts of our intellect. Our Lord put this truth under another figure when he said," No man can come unto me except the Father which hath sent me draw him." '£hose whom God knows, in the seuse of" approves," "reveals himself to," are those alone who, in any high, proper, spiritual sense, can be said to "know God." II. WHEREON BOTH THESE A.RE BASED. "If any man love God." Our best knowledge comes by love, not by intellect. '!'he mutual knowledge of husband and wife, of mother and child, come not by mental study of each other, but by the relations and revealings of love. And so alone can we know our heavenly Father. Let him come near to us in gracious communions, and our hearts will surely find out how precious •he is. " We shall see him as he is." Bodily vision will 11ot be needed, for souls can see. Intellect may stand back, for love can see and feel and know. It will be observed that the love of which St. Paul here speaks is seen, not on its sentimental but on its practical side. It is the charity which takes due account of the frailties of others, and acts with the desire to help them. Charity is the varied expression of the love cherished in the heart; somewhat as obedience is the expression of faith. Faith is seen in good works, and love is seen in charity. John 'l'auler, the mystic, suggestively says, '' Rightly is God called the 'Master of love,' for he rewards love; he rewards with love; and he rewards out of love." See the Revised Version on Luke ii. 14, "On earth peace among men in whom he is well pleased," or "men of good will "-of love, or charity. Impress how earnestly we should seek that disposition and character which will bring God near to us, and so give to us the saving apprehension of him. "We love him because he first loved us." And we can judge of our love to God by crur feeling concerning our brother; for" If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar;" "And this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth Go<l love his brother also."-R. T.

entries.title: 1CO 8:5
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Not gods, but God. Two primary and foundation truths of religion were committed to the keeping of the Jews as a nation. They were revealed to, and fully apprehended by, Abraham, and were the reason for his separation from his polytheistic surroundings in the country of the Chaldees, and for the subsequent remarkable isolation of his descendants in the small, compact, yet central country of Palestine. Those two truths were-the unity and the spirituality of Goel. "God is one;" "God is a Spirit." It is the first of these truths which St. Paul here reaffirms, in view of the pagan conception of many deities and divinities; and there can be no doubt concerning the clear-cut testimony which Christianity makes to the truth of the Divine unity. '£here is only one God, whose favour and reconciliation we have to seek, and whose claim to obedience and service we must meet. It is true that l\lohammcdanism also affirms the unity of God, but it adds the questionable statement, "and Mahomet is his l)rophet." Christianity does indeed declare that there arc " three persons in one God;" and that" Jesus Christ is the Son of God;" but both these truths are to be held, and can be held, consistently with our faith in the Divine unity. Vve havo to avoid the perils of tritheism, and of conceptions of the divinity of Christ which fall short of his .essential Deity; for "the Word was God;" "God manifest in the flesh." In the verses before us we have- I. THE COMMON NOTION OF GODS AND LORDS. "As there be gods many, and lords many." Paganism peopled earth and sea and sky with clifTercnt orders of divinities, -and imagined gods presiding over mountains, streams, and flowers; over flood and pestilence and fire; over virtue and over vice; over families and nations. lllustrato by the impressions made upon St. Paul when he first entered Athrns. The placo seemed to him crowded with idols," given over to idolatry." There was a. regular hierarchy; and probably a dim notion of one supreme god to whom the rest were subordinate, but as these lesser 0"Ods and iords stood in direct and close relations with men, it was inevitable that tliey should get all the worship. Illustrate from what is observed in heathen lands now; especially where heathenism is associated with iearning and civilization, as in India.. Show what complicated social questions arise in that coun.try out of the conflicting chums of the multitudinous gods and lords; and the 284 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. vm. 1-13.

painful uncertainty which men in idolatrous countries must feel as to whether they ha,·e propitiated the ri_qht god, or left an offended one still to executo his vengeance. In cont,.ast with elaborate heathenism, the worship and service of the one God is simple- and sati fyin~. Fear God, and there is no one else to fear, II. ·~·HE CHRISTIAN NOTION OF "GoD" AND "LORD." The two words may be taken to include the Divine Being as an Object of WOl'ship, and as our practical Ruler. Our God is at once the highest Being we can ccnceive, who ri"htly claims our reverence• and the Yery centre of all authority, to whose will we ~ust wholly bow. But tb; two terms may be used to indicate the oneness, yet distinction, of the Father and the Son. The term "lord" suggests the immediacy of Christ's relations to us, So the word "God" may stand for the essential being; and the word "Lord" for the mediatorial being. 1. The essential being-God. Four points are here noticed by St. Paul. (1) God_ is one. (2) He !s ~he Father-that rela!ion being t~e most suitable for repre- senting him, because 1t includes the personal interest of his love for each one of his. creatures, which such words as" King,"" Ruler,"" Judge,"" Moral Governor," do not. (3) All things are of him. He is the one and only Creator of thincrs and of nien. And ( 4) we are witnesses for him, who are bound to hold firmly, and sho~ forth fully, this first truth of the one Father-God. 2. His mtdiatorial being. Under this term we appre- hend the one God as the Lord Jesus Christ, and wo are to see that he is practically (1) our present Lord and Huler; (2) our only Mediator in his manifestation of himself in our flesh and upon our earth; and (3) our Christian standin~ and Christian hope are only in him and by him. Fully embracing this truth of the Divine unity, wo shall be wholly delivered from the fear of offending the" gods many or lords many," whether they be fellow-men or imagined divinities.-R. T.

entries.title: 1CO 8:9
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-0ur dealings with weak brethren. Our liberty may become a stumbling- block to others, and against this we must be constantly on our guard. There will always be around us some "weak brethren." 1. They may be intellectually weak, really unable to grasp more than the simplicities of the truth, and readily thinking that what they can neither understand nor appreciate must be error. 'l'here is also such a thing as mental bias, which prevents men from appreciating or receiving more than some particular side of truth. And this mental bias is often the affliction of men who are otherwise intelligent; and it becomes the occasion of much religious bigotry. 2. They may be weak in conscience. Instead of firmly attesting what is right and what is wrong, tbeir conscience may only pre.sent scruples and questions and doubts. It is the same thing to say that they have little power of decision; and feel restless and uncertain, and weakly full of fears, when a decision is made. 3. They may be weak through the relics of old habits. A man cannot immediately separate himself from all his surroundings; and it was very difficult for Gentile Christians to shake off their heathen notions. Missionaries now, in heathen land~, are gravely perplexed by tho lingering sentiments and habits of their converts. And in Corinth many could not get out of the idea that meat offered to an idol must be defiled and unfit for their eating as Christians. So it may be shown that there are" weak brethren" with us still; some who are offended with higher truths, which they are intellectually unable to reach; others who have scruples about what is permissible to Christians in social life, and yet others who fix narrow limits to the observance of the sabbath, and other details of Christian conduct. Now, St. Paul lays down some of the principles on which we should deal with these "weak brethren." I. 'l'HE PRINCIPLE OF FIRMNESS, More especially if our brother's weakness in any way imperils the truth. Concessions to our weaker brethren may go to the fullest lengtb so long as they concern only oor personal relations with them. But we may concetl nothing if our brother's weakness puts in peril vital truth. Then wo must be firm and stand our ground, and claim our full liberty to receive whatever truth God may be pleased to give us. And it is even found, in practical life, that our brother's weakness in matters of detail is best met by a firm and intelligent resistance. We need to be especially careful that our dealings with our brethren shall in no way foster and encourage their weakness. Modes of keeping sabbath, or relations of Uhristians to public amusements, will furnish necessary illustrations, 11. 'l'rrn PRINCIPLE OF HELPFULNESS; wherever we stand in such relations to th0

"weak brethren" n.s may give us a power of influence upon them. If we condescend to them, it can only be that we may lift them out of their weakness into strength. Such helpful influence we may exert (1) by direct teachings; (2) by our own personal example. Others may see that what they call "our Ii bert_y" in no way injures our spiritual life, and seeing that may best help them to correct their mistakes. III. 'l'HE PRL'fCIPLE OF SELF-SACRIFICING CHARITY. Actually depriving ourselves of pleasures, and what we think to be both permissible and good things, in order that we may be no hindrance or injury to others. lllustrate in the case with which St. Paul is dealing here; and show bow many good Christians nowadays abstain from such things as balls and theatre~ because they are anxious not to set a stumbling-block in the way of others. Our practical difficulties in life apply to things indifferent; and in such matters it is proper that we should regulate our conduct by the effects which it may have on others. 'l'he true Christian spirit would lead us to say, "Rather let me suffer by abstaining from what I should enjoy, and could do without any personal injury, than let my brother suffer, either by the judgrnent which be would form of my doings, or by his imitating my example to his own serious hurt."-R T.

entries.title: 1CO 8:13
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The law of Christian self-restraint. No more perplexing questions are presented to the Christiau than those which deal with the limitations of his Christian liberty. Were the Christian man alone in the world, or were he assured that his actions would in no way influence those around him, there are many personal enjoyments in which he could freely indulge, and he would have little call to selfrnstraint. He would at least be a "law unto himself," and need make no laws for himself upon consideration of others. But none of us can live under such conditions. \Ve are not only a "spectacle unto men and angels," but every act of ours beam influence on some one, affecting others either for good or for evil. And this fact we must take into solemn account. The relationships of life arc main sources of ou,· pleasure, but they brini:: us all our responsibilities, and, though our couduct in all essential things is to be determined only by what is right, in all matters that are le!'t to our decision we are bound to consider how others will regard our conduct; and we should eveu take into account how they may misunderstand and misrepresent, an,l so make mischief out of our actions. It is true that "the fear of man bringet h a snare," but it is also true that the love of man, and sincere desire for the blessing of others, will always help us to form good judgments concerning what is prndent and advimble. Sincere hearts are full of anxiety lest, by any personal indulgences or need loss displays of superior moral strength, they should "sin against the weaker brethren." It should bo observed that upon things doubtful God lays down no direct rnles. The Christian man is expected to make his own wise laws of self-restraint. If he be sincero r.nd earnest he will make for himself two supreme laws. I. 'l'HE LAW OF CHARITY TOWARDS OUR DROTIIER. '!'hat is, in every disputable or doubtful case he will give the advantage to his brother, and net taking iuto account even his weaknesses, It should be clearly understood: I. 'l'hat when, in a spirit of charity, a Cbristian man puts himself under strong restraints, he does not alter his views of the weakness of his brother's difficulty or of the possibility of his own actiug or enjoyiug without personal injury. 'l'he very point of his Christian virtue is that, while recognizing the rightness of the thing for himself, he refrains for the sake of others. 'l'here would be no virtue in his self-restraint if he changed his opiuion as to the rightness of the act. He holds his own opinion, but in Christian love he yichls to tho opinion of another. 2. We may also see that, when tho Christian puts himself under restraint for the sake of a weak brother, it is that he may p;ain inHuence upon him tbat shall lift him up out of his weakness. It can be no part of Christian duty to condescend to a brother's weakness, and leave him weak. lf St. Paul rcfrninc,l from eating the meat that had been offered to idols, it was iu the hope of presently getting the weak brethren to see that, since an idol is "nothing at all," he cannot defile any meat. Our charity rloes not conccm the particular case, but the entire 1vell-being of our weaker brother. 3. It may further be shown that tho restraints under which the Christian man puts himself, by the persuasions of his brotherly love, may be severe and trying at first, but become easier at'tcr a while, and will often turn i.uto blessing for himself at the last. 'l'his may bo cfl1cicntly illustrated in the ea,,• 286 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [ea. 1x. 1-:n.

of a man giving up all alcoholic drink for the sake of helping a brother who is in peril f~om the enticement~ of the drink-demon. If he be of a social disposition, it may cost bun a great deal to ~1ve up long-settled habits, but he may prove, in both health and means, that the self-restraint of Christian charity can become a blcssin" to him who manifests it, as well as to him for whose sake the sacrifices have be;n made. God ever graciously secures to us the rewards of right-doing, and makes "charity twice blessed." II. THE LAW OF LOY AT.TY TO CHRIST. Our one ~upreme purpose must be to serve him, and he has told ns that what is done unto "the least of the brethren" is "done unto him." ,ve think that, in the greatness of our loyalty, we would do anythin" for Christ, and put ourselves under any kind of restraints, were he really here with ~sin the flesh. But he puts our loyalty under a severe test when he says, "Do to your weak brother, do for your weak brother's sake, just what you would have done for me." ,ve think we could go without meat, or put away drink, at once and for ever, if Jesus wished. It is Christ's wish that is expressed to us when we are led to seethat our ''.liberty" is injuring a brother; and our Lord counts it loyalty to him when we restram ourselves !or a brother's sake. St. Paul makes this plain. To offend against a weak brother, to refuse proper limitations of our own liberty when such limitations would help a brother, is to sin against Christ, even against Christ whoat the uttermost self-sacrifi~c-even died that he might save and sanctify the weak brother. Conclude by showmg that the appeal may be made to us, in relation to this matter, which is made by the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews in a more general way, "Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin." Jn how few of us the self-restraints of Christian charity can be said yet to have reached the sublime heights of self-sacrifice !-R. 'l'.

entries.title: 1CO 9:1–21
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-T/ie leading characteristics of a truly great gospel minister. "Am I not an apostle? am I not free?" etc. 'l'aking these verses as a whole, they illustrate some of the leading characteristics of a truly great gospel minister, and I offer the following remarks:- I. 'l'he greater the minister of Christ, the MORE INDEPENDENT OF CEREMONIAL RESTilIC- TIONS. Paul was one of the greatest, if not the greatest, ministers of Christ that ever existed. He was an apostle, and had "seen Christ "-a qualification that distinguished him as a minister from all, but eleven others, that ever lived. Besides this, his natural and acquired endowments placed him in the very first rank of reasoners, scholars, and orators. He was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, etc. llut see how this great minister regarded the mere conventionalities of religious society. "Am I not an apostle? am I not free?" He refers in all probability to the preceding chapter, which treats of the eating of meat offered to idols, and concerning which he says, "If meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the -world standcth." As if he had said, "I am free to eat tbat meat, and free to reject it ; I am not bonnd by any conventional custom or ceremonial law, for I am' e.n apostle.'" Now, it may be laid <lawn as a universal truth that, the greater a gospel minister, the more independent of ceremonies. Indeed, the greater the man, always the more independent he is of forms, fashions, customs. Hezekiah called that which his countrymen worshipped "Nehush- tau "-a piece of brass. Cromwell called that glittering insii(Ilia of authority on the table of the Bouse of Commons, and at which most of the members, perhaps, trembled with .awe, a "bauble." 'l'homas Carlyle called all the pageantry of office o.nd the glitter of wealth "shams." Burns called the swaggering lordling a "coof." How much more would a man like Paul-who possessed that spirit of Christ which gave him an insight auto tbe heart of things-look down, not merely with indifference, but with contempt, ·Upon all that the world considered great and grand I 'l'he more Christly inspiration (I man has, the more he will discern degradation on thrones and pauperism in mansions. A famous French preacher began his funeral address over the coflin of his sovereign with these words, "'l'here is nothing great but God." 'l'o the man whose soul is .::barged with the great ideas of God, all the distinctions amongst men are only as the distinctions existing among the various bubbles on the flowing stream. Some are a little larger than others, some are tinged by the sunbeam, and some arc pallid in the shade; but all have the same common nature, and all, breaking into the abyss, are lost for ever. "Am I not free?" says Paul. A grand thing this, to be free from all tho conventionalities of society and the ceremonies of religion. What cared Elijah for the kings of Syria, or Israel, or Judah? Nothing. Agrippa trembled before the moral majesty of Paul, even in chains. Oh for such ministers as Paul in this ago of hypocrisies and forms l 11. The greater the minister of Christ, the HIGHER THE SERVICE HE RENDEns TO SOCIETY. "What high service did this great minister St. Paul render to the members of ,the Corinthian Church! "Are not ye my worK iu the Lord? . . . 'l'he seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord." Ye are, as far as ye arc Christians," my work." I converted you; I turned you away from idols to the one true aml living God, from the THE FmST EPISTLE TO THE COTII~THIANS. [cu. Ix, 1-21.

kingdom of Satnn to the kingdom of Chri,t. No work on earth equal to this, "He that cml\"ertelh a sinner from the error of lus ways," etc. This work which I e1Tectc1l in you "~n the Lord," or by the _Lo_rd, is a <lcmonstration of my apostleship. What work agarn, 1 ask, approaches this m grandeur and importance? It is the work of creating men "anew in Christ Jesns;" it is the work of cstablishincr that moral "mpire in the "·orld, which is "righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost." 'l'he man who succeeds in accomplishing tliis work thereby demonstrates the divinity ,!f his ministry. Hence Paul says, "Mine answer to them that do examine me is this." Those that question or deny my apostleship I refer to the spiritual work I have accomplished; "this is my answer," my defence. Truly it might be· said of Paul," No man can do the works that thou doest, except God be with him." The only way by which "·e can prove ourselves true ministers is, not by words, but by spiritual works. III. The grnater the minister of Christ, the MORE INDEPENDENT HE IS OF THE A!\--XMAL EXJOYMENTS OF LIFE. "Ha\'e we not power to eat and to drink? Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas?_" Pau~ claims the privilege to eat and drink as he pleased, and to marry or not accordmg to Ins pleasure, to be a celibate or a benedict. Perhaps some of the mcm bcrs of the Corinthian Church questioned Paul's apostleship because he was not married. Those who belonged to Peter's party-who was a married man-wouM. he likely to say," Paul cannot be an apostle, for Cephas, who is an apostle, has his wife, 11·hom he takes about with him in the prosecution of his mission." And then the "brethren of the Lord," too, they have their wives. Paul's reply to this is virtually," I have the power and the right to all connubial privileges and comforts, the right to feast at banquets, and to form domestic relations; but I forego them, I am independent of them, 1 have higher tastes and sublimer sources of enjoyment, '.For me to live is Christ.' He is the all and in all of my soul." 'l'he more brain and Christly inspira- tion a man has, the less carnal, and the less carnal the more independent of materia'l enjoyments. IV. The greater t'he minister of Christ, the MORE CLAIM HE HAS TO THE TEMPORAL SUPPORT OF THOSE WHOM HE SPIRITUALLY SERVES. The apostle goes on from the sixth to the fonrteenth verse to say that he and Barnabas would be right if they were to for- bear working for their livelihood, and claim their temporal support from those to whom they spiritually ministered. He goes on to indicate several reasons why be had a claim to their temporal support. 1. The general usage of mankind. " Who goeth a warfare any time at his own charges?" etc. He draws three illustrations from human lifu to show the equity of the principle-from the soldier, the agriculturist, and the shepherd. 2. The principle of the Jewish Law. "Say I these things as a man? or saith not the Law the same also?" etc. On a space of hard ground called a threshing-floor the oxen in Jewish times were driven to and fro over the corn thrown there, thus separating the husk from the grain. "God,'' says Matthew Henry, "had therein ordered that the ox Bhould not be muzzled while he was treading out the corn, nor hindered from eating while: he was preparing the corn, for man's use, and treading it out of the car. But this law was not chiefly given out of God's regard to oxen or concern for them, but to teach mankind that all due encourao-ement should be given to those who are employed by us or labourino- for our good, that the labourers should taste of the fruit of their labours.'' "Doth God take care for oxen?" Yes. He enjoined that the mouth of the working ox should not be muzzled, but should have food to eat. Is not man greater than thu ox? And shall he work and be deprived of temporal supplies? 3. The principles of common equity. "If we have sown into you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal thincrs?" 'l'hey had given to them far higher things, infinitely more important than the t;mporal support which they required. He who ~ives to h_is race Divine ideas gives that which alone can secure the progress of humamty, both in temporal and spiritual good. 'l'rue ideas destroy bad institutions and create good ones. 4. Other apostles and their wives were thus supported. " Or I only and Barnabas, have· not we power to forbear working?" ... If others be partakers of this power over you, are not we rather?" This language implies that all the others who worked amongst them obtained their temporal support. Why should not we? Have we done less? Is our authority inferior? 5. The support of the Jewish priesthood. "Do )'0 not kno,v that tbey which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they CII. IX. 1-127.] '!'HE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE cor.rnTI-IIANS.

which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar?" "The first part of the pa8~,1~c refer, to the general principle that the priests who were engaged in the temple se?·vice, were supported from the various offerings which were brought there; and the seconi i clause mure definitely alludes to the particular fact that, when a sacrifice was oITered on .the altar, the sacrificing priests as well as the altar had a share of the animal." 6. The -ordination of Christ. "Even so bath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel" (see Matt. x. 10). "Should live of the gospel," not grow rich on the gospel, but have from it that which is needful for subsistence. Looking at all that Paul says on that question here, and at the immense service that a true· minister renders to society, the conviction cannot be avoided that no man has a stronger claim to a temporal recompense for his labour than a true gospel minister. Albeit nu claims are so universally ignored. "What Churches in these modern times tender to their ministers as an acknowledgment of their service is regarded as a charity rather than a claim. Charity, indeed I Call the money you pay to your butcher, baker, lawyer, doctor, charity; but in the name of all that is just, do not call that charity whic!-: yon tender to the man who consecrates his entire being and time to impart to you the -elements of eternal life. V. 'l'he greater the minister of Christ, the MORE RF.ADY TO SURRENDER HIS CLAnrn TOR THE SAKE OF USEFULNESS. Great as were the claims of Paul, he magnanimously surrenders them all in order to become more useful. He would not feast at banquets, enjoy conjugal life, or take payment for his services, lest his usefulness should be in the I-east impaired. "But I have used none of these things: neither have I written these things, that it should be so done unto me; for it were better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void." I would sooner die than be dependent on you for a livelihood. Grand man! He stood before his congregations and said, "I have coveted no man's silver, or gold, or apparel. Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with rue."
