entries.title: 1CO 9:22
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
- Soul-saving. The great apostle of the Gentiles was a singular man and lived a strange life. Some looking at him pronounced him to. be a fool; others, a madman. He seemed, indeed, strangely destitute of that wisdom which places selfinterest in the front, and incites to the pursuit of position, power, and the praise of men. "When brought to a knowledge of the truth, the future apostle relinquished the course which he had mapped out, and his association with Gamaliel and the great teachers. He commenced with gigantic self-sacrifice: why? He desired to save souls. He became a great traveller-from city to city, town to town, village to village, he went on untiringly: why? To save souls. He underwent extreme sufferings (2 Cor. xi. 24-29)-to save souls. He exposed himself constantly to danger and death-to save 11ouls. With the Jew he banished from his mind all Gentile tendencies-to save the Jew. With the Gentile he severed himself from all Jewish partialities-to save the Gentile. He was willing to be anything or nothing, to do this or that, if by any means he might "save some." Soni-saving had become a master-passion of his soul. He was in the world for it. Everything must be subordinated to it. . I. WHY WAS PAUL so DESIROUS TO SAVE SOULS? He remembered: 1. The value of the soul. Of this he had the deepest conviction. To him the soul of man was the most. e,::. 1x. 1-2i.] THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIA~S. 30fi"

precious thing in the world. Whilst men were seeking to save all other things, be would seek to save this. All other f(ain was as loss compared to the gain of a soul. 2. The fate of the lost soul. He saw the unsaved soul going down, getting further and :further from God, becomin~ viler, ripening for hell. The fearful words of his Master rang loudly in his ears. He believed them, he did not refine them down until they meant nothing. He saw the souls "cast out;" he beard the dread "Depart;" the "weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth" sounded in his heart; and he resolved that, as an instrument in the Divine hand, be would do his utmost to "save some." 3. The future of the saved soul. (1) In this life. Tending upwards; becoming purified; increasing in joy, peace, usefulness; indissolubly united to God. (2) In the next life. "With Christ." 'l'he fulness of joy. Every soil of sin removed. All powers becomfo~ developed. The "higher ministry" commenced and continuing. 4. The glory of Christ. This was supreme in the apostle's mind. The Master was first. P,rnl was pre-eminently a" Jesus Christ's man." Soul-saving redounded to the honour and praise of his Lord. Christ had come "to seek and to save that which was lost." The pur- pose of the Master became the all-absorbing desire of the servant. Paul saw that bis Master was glorified by the victories of the cross. So in season and out of season the apostle preached "Jesus Christ and him crucified" that he might "save some." He lived, laboured, suffered, for the day when" the multitude which no man could number" should sing ta the praise of Christ the sweet stanzas of the "new song." The love of Christ constrained him. II. NOTE SOME WAYS IN WHICH PAUL SOUGHT TO SAVE SOULS. 1. He used all ni~ans at hand. (1) Preaching. He had a definite object in preaching. (2) Conversa- tion. He could preach well to a congregation of one! (3) Writing. What a gift ho haci for "Epistles"! Letter-writing with a view to saving souls is an excellent means, but it requires dexterous use. P,1.ul could not" drivel," or be "goody-goody," or" talk cant." Many religious letter-writers can. Hence the contrast between ancient and modern epistles. (4) Prayer. He" bowed his knees." Stiff-kneed preachers often have ~tiff-necked people. (5) Living the truth. Here, perhaps, lay the tro.nscendent power of Paul. He not only prayed, wrote, talked, preached,-he was. Satan is more afraid of the gospel in the concrete than of the gospel in the abstract. 2. He complied with pre- ;"iulice and prepossession. If we would make others like ourselves in things essential, we must first make our$elves like them in things indifferent. Paul tells us thnt to the Jf'w he became a Jew-remembered Jewish feeling, looked at things from a Jewish standpoint, accorcled with Jewish observances. 'l'o the Gentile he became a Gentile- ~ccomruodating his utterance, manner, form of thought, mode of presenting the truth, to Gentile predilection. You can talk to a man more easily if you stand on the same J)latform with him. 'l'o the weak Paul became as weak ; not insisting upon his liberty or ruthlessly running counter to imperfect conceptions. In fact, he asserts that ho 1iecame "all things to all men" in order to realize his supreme object. Personal pre- Jilections must be sacrificed, and unpleasant restraints submitted to, if we would do elTectively tho greatest work under heaven. An unbending preacher will preach to unbroken hearts. An insistence upon our rights and privileges is a short method, often adopted, of ruining all hopes. A spirit of holy compliance, a disposition to stand :j11st alongside the one wo would gain,-these are potent. We often bar and bolt the very door titat ive are trying to unfasten. Often we forget that we arc speaking to very imperl'cct men, and that we are very imperfect ourselves. Complianco must, of course, not be unlimited. (1) \Vo must exercise discretion. We must abido in the realm of "the lawful," and select what will be truly "expedient." Sound judgment need be exercised. \Ve must look to 1irobable results. (2) \Ve must never sacririce the right. Paul was most compliant in things indifferent, but most unyielding in thingsess~ntial. ·when he yielded he not only confined himself to things indifferent, but made it lo bo understood that the things were indifferent. When they were regarded as essential ho refused to comply. 'l'his is strikingly illustrated in his permitting the circumcision of Timothy, but resisting that of Titus. 3. He practised great self-sacrifice. He di,! not think of himself, but of those he sought to gain. Vv e have seen how willing he was to sacrifice his personal predilections. He went further. (1) In some instances ho sacri ficc,l his maintenance, supporting himself by,the la.hour of his own hands. (2) He sacrifice,! his 1msonal case and comfort. (3) He sacrificed much of his freedom-he made himself I. CORI!':TIIIA NS, X. 306 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. IX. 1-2,.

"serrnnt unto all" (ver. 19). A man who is prepared for illimitable self-sacrifice can do, much. No sacrifice is too great for the attainment of Paul's life-objact. Christ laid down his life for it. He who bore the great cross spoke of crosses for his followers. His ministers often have heavy ones, but it is worth while to carry them, if by doin" so we become instrumental in saving souls. Souls saved will be our "joy and crown f.. at last. What vast possibilities life presents, when we think that in it we may be· the means of saving souls! This applies to all Christians. Every saint should toil for the sah·ation of men. All the sorrows endured and sacrifices made will seem. like "the dust of the balance" when we see our spiritual children welcomed home.-H .. Vers. 24-2T.-Spiritual athletics. Paul compares the Christian life to a foot-race and to a boxing contest. These were familiar to the Corinthians bein" conspicuous. features of the celebrated Isth~ian gam_es. A wise teac~er spe;ks through things known of thrngs unknown. Chnst spoke m parables. PassJn" events may be made the .chicles of a biding truths. The secular may often illustrate th~ sacred. There is no loss of dignity or impropriety in such modes of instruction. Some people are shocked by references to everyday life; but such people ought to be shocked. Homely garb, sometimes wins the readier admittance. Note some points of resemblance. I. CHRISTIAN LIFE IS A PASSAGE-FROM SIN TO HOLINESS, FROM EARTH Tn HEAVEN,. It is a daily movement. '\Ve need beware of stumbling-blocks, of strayin" from the right course, of indulgence which may hinder, of violation of laws, of loit;rin"0 since the time is short. '

II. CHRISTIAN LIFE IS A COl. . 'I'EST WITH ENEMIES. The" race" does not fully illustrate- it. We have opponents, many and resolute. We have a trinity against us as well as for us-the world, the flesh, and the devil. We have not only to "run," but to "fight." 111. Fon SUCCESS ARE NEEDED: 1. Preparation. For athletic contests how much, "training" has to be undergone, often very painful and wearying! Our preparation for Christian life is arduous and long, but it does not commence before we enter upon Christian life, but as we enter, and continues until the close. We "train" as we run and as -we fight. 2. Earnestness. No indifferent competitor was likely to win in ancient races or boxing contests. Indifference kills Christian life. The half-hearted go not far from the starting-point. Many have only enough earnestness to "enter" for the race and ·fight; as soon as they have "entered," they think all is done. 3. Striving. To be amongst the runners is not enough; we must exe1t our powers; we must call into activity all our energies. We must not be as those who" beat the air," but as those who beat their enemies. Christian life is real, with issues of infinite importance. It is not for exhibition of skill, but for stern work. "Strive [agonize] to enter in at tho strait gate." Paul would have each Christian to be as the winner, who" spent himself" in snatching the victory (ver. 24). We do not hinder others from attaining, and for this we may be not a little thankful; but we each need to use the utmost effort. 4. Patience, Christian life is not soon over. At first we may do well, but when difficulties arise we shall be tested. Some who run fastest at first run slowest at last. Our all-wise Master spoke· of "enduring to the end." 5. Watclifulness. Lest we trip. Lest our enemy gets an ad,antacre. The great Preacher's text was often" \Vatch!" 6. Resolution. If we are to endure t~ the end, we shall need stern resolve. Fixedness of purpose is an essential for Christian life. '\Ve should determine in God's strength to go on, whatever may lie in our path: to fight on, no matter what enemies confront us. Christian life demands courage and fortitude; we must not be too easily frightened. 7. Concentration. "This one thing I do." The "whole man" must be given to religion. Home professors are "called off" from the race, and lose it. They lower their guard, for their hands must be about earthly things, and then their enemy overthrows them. 8. Continuity. This tries many. If religion were spasmodic, they could be religious. There are many "now-and-then" Christians. People like to be pious at intervals. 9. Mortifi- cation of the flesh. Ancient athletes knew, as their modern brethren do, what this means. The victor was" temperate in all things." A pampered body meant disappoint- ·ment, disgrace, loss. Paul said, "I keep under [I buffet, I bruise] my body." Our lower nature must be dealt severely with. Indulgence is disaster; we must practise .fclf-control, self-denial, self-sacrifice. 10. Confidence, bul not excess of confidence.

Confidence that will prompt to exertion, not confidence which kills effort. "Lest ... I myself should be a. casta.way." IV. Succ~;ss MEETS WITH REWARD. Contrast the crowns of earth with the crown of heaven. Many do so much for a corruptible crown, and we so little for an incorruptible one. A garland of leaves and a day's popula1ity: paradise and life eternal. V. MANY SPECTATORS WITNESS THE CON'l'l\ST. The eyes of the ungodly arc upon us. Fellow-Christians watch us closely. 'l'he angels behold us, and are" ministering spirits" to us. Perhaps victors of the past, perhaps those who have failed in race and fight, watch us. 'l'he King sees us-the Judge-he who holds "the crown of righteousness" for those .who have "fought a good fight" and "finished the course." "Wherefore seeing," etc. (Heb. xii. 1,- 2). When we think of the race and fight, we should ponder Phil. iv. 13, "I can do all things through Christ which strengtbeneth me."-H.

entries.title: 1CO 9:1–3
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -The marks of apostleship. 'l'his chapter grows out of the noble utterance of self-denial with which the previous one closes. 'l'he apostle illustrates and enforces the duty of curtailing our liberty iu things indifferent for the sake of weaker brethren, by a reference to his own example in foregoing the right of maintenance by the Church. Was he not free? Had he not all the rights belonging to Christians, unfettered by obligations to men? Nay, more, was he not an apostle? At Corinth, as elsewhere, there were some who questioned the full apostolic authority of Paul, on the ground that he was not one of the twelve; and his self-denial seems to have been turned into an argument against him. It was insinuated that he refrained from asking the support of his converts, as the other apostles were in the habit of doing, because be was conscious of bis inferiority. It is apparently for this reason that he here presents the marks of his apostleship. I. HE HAD SEEN JESUS THE LoBD. There is no evidence that he had seen Jesus in the days of bis flesh, but the reference is mainly to the appearance near Da.mascus (Acts ix. 4-6). On that occasion the Lord met him and gave him his commission as an apostle; and this was regarded as an essential mark of apostleship in the highest sense, as we see from the election of Matthias (Acts i. 22; comp. eh. xv. 8). In this respect the apostles can have no successors. 'l'he office was a special and temporary one, needful for the pla.nting and organizing of the Church, and was intended to expire with the men who held it. Ha.ving set the house in order, they were to deliver the keys to the ordinary servants who were left in charge. Still, every one whom Christ sends forth to do his work must first have bad the sight of him that faith gives. Only when we ha.ve beheld him in his glory, invested with" a.ll authority in heaven and on ea.rth," and heard from bis lips the call to go forth, shall we feel ourselves clothed with power as his ambassadors (comp. Isa. vi.; Matt. xxviii. 18, 19), II. TliE CORINTHIAN CHRISTIANS WERE THE SEAL OF ms APOSTLESHIP. Whatever reason others might have for questioning his standing, they at lea.st ha.d none; for as the instrument of their conversion, he could point to them as "bis work in the LorJ." The power which accompanied his preaching, and which ha.d wroug;ht so mighty a. chang;c in them, was a proof that be had not run unsent. 'l'his of itself did not prove apostleship in the high sense in which Paul claimed it, but it proved that the Lord was with him. 'l'his kind of evidence requires to be adduced with caution, inasmuch as it is difficult for us to estimate the real success of e. ministry; but where there aro unmistakable proofs of the con version of sinners and the edification of saints, we are warranted iu viewing these as the seals of our mission. In seeking these high ends, we aro doing truly apostolic work. Happy the minister who can say to his congregation, "Ye are my work iu the Lord "1-ll.

entries.title: 1CO 9:4–18
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Jllinisterial support. Having vindicated his claim to be reckoned among the apostles of Christ, Paul proceeds to assert his right to a temporal maintenance at the hands of those to whom he ministered. 'l'ho other apostles received support, not only for themselves, but also for their wives: why should he not make the same claim? '!'hough he was unmarried, and though he bad hitherto supported himself hy the labour of his own hands, this did not invalidate his right. Consider- I. 'l'IIE RIGHT OF MINISTERS TO A BUITADLE MAIXTENANCE. 'l'his is upheld by various arguments and analogies. 1. The labourer is w11rcliy <!/ Ms reward. 'l'hree 308 THE FIRST EPISTLE 'l'O THE CORINTHIANS, [en. IX. 1-27.

i_nsk1?ccs are adduced in illmtr,1tion ~,·er. 7). (L) 'l'he soldier. 'l'he duty of fighting !or Ins country throws the ~urden of Ins support upon others. ·why should it be other- wise with the Christian soldier (2 Tim. ii. 4)? (2) The husbandman. His labour is rewarded by the fruit. The minister of the gospel is also a husbandman ( eh. iii. 6-9). (3) The shepherd. Does he not receive the milk of the flock, partly for food and partly for exchange? "Thy should not the Christian pastor, who tends the flock of Christ, have a similar return (1 Pet. v. 2)? The principle in these instances is that every occupation in common life yields support to the worker, and that he does not require to go beyond it for daily sustenance. In like manner, the minister of the gospel is entitled to an adequat~ maintenance without having to resort to secular work to supply his wants. 2. The teachin9 rf the Mosaic Law. "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox," etc. (ver. 9; Dent. xxv. 4; comp. 1 Tim. v. 18). What was the meanincr of this injunction? It shows, indeed, the care of the Lawgiver for the brute creation, b~t it is only a particular application of a great principle. Tbe Law has regard for oxen, not for their own sake, but for the sake of him to whom they are in subjection. And if even the labouring ox \Yas to_ be fed, !low much more should the plougher and the thresher work in hope ot partakm~ ! The La:w o~ Moses t~us confirms the teaching of natural analogy, that the labourer 1s to be mamtamed by his work. 3. The fairness ef the claim. "If we sowed unto you spiritual things," etc. (ver. 11). In every case the sower expects to reap; but the1:e is mo~e than this in the apostle's argument. 'l'he preacher of the gospel sows spintual thmgs-those great truths that minister to the spirit: is it a great matter if he looks for carnal things in return-those things that minister only to the flesh? If he is the instrument, in God's hand, of saving the souls of his hearers, what amount of gold can be an adequate recognition of the service rendered? 4. .Analogy of the Jewish priesthood. (Ver. 13.) The rule was that they who served at the altar should receive a portion of the sacrifices and other gifts that were constantly brought to the t~m pie. A sufficient support-was thus secured; and the Divine sanction implied in that ancient rule applies equally to the case of the Christian ministry. 5. The express ordinance of the Lord Christ. (Ver. 14.) When he sent forth his apostles to preach, he said," Get you no gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses; . . . for the labourer is worthy of his rood" (Matt. x. 9, 10). 'l'his was their marching order. 'l'hey were to depend on the offerings of the people among whom they la.boured ; and the reference here shows that this was no temporary arrangement, but that it was intended to be the New Testament rule for preachers of the gospel. Instead of having to turn aside to secular pursuits, they are to be free to give themselves wholly to their work. By these various arguments the apostle establishes the right of ministers to claim support at_ the hands of the Cbristian people, and the corn:sponding duty of the people to contribute that support. Both the right and the duty have been but imperfectly recognized by the Church. This will appear if we consider: (1) The average rate cif ministerial support. Compare this with the incomes of men in the other learned professions or in mercantile pursuits, (2) The manner in which giving tu the cau~e of Christ, is fre~uently 7:ega:ded. How many either give with a grudge or do not give at all! The e~1l resultmg 1s twofold-;- spiritual loss to the individual, and a crippling of the Church m her work. Not until all the tithes are brought into the storehouse wil! the Lord open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing (Mai. iii. 8-10). II. THE RENUNCIATION oF THIS RIGHT. (Vers. 15-18.) Strongly as Paul insists upon b:s right to temporal maintenance, i~ is ~ot with a_ vi~w to ~rge h\s claim upon the !Corinthians but to brin" into clearer relief his renunc1at1on of it. 'lhat he preached , the gospel free of c!UJ.rg: was to him a matter of boasting which he would rather die ·than be deprived of. It was no glory to h!m ~hat he was a preac?er; for, as a stewa1;d 1iut in trust with the gospel, this was !us s1mp)e duty. . But 1t was no part of h!s stewardship to labour without support; and tb1~, accordrngly,· ,~as a proof of his sincerity in which he was entitled to boast. In this act of self-demal he had a reward in making the gospel entirely free, and in securing tha_t on this_ grou~d no hindrance ~bould be put in its way (ver. 12). Here some practical considerations emerge. 1. How a minister of the gospel should bear !timself towards pecuniary support, 'l'h~re arc cases in which he may forecro his fr,]it, especially where he sees that thi~ renuncia- tion will tend to the advancen;cnt of tl1e gospel. -Usually, however, it is his duty to accept a stipend at the hands of the Christian people, and that for the reason which led

Paul to decline it. To receive a rea~onable maintenance is to be in the best position for devoting one's self entirely to the mi11istry of the \Vonl. Ilut at all times it sbouhl be manifest that the servant of Christ does not act from mercenary motives. '1.'be shepherd is not to tend the flock for the sake of the fleece. " Not yours, but you," should be his motto (2 Cor. xii. 14). 2. The obligation to preach the gospel. "Necessity is laid upon me." '!'here is a Divine must in the case of e,ery true preacher, as there was in the case of Jesus (comp. Mark viii. 31; Luke iv. 43; xix. 5; Jolm iii. 14). '1.'he love of Christ, not less than the command of Christ, constrains him. It is with him as with the prophet : "Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his Name. But his word was in mine heart. as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stny" (Jer. xx. 9). 3. The doctrine of reward. '1.'he apostle's statement regarding the reward he expected fur his optional renunciation of support has been adduced by popigh dh·ines in support of their doctrine of supererogation; but it will not bear such an application. The distinc- tion be makes is between what was plainly a part of his bounden duty as a steward, and what seemed best for the furtherance of the gospel in his peculiar circumstances. In one sense it was a matter for bis own choice whether be should accept a temporal maintenance, but this is not the sense required by the Romish argument. \Vhatever promises to conduce to the furtherance of Christ's king,lom, becomes thereby a duty to the apostle; for "to him that knowetb to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin " (Jas. iv.17). There is no act which is not included under love to God and love to man. There is no selJ'.-denial to which the love of Christ should not prompt us. The gospel doctrine of reward does not rest on any theory of supererogation, but rather on the principle that God is pleased to recognize the fidelity or his servauts.-Il.

entries.title: 1CO 9:19–23
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Theprinciple of accommodation . .Paul's resolve to preach the gospel without charge was but one instance of the general rule which guided his life. Though under obligation to none, he yet became the servant of all-" all things to all men." He accommodated himself to the Jews (ver. 20), as when he circumcised Timothy (Acts xvi. 3) and purified himself in the temple (Acts xxi. 2o). He accommo,lated himself to the Gentiles (ver. 21), by refusing to impose the Law of Moses (Gal. ii. 5) and by meeting them on tLeir own ground (Acts xvii. 22-31). He accommodaled himself to the weak (ver. 22), as when he abstained from meat because of their scruples (ell. viii. 13). Consider- I. AccOMMODATION AS A RULE OF MINISTERIAL PIIACTICE. There is a high sense in which every minister of Christ is called to becomo "all things to all men." We are to adapt ourselves to the circumstances, modes of thought, and oven the liarmless pre- judices of those among whom we labour. In dealing with human souls, we must not stand upon points of etiquette, hut bo ready when occasion requires to sacrifice our preferences and sometimes our rights. 'l'his principlo will cover matters of dress a!lll modos of living, as also our choice of recreation and amusement. ,villiam llurns, missionary to China, adopted the Chinese dress that he might the more easily gaiu access to the people. On the same ground we shall present the truth iu language which our hearers understand, whether they are chil,lrcn or adults. '1.'l1is happy faculty of adaptation has frequently proved of grel\t service to the gospel. II. LIMITS TO BE ODSEIIVED IN FOLLOWING TIIIS RULll. 'l'be highest things may frequently be mistaken for the lowest. Christian nccommotlation may be confounded with time-serving, but nothing is moro unlike. 'l'he man whose principles aro flexible, who t.rims and carves to serve his purpose, who is a devout Christian in this company and a railing scoffer in that, may be said to be "all things to all men ; " but such a man is a mere jelly-fish chamcter, a mass of moral pulp. For such accommodation ns ' Paul practised there is needed the highest principle, the stron~cst consistency; and in order to this, certain limits are to be observed. 1. It must not Zc,Hl us to do or tolerate that which is sinful. 1'his limit is transgressed by Jesuit missionaries when they suffer their converts to retain part of their old idolatrous worship. 2. It must not lead 11s to l.eep back any essential truth because it is unpopular. 'l'his were cowanlice aml infidelity to our trust. 3. It must not lead us to do unytl.in_q which would compro11,ise the Christian name. "Lot not your good be evil spoken of" (llom. ,;iv. lG). Ill. MoTin:s 'l'IIAT l'R0MPT U9 TO FOLLOW THIS RULE, 'l'llese arc: 1. ..d. de3ire tc 310 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [err. 1x. 1-27.

sure others. It is not a wish to please men, but a desire to remove every hindrance to the reception of the gospel. With this end in view, we shall not find it diflicult to become "all things to all men." A human soul is not too dearly won at the cost of a little self-sacrifice. _In this a~pect th~ rule we are considering is but a faint copy of the great accommodation-the mcarnat10n and work of Jesus Christ. 2. A regard to ow· personal salvation. (Ver. 23.) Paul connects his work '' for the (Tospel's sake" with his being a "joint partaker" of its blessings. In work for the cr0od of others we must not be unmindful of our own good; and there is nothincr more "conducive to our spiritual benefit than faithful, self-denyin~ service for Chri~t. "Continue in these things ; for in doing this thou sbalt both save thyself and them that hear thee" (1 '.l'im. iv. 16).-B.

entries.title: 1CO 9:24–27
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The i·ace for the prize. The thought introduced in ver. 23, that Paul's self-denial bad a reference to his own salvation as well as the salvation of others is here carried on and applied generally to all Christians. The imagery is derived from the Isthmian gan,cs celebrated in the neighbourhood of Corinth and therefore "·ell known to his readers. These games occupied a place in the nationa'l life of Greece corresponding to that occupied by the great yearly festivals in the life of Israel. There is no reference to them in the Gospels, as they were unknown in Palestine but more than once they are used in the Epistles as a metaphorical representation of the Christian life (comp. Phil. iii. 14; 2 Tim. iv. 7, 8; Heb. xii. 1). Consider- I. THE RACE. The stadium presented an animating spectacle. At th.is end stand the competing athletes, awaiting the signal to start; at the other end is the judge, holding in his hand the prize; whilst all around, rising tier upon tier, are the seats cruwded with spectators. The Christian life is a race for the great prize offered by God to the successful runner. At conversion we take our-place in the racecourse and ha,e our names proclaimed by the herald. The leading ideas in the figure are: 1. Progress. "Forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on," etc. (Phil. iii.13). 2. Earnestness. The Christian life is one of strenuous effort-every muscle strung, every faculty called into exercise. No place for lukewarmness or indifference here. 3. Concentration. "One thing I do." The runner, with eye on the goal and all else out of view, bends his whole strength to this single effort. Dissipation of energy, the multa rather than the multum, is a source of "·eakness in spiritual life. '' One thing is needful." 4. Endurance. "Let us run with patience" (Heb. xii. 1). To faint or fall is to lose the prize. The cross must be borne to the end. Nothing but "patient continuance in well-doing" will conduct us to the goal (comp. Jas. i. 12). II. Co:in>ITJONS OF SUCCESS L\1 THE RACE. To run well we must run as the successful racer. The end in view must be clear: we must know what we are running for (" not uncertainly"). Here specially emphasize the preparatory condition-self-restraint. The athlete under training was required to avoid excess in eating and drinking, and ernry form of fleshly indulgence. The Christian athlete must practise a like temper- ance if he would run his course with success. In this point of view the body is the ::mtao-onist with which we contend, and which must be buffeted and bruised rather tban°suftered to gain the mastery over us. How rnan_y Christians are hindered in their spiritual course by lack of self-restraint I The worship of comfort, the love of luxury, not to speak of such indulgences as are clearly sinfol, cause many to lag in the race. An intemperate use of, or affection for, things in themselves good, is a most insidious ~nare in the path of spiritual advancement. Bodily mortification is not spirituality, but it is often helpful towards its attainment. 'l'he Christian runner must lay aside every weight as well as every sin (Heb. xii. 1). !II. THE PHIZE. This consisted of a chaplet of leaves-olive, parsley, pine. In addition, the name of the victor was celebrated in a triumphal ode and a statue was ~rected to his memory. It was a great honour-one of the greatest in a land where the gymnastic art was so highly appreciated; and e~en Homan emperors (Nero, e.g.) did not hesitate to enter the lists. But at best It was, hko all earthly honours, corruptible. These crowns would quickly fade, that applause would soon cease. The prize for which the Christian ~ontenJs is an incoi·ruptible crown. It is the "crown of nghteousness" (Z 'J.•Ul. iv. 8), the" crown of life" (Jas. i. 12; Rev. ii. 10), the "crown -en. Ix. 1-27.J 'l'HE E'lllST EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIA,NS. 311

of glor:r ''. (1 Pet. v. 4). To have ri~hteousness and life in perfection is our true glory, and tl11s 1s the very crown of our bel.llg. A crown composed of such materials cannot fade away. All the trees in that country are evergreen. What an object to nil the eye and fire the soul! A proud moment when the successful runner had the chaplet of leaves put on his brow ! A grander moment for the Christian athlete when the pierced hand of Jesus places on his head the crown of glory! And if men endure so much and strive so earnestly for the corruptible, how much more should we endure and strive in order to obtain the incorruptible! REMARKS, 1. The human side of the Christian life is strongly emphasized in the figure of the race; but along with this we must take the other side of the truth. Without the grace of God we cannot run. Mark the striking combination in Phil. ii. 12, 13. 2. Notice the apostle's self-distrust. He is not ashamed to confess that he brings his body into subjection, "lest by any means, after that I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected." Compare such outbursts of confident assurance as Rom. viii. 38, 39, and 2 Tim. i. 12, and regard the one as the complement of the -0ther, Self-diffidence goes hand-in-baud with genuine assurance. A lesson for all Christians, and especially for all preachers.-B.

entries.title: 1CO 9:16
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-0ompulsory service. The apostle here affords us a passing glimpse of his own state of mind in reference to his high calling as a "preacher of the gospel." The revelaticn of the secret workings of an earnest human spirit must needs be deeply interesting to us, and most of all in the case of a man of such noble nature as Paul, and in reference to a matter of such supreme moment. We could scarcely have a finer view of the ministry of the ·word, a finer model of right thought and feeling about it, than is presented in these simple but lofty words. Chiefly three elements of feeling are here expressed. I. A SENSE OF THE DIGNITY OF THE PREACHER'S OFFICE. The preaching of the word i.s evidently regarded here as a fixed and permanent institution of the Church, a work to which men are divinely called to consecrate themselves, and from which they may draw the necessary support of their life (ver. 14). And the fact that Paul disavows all self-glorying on account of it, implies that there is that in the office which might lead a man unduly to exalt himself. But what is the real nature of its Jignity? It is very different from that which belongs to social rank or any kind of worldly distinction. Much mischief springs from losing sight of this difference. Ever since the time when a halo of worldly glory began to be thrown around the witness for Christ, and the ideas of social elevation, priestly supremacy, large emolument, luxurious ease, came to be associated with it, it has been degraded by the intrusion of false motive, and by bemg made the prize of a purely carnal ambition. '1.'he dignity Paul recognizes in it is that which is inhP.rent in all high and holy service; the honour he would havo paiJ to it i~ that which is due to a faithful discharge of sacred responsibility. The dignity of the preacher's function lies in such facts as those: 1. It brinys a man, more thau any other office does, into habitual contact with the mind of God and with the realities of the invisible world. Not that he who sustains it has in this respect a privilege deuietl to others. Every path of human life may be thus gilded and gladdened by the heavenly glory. But it is his special business, by habits of thought and prayer, to become moro deeply conversant than other men with the revelations of God and the things unseen and eternal. Aud the fact that his work demands that mind aud heart shoulJ be ever dwelling in such a high spiritual region, imparts a greatness and dignity to it surpassing that of all others. 2. It brings him into a purely spiritual relationship with his fellow- men. Other human relations arc more superficial. 'l'he world recognizes no bonds of union but such as grnw out of the passing interests and experiences of this present life. To the preacher of the gospel, as such, the seculur aspect of the position men occupy is nothing as compared with the spiritual. He "knows no man after the flesh." lfo has to do with the nobler, the immortal part of them, " to watch for their souls as one that must give account." 3. It leads on to eternal issues. All the granucnr of the endless futurity overshadows it. None of our eartlily businesses have rel"crence merely to the issues of time. Lines of moral influence arc connected with them that stretch out into the great hereafter. Dut this is specially tho case with the work of the Christian teacher. It must have infinite developments. It is the seeJ-su1\iug for an Jl2 Tl, •~ FIHST EPISTLE TO TIIE COilJNTHIANS. [c:11. 1x. 1-2,.

eternal harvest. It is to C"l'ery man "none other than the savour of life unto life, o, of death unto death." II: THE SENSE OF PERSO:S-AL ~Nwo~TIIINESS. "Though I preach the gospel, I have nothmg to glory of." The consc10us dignity of his office is coupled with deep humility. "Who is snflkicnt for these things?" (2 Cor. ii. lG). Paul's humility, indeed, was not that of the man who is always doubting his right to the position he occupies, and fitness for the work he is doing. He knew that he bore the stamp and seal of a Divine com- mission. And every true preacher of the Word must in a measure share this feeling. If a man has no conscious or acknowledged fitness for the work, he bas no business to undertake it. But it must needs be that, in hours of calm reflection, in the solitude and silence of the night, he will often lie "Contemplating his own unworthiness." Many thinzs will serve to bumble him. 1. The thought that he is but an instrument in t!ie hands of Goel (eh. iii. 5-7). 2. The fact that, in proclaiming the mercy of God to smncrs, he has to look upon himself as the foremost of those who need that mercy (1 Tim. i. 15, 16). 3. The light the Word he preaches continually sheds on the evils- ,,f his own heart and life. 4. The sense of the subtle spiritual dangers th:::.t beset his ,acred calling. 5. The fear "lest that by any means, having preached to others, he himself should be a castaway" (ver. 27). III. A. SENSE OF MORAL coNSTI\AINT. "Necessity is laid upon me," etc. The ap0stlc felt that he had been invested by the risen Lord with a very solemn stewurdship, and 1 hat J,e dared not be unfaithful to it. The heaviest of all "woes," the woe of a remorse- ful conscience, the woe of a spirit that has fallen from the heis;ht of a glory that mi 5ht have been its own for ever, would fall upon him if he did. His would be the misery of being basely untrue to himself as well as to his Divine Master. '!'here are two kinds of moral "necessity "-the necessity of an external force and that of an internal: the necessity of an outward law, backed by some form of outward penalty; and the necessity of an inward impulse, backed by the sacred fear of inward shame and loss. It wns this latter kind of necessity of which he was supremely conscious. It was consistcnL with perfect moral freedom, because it was of the nature of a resistless force in the depths of his own soul, the decision of his own will, the impulse of his own heart. The will' d God had imposed this stewardship, this "dispensation of the gospel," upon him. Ho ,,ad been separated unto it from his very birth (Rom. i. l; Gal. i. 15). And God's will had become his will, God's purpose bis purpose. The manifested Jove of Christ had become a constraining power wit.hin him, leading his whole being into captivity, ,lrawing forth every energy of his nature in a holy and joyous service. This kind of "necessity" is the loftiest principle by which any human spirit can be actuated. Never is a man so great, so free, so royal, so divinely blessed, as when be is intelligently conscious of it. This is the true inspiration of gospel ministry. 'l'he harvest is great. May the Lord of the harvest "scnii forth labourers" thus inwardly constrained to serve him!-W.

entries.title: 1CO 9:22
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-" By all means sai,e some." 'l'wo points present themselves for our cousideration here-(1) The end the apostle had in view; (2) the method by which lie sought to secure it. I. Tim END. "To save some." What does he mean by this? \Vhat to him was the salvation of men? 1. It certainly means deliverance from a dread future calamity. " The wrath to come," "the perdition o_f ungodly men," was t? St. Paul no dream, b~t· an awful realitv. It was worth all possible effort and self-sacrifice to sav(l men from It. If be had no other impulse than that of mere human sympathy to movo him, we havehere a sufficient explanation of the enthusiasm of his zeal. It is often said that if Christian people really believed the future that is before multituJes of their fellowcreatures to be so dark and dreadful as they say it is, they could nevor rest as they do- Ill their own natural or spiritual satisfactions. 'l'hey would rather be beside themselves with a frantic agony of sympathetic sorrow and desire to save. There is truth ln this. 'J.'he easy indifference with which too many of us regard the condition and prospects or tLe godless world around us, belies the reality ~f. our faith. Our con~eptions of what the solemn issues of the future shall be may d1f1er. Some, after anxious and earnest

thought, may hnve arrived at the conclusion that to forecast the nature or the duration of the penalty that will then fall on the transgressor is beyond our province, and that we can only take the l:rnguageof Scripture as it stands, without attempting to penetratethe haze of 1lreadful mystery that hangs around it. But the broad and certain factsof the case are such as may well affect us far more deeply than they do, and bring forth in us far richer and more abundant fruits of practical beneficence. It is to be feared that doctrinal controversy abon t the future teads to weaken rather than deepen and strengthen our impressions. We lose in speculation and debate the practical earnestness the subject itself might be expected to awaken. St. Paul lived in the clear iight of the future. His soul was thrilled by the sense of its tremendous reality. And though its issues probably were no more distinct and definite to his apprehension than they are to ours, yet his faith in their certainty was such as to stir up all the noble energies of his being in the endeavour to save his fellow-men. 2. But the foresight of the future was far from being the only thing that moved him; it was a present deliverance from a present calamity that he had in view. To save mcu now from the evil that enthrallc<l and cursed them, ruining their Godlike nature, darkening all the glory of their life,-this was the end he sought. He was no visionary. It was no object of remote and uncertain utility, but one of most practical and immediate urgency at which he aimed. Whatever its bearing on the future may be, the influence of the gospel on the present passing life of men is so benign and blessed that our utmost zeal in diffusing it is fully justi6cd. If we think of nothing more than the superficial social changes that Christianity has introduced, how it is at this very hour the prolific root of all social progress in every Janel, we see here an ample reward for all the sacrifice8 that have ever been made for its extension. But beneath all this there lies the fact that, as sin is the ruining, destroying power in man's nature and life, it must needs be a Godlike purpose that seeks to deliver him from it (Matt. i. 21; Acts iii. 26). "That I may by all means save some." He could not hope for all, but if "some" only yic!ded to his persuasive word, it would be a blessed recompense. This is the inspiring hope of everr true preacher and worker for Christ. The net is cast, the arrow is shot at a venture; the issue is not now runde mnnifest. But a seemingly profitless work may be linked indirectly with results that are very great and glorious. Waves of spiritual influence, from a narrow circle, travel out where none can follow them. \Vhile there are those who shall find at last that the "great and wonderful things" they supposed they had done in the name of Obrist are little recognized, thero are others who will bo arnazerl todiscover that their l0wly endeavours hnve yielded fruits of which they ucver dreamed. And to "save some," to be able to lay some trophies nt the Master's feet, will \Jo a blessed reward. II. THE METHOD. "I am becomo all things to all men." It is rcmnrkablo that words which express the highest nobleness of nn npostolic spirit should have come to be used by us in familiar discourse ns descriptive of a typo of character and mode of conduct that is mean nnd despicable. It is suggestive of tho behaviour or oue who hns no steadfast principle, no honest outspokenness; tho mere obsequious time-server, full of smiles and gilded insincerities; who, to serve his own ends, can put on any· face that suits tho occasion; "Aman Versed in tho world ns pilot in his eomp11ss, Tho noedle pointing cvor to that interest Which is his lode-st11r, nml who spreads his sails With vantngo to the g11lo of others' p11ssion."

There wae nothing of this sort in Paul. Nothing could be more abhorrent to his spirit than a time-serving policy or a habit of smiling, plausible deceit. 'l'heso won'.s from his lips simply indicate that his strong desiro to save men and wi,~ them to Christ led him to enter as much as possible into their circumstances, to placo himself on their level. '!'bus would he disarm their prejudices and bring his heart into sympathetic contact with theirs. '!'bus would he commend to them the Jovo of him who" was made under the Law that he might redeem them that were under the Law;" "who for our sakes became poor, that wo through his poverty might be rnado rich.'' (Examples: Acts xvi, 3; xvii. 22-31; xxi. 26.) The lesson for nil Christian preacher:. 314 THE FJRST EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIANS, [cu. Ix. 1-27.

:and workers is this: Cultivate a broad and generous human sympathy. In dealing with men in various conditions-doubt, error, poverty, sorrow, temptation, subjection to the power of evil-put yourself as much as possible in their place, if you would hope to guide, or comfort, or save them.-\V.

entries.title: 1CO 9:24–27
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Runningandfigliting. The crown of eternal life is here set forth as the issue of successful conflict with difficulties and foes. It would seem as if all Divine excellence must needs present itself to our minds as the negation of opposite forms of e"l'il. \Ve cannot think of God but as the "Licrht" that contends with our darkness, the "Fire" that consumes our corruption. God's Law is but the Divine restraint of our wayward propensities, the Divine rebuke of our traacrressions. The Divine life in the soul is an energy that reveals itself in ceaseless stru.;'crle with forces that would otherwise destroy it, a perpetual battle with the powers of d;ath. Heaven is victory, the rising up of the soul out of the region of trial and strife and sufferincr to its true destiny and inheritance in the glorious presence of God. Look at this pass';cre 0 as suggesting certain conditions of success in this spiritual conflict. l. CoKCE~TRATION OF THOUGHT ON THE PRIZE AS A MATTER OF INTENSE PERSONAL I:S-TEUEST. " .A.II run, but one receiveth," etc. The analogy here instituted is not complete, inasmuch as in the Christian race all who "run with patience" will attain. But it serves to enforce the need of great fixedness of thought and purpose, as if each runner felt that only one could win, and he would be that one. There is nothing Darrow, envious, selfish, in this. .A. great difference lies here between the heavenly and the earthly striving. He must be a man of very elevated spirit who is able to r.ise <!ntirely above the narrowing influence of secular rivalry. In urging his way to success along the crowded thoroughfares of the world, a man almost inevitably thrusts some -0ne else aside. The gigantic system of commercial competition means this. And it is an important problem of social life to determine how one may claim as he ought that personal inheritance in the world that God has placed within his reach, and yet not fall into the sin of a selfish violation of the rigb ts of others. There is no room, however, for anything of this kind in the spiritual race and warfare. Mutual emula- tion is mutual profit. The success of each one is to the advantage and the joy of all. Strive to \Yin the heavenly crown as if you alone could wear it, and the more intensely earnest you arc in your striving, the more does your example inspire your fellow- combatant, the more do you become a fount of healthful influence, a source of enrich- ment and blessing to all around you. II. SELF-llESTRAINT AND SELF-DISCIPLINE. 'l'he severe physical discipline to which the athletes subjected themselves was gladly borne for the sake of the "corruptible -crown" they sought to win. Not that the perishable wreath of wild olive encircling the vict.or's brow was in itsdf the thing he cared for. It was but the symbol of something else. 'l'o be conscious of the mastery, to have his name proclaimed by the herald before the assembl.ed multitude as one who had conferred honour and renown .aa his family, his tribe, his country,-that was his reward. So that the very ephemeral character of the crown made it the more striking witness to the nobility of man's nature, to the truth that he can never find his satisfactions in the region of sense; they belong, after all, to the super-sensible, the ideal world. Every form of ambition greater than the apparent object will account for or warrant, is proof of this. The enthusiasm that magnifies its objects beyond their real dimensions, and invests them with a fictitious charm, is always a significant memorial of man's relation to a higher and a better world. At the same time, this striving for the corruptible crown reminds us how ,·ain often are the rewards of earthly ambition, and how the price men pay often for their successes is a very costly one. They surrender that which is far more precious than the thin<T0 they gain. '!'hey "spend their money for that which is not bread, and their labour for that which satisfieth not." In "seeking. to save their life, they lose it." '!'he law of the heavenly race is the reverse of this. As the unsubstantial, the delusive, the perishable, is relinquished, the soul wins for itself the "inheritance incorruptible, and uncleliled, and that fa<lcth not away." You lose tlie lower life to gain the higher. "Temperate in all things." Let not the word "temperance" have to our minds a limited ~nd ~xc_lusive meaning, one ";~ich, howe~er important, does not cover the whole field of its Scnpture appl1cat10ns. l be Clmst1an ell. ix. l-2i.J 'l'HE J<'InST EPISTLE 'l'O THE CORIN'rHIAKS. 315

is called to be tempemtc alike in all his thoughts, emotions, worc!s, and ways; in his joys and sorro,vs, his schemes and activitic's, his personal indulgences and personal mortifications; in his worldly ambitions, and even in the zeal of his religious life. But " the flesh" must needs be the chief occasion for the exercise of this self-regulating grace. "I buffet my body, and bring it into bondage." Nothing could be more expressive of that subjugation of our lower nature by which we can alone win the crown of the spirit, Not that there is any essential virtue in mere physical austerities and mortifications. Suppose ono to attemJ.,t that course without his mind made up as to the reason why or the goal to which he shoultl run, moving without spirit or purpose, looking to this side and to that; he could take no }lrize. He fights well who plants his blows skilfully and makes them tell. The apostle was a man of pence, but he neeclcd bolclness and firmness, as well as love and patience, for his hard service. He had journeys to make, trials to bear, testimonies to raise, controversies to conduct, difficulties to adjust, calumnies to refute, sorrows to assuage-a great and arduous career; and, by the grace of Gou, he put all his force into it, ran his race of duty with ardour, fought his fight of faith with resolution, II. '!'RAINING AND DISCIPLINE FOR sucn SEllVICE. "I buITet my body, and bring it into subjection." He who woultl subdue evil in others must suppress it in himself. Now, the apostle found that the gospel was hinclcrcd, not so much by intellectual -0bjection, as by moral depravity. The flesh lusted against the spirit. He had felt this hi himself, and knew that the flesh prevailed by fastening on the organs of the body. and induciug indulgence or excess. So he brought himself into goocl training for activo Christian work by bruising the body and "mortifying its deecls." He would not sLir- foit or pamper it, lest he should stupefy the soul. disable the powers of the mind in hope of purifying the soul. Such has been the practice of men and wonien in the ascetic life, :ind ,it one time it took the form of a· frenzy, when the Flagcllants traversed a consideraLle part of Europe in long proces- sions, with covered faces, chanting penitential hymns, and continually applying the scourge to one another's naked backs. We do not hold the body sufficiently under control. \Ve give it ease and luxury and orna- ment; we allow dangerous scope to those cravings and passions which have a physical basis, and so our spiritual life languishes, and we can put no o-low of feelin" or stren"th of p_urpose into the service of Christ. Paul had preached to others, and called them to the Christian race, like the herald at the public games of Greece, who proclaimed the rules and co11ditions of the contest, and summoned runners or combatants to the lists. Alas for him if, through self-indulgence or want of thoroughness in his ministry, he should be disapproved by the great Judge at the close of the day! 'l'be question here is not of a sinner's salvation, but of a believer's service-of doing well or ill in ministry; and fear of failure was an<l always is the obverse side of the desire of success. "They that wait on the Lord shall renew their strength."-F.

entries.title: 1CO 9:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The rights of apostleship. One of St. Paul's chief difficulties arose from the efforts of his enemieM to <lisprove his claims to apostleship. There does not seem to have been in the early Church a common understanding as to what constituted an apostle, aud it was readily observed that the groumls of 8t. Paul's claim differed from the grounds on which the older apostles claimed. '!'his, indeed, was but a surface appearance of difference, and did not reach the heart of the matter; but it sufficed to give the enemies of St. Paul an opportunity of questioning his authority, and oven of asserting that, in the extravagance of his self-esteem, he had assumed r. position nn,1

office which in no sense belonged to him. It will be seen from his letters that he was very jealous of his position as an apostle, and persisted in claiming the rights which belonged to the office. We may, therefore, recall to mind the general grounds on which he believed himself to be an apostle, and the more special signs of his apostleship wbid: ought to have commended his rlaim to the Corinthians. St. Peter, on the occasion of filling the betrayer's place, 1·,,,l declared a condition of apostleship for which he gives no kind of authority. Accc•du,g to his idea (Acts i. 21, 22), "Of the men therefore which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John, unto the day that he was received up from us, of these must one become a witness with us of his resurrection." Probably St. Peter was led to this idea by our Lord's appointment of the apostles as his witnesses, and he conceived that an apostle must have a complete knowledge to be a true witness. But the essential condition of apostleship is rather to be found in the direct per:;hnal call to the office by the Lord Jesus Christ himself. Each one of the first twelve our Lord personally called. St. Paul he directly and personally called. No man can cl::.im the office. 'l'he number can never be increased, unless Christ should be pleased to make himself manifest again, and call men to the office. St. Paul saw the Son of man, and heard his voice, and received his direct call, when smitten by the light near Damascus. ,vhere there had been this direct personal call of Christ, there would surely be a seal of the call in a Divine endowment of miraculous power. 'fhis the first twelve apostles had, and this it is certain St. Paul also had. This, then, was the general ground of his claim; but he further urges upon the Corinthians that they had special reasons for accepting him as an apostle. 'l'hc power of Christ which bad come to them through him carried its own testimony. "The seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord." God had witnessed to him by crowning his labours with success; and the Corinthians had felt his apostolic power. Now St. Paul had to vindicate his personal dignity and liberty and right as an apostle. He had persisted in working for his own living at the trade of the tent-maker, in which he had been brought up, and his malicious enemies argued that he did so because he felt that he could not press his claim to maintenance, as did the other apostles. "The followers of St. Peter, with malicious ingenious logic, argued from this practice of St. Paul that his dignity and authority were thereby proved to be somewhat inferior to that of St. Peter and the Lord's brethren, who were supported by the Christian Church." In this chapter St. Paul declares his apostolic liberty and rights, especially iu three matters. I. His RIGHT OF ENTERING INTO SOCIAL RELATIONSHIPS. St. Peter had a wife. Other apostles were married men. .A.nd St. Paul might have been had he choseu to be. H he voluntarily refrained from entering into this social relation, because of the limitations which its responsibilities would entail on him, and because of the itinerant character of his labours, no one need assume that he abandoned his rights or fai:ed to recognize them. Had he so minded, he could have made both wife and family chargeable to the Churches, and the burden those who loved him would gladly have borne. Voluntary abstention from the pressing of a man's rights ought never to be construed as the surrender of those rights. So St. Paul lays down the true and only principle upon which the celibacy of the clergy can be recognized. Every clergyman has tho riqht to "lead about a sister, a wife," but any clerµ;yman may refuse to exercise his right, an<l may voluntarily set his own liberty in bonds, if he thinks that ho may thus gain o. higher power in the service of his Divine Lord. 'l'he principle is equally applicable in the life of the ordinary Christian. Abridgments of liberty are oftentimes necessary, and yet more often advisable, but they never involve abandonments of rights. Constantly the Christian man says, " I may, but I will not-I will not for Christ's sake." II. His RIGHT OF WORKING FOR l!'IDEPENDENT MAINTENANCE. This was certainly a peculiarity in St. Paul, and no doubt other teachers felt it to be a kind of reproach upon them. llut St. Paul never argues that it was a necessary duty for others. Any other man might feel it a duty, just as he did; but he had no intention of making his conduct in this respect even an example. He was placed in peculiar circumstances; he was of a singularly sensitive temperament; he laboured among all classes, and was anxious to keep away everything that might be rua<lo a reproach of the gospel; ho was determined to make his motives quite clear, aud so he would receive from the Churches uo mainteuance, only, iu times of necessity, some kindly and helpful gifts. Now, wo 31S THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. 1x. 1-27.

nc~d not even sa:i: that St. P~ul was right in this. He had an unque~tioued ministeriat ch11m to support m carnal thmgs. \Ve can only say he had a ri<>ht •~!so to exercise his liberty, and work for his own living, if he chose so to do. Tho~e who work for their li,·ing may serve Christ in the preaching of his gospel· and those who preach his gospel may work for their living, if they prefer so to do. ' lll. Hrs RIGHT OF CL.\I:MING TIIE DUE REWARDS OF ?;-- WORI[. (Ver. 7.) Th'l.s is urge_d by three figures: ~he support of the soldier in "., r; al.IC 1>artaking of the fruitage of 111s vmeyard by t?e vmc-dresser; and the sharing of the milk, given by the cattle, by hin~ wh~ has them Ill charge. The true rewards of Christian s•irvice for others are (1) thelf lovmg confidence and esteem; (2) the expressions of that love in their holy lives and la hours; and (3) the more personal expressions of their love in <>ifts and care and kindly concern for the temporal well-being of their teachers.-lt. T. " ,

Vers. i-12.-The duty of supporting the ministry. The separation of certai11 rncmhcrs of the Christian Church to the specific work of the pastor, the teacher, or thc missionary, may be said to have begun at the election of the "seven," commonly called "deacons," which is nar:a~ed in Acts vi. 1-6. Then certain persons gave themselves up to the study and mm1stry of the Word and to prayer. The question how they were to be fed and supported was at once met by the members of the Church, who, in response to a natural and reasonable demand, and in full accordance with the principles. and practices of the Mosaic dispensation, made provision for their material necessities. Our Lord, in sending out his disciples on their trial mission, had laid down the principle that they should not supply their own material wants, because "the labourer is worthy of his hire." Much has been said in recent times against an organized Christian ministry, dependent on the good will of the several Churches they may serve; but the Scripture cannot be read with unprejudiced mind, and the reader fail to perceive that "they whopreach the gospel should live of the gospel." In the verses now before us St. Paul urges the duty of supporting the ministry by three lines of argument and illustration. I. BY COMMON WORLDLY ILLUSTRATION. 1. The soldier, who, if he fights the battles of his country, reasonably expects his country to provide for his maintenance and his comfort. 2. The vine-dresser, who expects to reap in fruitage the reward of his labours in the vineyard. 3. And the keeper of a flock, who day by day lives upon the milk of the flock. These illustrations only touch the general principle that the worker has a claim to a portion at least of the results of his labour. The illustration of the soldier is the one most to St. Paul's point, because, while doing a special kind of work for us, he looks for our care of his temporal necessities. So the minister, in doing. a spiritual work for us, commits to us the care of his" carnal things." II. BY SCRIPTURE RULES. (Ver. 9.) The law is taken from IJeut. xxv. 4. The figure is that of the oxen, who were driven to and fro over a hard space of ground, called a. threshing-floor, on which the corn-stalks were spread, so that by their "treadings" the grain might be separated from the husk. Those oxen were engaged in doing work for the good of others, and it was only fitting that they should be provided for while they laboured. . III. BY THE RITUAL LAWS oF THE OLDER MosAISM. (Ver. 13.) Priests and Leviteshad special maintenance, and this almost entirely by the offerings and good will of the people. They had certain towns allotted for their residence, certain portions of the sacrifices for their food, and certain tithes for the supply of their other necessities, and such a regulation could in no sense be regarded as an unreasonable burden. St. Paul even, declares, upon his apostolic authority, that" Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." When we have sufficiently proved that the material support of a spiritual ministry is one of the first duties of the Christian professor, we are prepared to argue and to illustrate further that a genei-ous, liberalr hearty, and even self-denying provision is comely and noble; and that in securing such. generous provision our thankful love may find a most fitting expression.-H. T.

He had persisted in working for his own living at the trade of the tent-maker, in which he had been brought up, and his malicious enemies argued that he did so because he felt that he could not press his claim to maintenance, as did the other apostles. "The followers of St. Peter, with malicious ingenious logic, argued from this practice of St. Paul that his dignity and authority were thereby proved to be somewhat inferior to that of St. Peter and the Lord's brethren, who were supported by the Christian Church." In this chapter St. Paul declares his apostolic liberty and rights, especially iu three matters. I. His RIGHT OF ENTERING INTO SOCIAL RELATIONSHIPS. St. Peter had a wife. Other apostles were married men. .A.nd St. Paul might have been had he choseu to be. H he voluntarily refrained from entering into this social relation, because of the limitations which its responsibilities would entail on him, and because of the itinerant character of his labours, no one need assume that he abandoned his rights or fai:ed to recognize them. Had he so minded, he could have made both wife and family chargeable to the Churches, and the burden those who loved him would gladly have borne. Voluntary abstention from the pressing of a man's rights ought never to be construed as the surrender of those rights. So St. Paul lays down the true and only principle upon which the celibacy of the clergy can be recognized. Every clergyman has tho riqht to "lead about a sister, a wife," but any clerµ;yman may refuse to exercise his right, an<l may voluntarily set his own liberty in bonds, if he thinks that ho may thus gain o. higher power in the service of his Divine Lord. 'l'he principle is equally applicable in the life of the ordinary Christian. Abridgments of liberty are oftentimes necessary, and yet more often advisable, but they never involve abandonments of rights. Constantly the Christian man says, " I may, but I will not-I will not for Christ's sake." II. His RIGHT OF WORKING FOR l!'IDEPENDENT MAINTENANCE. This was certainly a peculiarity in St. Paul, and no doubt other teachers felt it to be a kind of reproach upon them. llut St. Paul never argues that it was a necessary duty for others. Any other man might feel it a duty, just as he did; but he had no intention of making his conduct in this respect even an example. He was placed in peculiar circumstances; he was of a singularly sensitive temperament; he laboured among all classes, and was anxious to keep away everything that might be rua<lo a reproach of the gospel; ho was determined to make his motives quite clear, aud so he would receive from the Churches uo mainteuance, only, iu times of necessity, some kindly and helpful gifts. Now, wo 31S THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. 1x. 1-27.

nc~d not even sa:i: that St. P~ul was right in this. He had an unque~tioued ministeriat ch11m to support m carnal thmgs. \Ve can only say he had a ri<>ht •~!so to exercise his liberty, and work for his own living, if he chose so to do. Tho~e who work for their li,·ing may serve Christ in the preaching of his gospel· and those who preach his gospel may work for their living, if they prefer so to do. ' lll. Th'l.s is urge_d by three figures: ~he support of the soldier in "., r; al.IC 1>artaking of the fruitage of 111s vmeyard by t?e vmc-dresser; and the sharing of the milk, given by the cattle, by hin~ wh~ has them Ill charge. The true rewards of Christian s•irvice for others are (1) thelf lovmg confidence and esteem; (2) the expressions of that love in their holy lives and la hours; and (3) the more personal expressions of their love in <>ifts and care and kindly concern for the temporal well-being of their teachers.-lt. Vers. i-12.-The duty of supporting the ministry. The separation of certai11 rncmhcrs of the Christian Church to the specific work of the pastor, the teacher, or thc missionary, may be said to have begun at the election of the "seven," commonly called "deacons," which is nar:a~ed in Acts vi. 1-6. Then certain persons gave themselves up to the study and mm1stry of the Word and to prayer. The question how they were to be fed and supported was at once met by the members of the Church, who, in response to a natural and reasonable demand, and in full accordance with the principles. and practices of the Mosaic dispensation, made provision for their material necessities. Our Lord, in sending out his disciples on their trial mission, had laid down the principle that they should not supply their own material wants, because "the labourer is worthy of his hire." Much has been said in recent times against an organized Christian ministry, dependent on the good will of the several Churches they may serve; but the Scripture cannot be read with unprejudiced mind, and the reader fail to perceive that "they whopreach the gospel should live of the gospel." In the verses now before us St. Paul urges the duty of supporting the ministry by three lines of argument and illustration. I. BY COMMON WORLDLY ILLUSTRATION. 1. The soldier, who, if he fights the battles of his country, reasonably expects his country to provide for his maintenance and his comfort. 2. The vine-dresser, who expects to reap in fruitage the reward of his labours in the vineyard. 3. And the keeper of a flock, who day by day lives upon the milk of the flock. The figure is that of the oxen, who were driven to and fro over a hard space of ground, called a. threshing-floor, on which the corn-stalks were spread, so that by their "treadings" the grain might be separated from the husk. Those oxen were engaged in doing work for the good of others, and it was only fitting that they should be provided for while they laboured. . III. BY THE RITUAL LAWS oF THE OLDER MosAISM. (Ver. 13.) Priests and Leviteshad special maintenance, and this almost entirely by the offerings and good will of the people. They had certain towns allotted for their residence, certain portions of the sacrifices for their food, and certain tithes for the supply of their other necessities, and such a regulation could in no sense be regarded as an unreasonable burden. When we have sufficiently proved that the material support of a spiritual ministry is one of the first duties of the Christian professor, we are prepared to argue and to illustrate further that a genei-ous, liberalr hearty, and even self-denying provision is comely and noble; and that in securing such. generous provision our thankful love may find a most fitting expression.-H. entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-St. Paul an exception. He wishes it to be understood that he does. precisely what he thinks to be right, but does not wish the peculiarity of his conduct to be made a model for other~. '!'here arc things in lifo concerning which each man muBt make his own individual stand, upon which he may find himself compelled to·

take an individual and exceptional line. And he may do this withont opposition to others, without making himself in any way objectionable. St. Paul found sufficient reason for the adoption of a singular course of conduct in relation to his apostleship or ministry. He would receive nothing in a way of payment or reward from the Churches amon"' whom he laboured. His reasons probably were: 1. That the older apostles never quit; approved of his work, and he found it better to act in an independent way, and make no one responsible for his modes of work, or the advanced truths which ,vere given him to teach. 2. That he was, throughout his missionary labours, keenly watched by active and bitter enemies, who were ever ready to misrepresent his· conduct, and fashion accusations against him. He well knew how promptly they would seize on his receiving payments, and declare that he was mercenary, and only preached for selfish eDds. 3. That he had, in his hands, a kind of skill-that of tent-making-which he could readily turn to account wherever he went. It was most important that he should give his enemies no opportunities or advantages against him; an<l he would even refuse some of his rights and privileges, if the assertion of them could be made into a. hindrance of his work. We must ask both what is lawful and what is expedient, both what is necessary and what is htcoming. ,ve must beware of forcing our rig/its, as they may stand by the rule and by the law; an<l we should see that our personal and individual conduct must be ordered so that the impressions which others receive from it shall be helpfnl to them and to the Church. We must watch against even unintentionally causing offence and hindering Christ'swork.-R. T.

They cannot be precisely compared with anything that we 1rn"l"e in modern times, because they were regarded by the Greeks as great national .and religious festivals. Dean Stanley, writing of these Isthmian games, says, "This was one of the festivals which exercised so great an influence over the Grecian mind, which were, in fact, to their imaginations what the temple was to the Jews and .the triumph to the Romans." The training was very severe, conducted upon carefully prescribed rules, and desi<Tned to nourish vigorous physical power and precise skill for the kind of contest in wbiih the man was to engage. 'l'he providential dealings with men are meant to afford opportunities of training for their life-work. 2. How men .are required to meet the" law of training" by making personal efforts to secure fitness for the work to which they are called, such training taking the general form of sonl- culture, and the specific forms of adaptation to work. It applies to all the passions of the body, indul~ences of the appetite, and relationships of the life. The Grecian philosopher says," Wouldest thou conquer at the games? any. Everything is at our service and for our use, within careful limits, and these limits :no rules can fix, only our own good juclgment decides them. Ill. '1'1rn LAW OF SELF-MASTERY. (Ver. ~7.) '!'his reminds us that training means trial, and temperateness means severe and painCul dealings with self. '!'he contest ~1· life is between the regenerate will and the enslaved and corrupt body with its inclinations and motions (see-Rom. vii.). St. Paul says that the renewed will must hold tl11: body in subjection and service. But such complete ~elf-mastery is the product of Ion'..'. struggle. '\"er. 21.-The relation of personal consistency to public labours, The expression use,1 by the apostle here, and translated, "I keep under my body," is literally, "I strike under the eye; I beat black and blue" (comp. Luke xviii. 5). Mastery of the body, repression of the lusts and indulgences and evil inclinations of the body, a strong hand upon the "self," are necessary to ensure "consistency;" yet what is the worth of a Christian teacher whose life tells one story and his lips another? St. Paul contemplate, with horror the possibility of his preaching the gospel to others, and, by reason of hi, personal inconsistencies, proving at last a" castaway." No amount of religious profession, no fervour in religious work, no mere utterance of religious sentiment, can avail without personal and practical consistency of life. On this point we dwell further. J. THE SENSES IN WHICH PERSONAL CONSISTENOY AND PUDLIC LADOUR ARE DISTDICT THINGS. It may be urged that the question is one of gifts for a particular work, and not of personal character. It may be said that we do work with the skill and power entrusted to us, and the good workman may be personally of good or bad character. However true that may be in common life-and we should be prepared to contest its truth even there-it cannot possibly be true in the religious spheres, because all Christian work is the impress of the man himself, is inseparable from the force which his character gives to it. Exactly what we ask for in religious spheres is not mere truth, but truth with some stamp of personal conviction upon it; not mere duty, but duty pressed on us by the force of some holy example. The true preacher is the man who bears in on us the force of his own life and feeling. The true teacher is the man who can win our confidence in himself. '!'he true visitor benefits and blesses the poor and the sick by the resting~ and comfortings of his own quick sympathies, that come from sanctified character. So in the religious spheres there can be no separation between holy character and faithful labour. Show that, just here, serious mistake is made, and much seeming service is unacceptable to God and of no real value to men. II. THE P0SSIDILITY OF THE INCONSISTENT MAN DOING GOOD WOJll{. In view of what has been said in the previous division, it would seem to be an impossibility, but those remarks may be limited to the higher forms of Christian work and tho exertion or spiritual influence. Scripture teaches us, by its examples, that God claims tho service of oven ungodly men, and deigns to work by them. Of Cyrus Goel says, "I girder! thee, though thou hast not known mo," etc. But perhaps thero is no distress in life like th:i:. which we feel on finding that those who have helped us in our religious life fail morally. When such distress comes to us, we are almost ready to make shipwreck of our faith. III. 'fHE FORCE ADDED TO ALL GOOD wonK DY THE CONSISTENT CHARACTER OF Tm: WOllKER, Reviewing tho influences for good which have rested upon our life, wo can but feel that the holiest and mightiest and best have come from consistent and holy mcu and women, who bore upon us the force of saintly character, and whose memories still keep us true and faithful. Vvhen McCheyne died, 11 noto was found unopened on his study table. It was from some one who had recently been brought to God throu;;h his preaching, but the note said it was not so much the truth that had impressed, as tho 11incerity and holy fervour of the preacher. It is the great secret of the highest work. What a man is tells more for the honour of God o.nd the blessing of men than merely what II man does. So we may be warned by the apostle, and take heed lest, while working for others, we ourselves should prove "castaways."-H, 'l'. I, CODINTIIIAISB, V THE: FIRST EPISTLE '1'0 THE CORINTHIANS. It may be urged that the question is one of gifts for a particular work, and not of personal character. It may be said that we do work with the skill and power entrusted to us, and the good workman may be personally of good or bad character. However true that may be in common life-and we should be prepared to contest its truth even there-it cannot possibly be true in the religious spheres, because all Christian work is the impress of the man himself, is inseparable from the force which his character gives to it. Exactly what we ask for in religious spheres is not mere truth, but truth with some stamp of personal conviction upon it; not mere duty, but duty pressed on us by the force of some holy example. The true preacher is the man who bears in on us the force of his own life and feeling. The true teacher is the man who can win our confidence in himself. '!'he true visitor benefits and blesses the poor and the sick by the resting~ and comfortings of his own quick sympathies, that come from sanctified character. So in the religious spheres there can be no separation between holy character and faithful labour. Show that, just here, serious mistake is made, and much seeming service is unacceptable to God and of no real value to men. II. THE P0SSIDILITY OF THE INCONSISTENT MAN DOING GOOD WOJll{. In view of what has been said in the previous division, it would seem to be an impossibility, but those remarks may be limited to the higher forms of Christian work and tho exertion or spiritual influence. Scripture teaches us, by its examples, that God claims tho service of oven ungodly men, and deigns to work by them. Of Cyrus Goel says, "I girder! thee, though thou hast not known mo," etc. But perhaps thero is no distress in life like th:i:. which we feel on finding that those who have helped us in our religious life fail morally. When such distress comes to us, we are almost ready to make shipwreck of our faith. III.
