sbo?ld protest eo_ stron~ly agai!1st ~be shocking abuse of the Lord's Supper among the Co_nnth1ans.. W1!h this fe~st, msti~ute~ and consecrated by Christ himself, its puq,ose bemg to brmg him back mto their midst and to enable them to realize his comin~ a_gain, the two ideas _being closely joined,-with _this tender. re'!1em bra nee and expect,:= t1on they h_ad associated se!1~ual pleasures, eatmg and drmkmg to excess, separatin::=; themselves mto classe~, desp1smg the Church of God, and bringing condemnation upon themselveH. What of Christ was in all this? Instead of memories of bis sacrificin.l death, instead of their personal recollections of his providence and grace in their behalf, instead of touching and humbling recallings of how he had dealt with each of them, what utter forgetfolness, what a closing up of every avenue of the past opening inw the present, and what a concentration in the animal gratifications of the hour! Instearl of anticipation and joyous hope, looking to the Lord's comin"', what blindness to all but the transient festivities of the carnal senses! On this acciunt (therefore) "many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep." The reference is not to the weakness an~ sickliness that folio~ the violations of natural laws, nor is the sleep the falling asleep ID Jesus, but a punishment sent from God and executed under the directive agency of providence. Just in proportion as a man realizes Christ in the past will be realize him in the future. Just in the degree that he loses him from the past of his own heart, in that same degree will he vacate the future of his glorious image. 'l.'he present is all, and it is all of the senses. And when God ar;ses to judgment, as in the case of the Corinthians, what a sudclen intensity surcharges the present, the blessedness of the old yesterdays and the awaiting to-mon-ows nil extinguished, and the immediate moments, once so fugitive and so eager to glorify themselves by larger additions, lingering now and lengthening in the keener consciousness of pain and remorseful anguish! "Judge yourselves," 0 Uorinthians ! Examine your hearts ; return to your memories and expectations; go to the cross of Christ and learn the lesson of its self-sacrifice; condemn and punish yoursel.es for the guilty past; and make this discipline of self a chastening for future well-being. But let no true and humble soul be tortmed by the thought of eating and drinking "unworthily," and thereby incurrin:2: "condemnation." Whoever comes to the Lord's Snpper after a close self-exarninntion nidcd by the Spirit, and brings to it a meek and trustful mind; whoever repnirs to it after he hns communed with his memories of Christ's goodness to him,-will be a worthy participant in the sacred rite, and rnny surely expect the seal of God's approbation. A Christian child may understand the essential idea and spirit of the institution. And yet it has connections that transcend all thought, and the soul of every devout communicant welcomes the mysterious glory with which it is invested. Charles Wesley sings for every believer when he says- " His presence mokes the fenst, And now our bosoms fool The glory not to be expressed, The joy unspenkoblo." L.

entries.title: 1CO 11:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Imitation. The personal feelings of the npostle come out in these Epistl~• to the Corinthians perhaps more than in any othor of his writings. '!'his may woll have been because at Corinth his authority wns questioned, and other teachers were by some exalted as his rivals or superiors. 'fhat he should resent such treatment from those who were under peculiar obligations to him we cnn well umler8tn.ml; and it is very natural that he should be led all the more boldly to vin,licnte his npostolic character and to assert his apostolic authority. '!'hero is self-con(hlence of a ju~t and warrantable kind in the admonition and challenge of this language: " De ye imit,1tors of rue." I. THE PRINCIPLE TO WHICH THE APOSTLE HERE APPEALS-IMITATION. 1. It is 0. principle natural to all mankind. Most conspicuous is it in the co.se of chilclren and young people, and in the case of the uncivilized and unt1~tored, who ~a.nnot ensily acquire knowledge through symbols, but who le_arn arts with great facility t,hrough imitation. 2. Its range of operation is as extensive as the nature of man. V,i c trn.ce it in exercise in tho bodily life, for multitudes of acts and of arts nro acquired by those 374 THE FIUST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cH. u. 1-34.

,vho carefully copy the proceedings of others. We trace it in the mental life: wavs of thinking, of regarding life generally and one's fellow-men in particular, moral judg- ~nents and b~bits,-all are _oll'.in~ largely to imitation. 3. It is of set purpose employed m all educat10n; for the d1sc1plme and culture of the young is almost dependent upon the operation of this interesting and most powerful principle of human nature. II. TIIE GREAT AND GENERAL uSE WHICH CHRISTIANITY MAKES OF THIS PRINCIPLE. 1. In the Holy Scriptures, espcci:\lly of the New Testament, men are summoned to be followers, imitators of God, in all his moral perfections. It is represented that the excellences which are supreme and glorious in him may inspire us with the desire and resolve to copy and to acquire them in our measure for ourselves. 2. Jesus Christ is set before us as the especial Object of our reverence, as the hio-hest Model for us to study and to imitate. It is possible that, through our reverence for him as our Divine Sa,iour, we may lose sight of the fact that he is also our human Exemplar. We are summoned to grow up in all things unto him. 3. Yet this grace of imitation is to be ours, through our response to the love of Jesus and our participation in the Spirit of Jesus. It is not a mechanica.J, but a spiritual, intelligent, living process. We must love with the love of admiration, sympathy, congeniality, in order that we may be changed into the same image. Ill. THE SPECIAL APPLICATION PAUL MAKES OF THIS PRINCIPLE. 1. Religion permits us to study human models of excellence and to aim at conformity with such. Thus the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews sets before his readers illustrious examples of faith, as a practical and powerful principle governing and inspiring human nature and life. And here Paul requires of the Corinthians that they should be imitators of him. How many Christians in all ages have been fired with this noble ambition! And how wonderfully has it proved for the advantage of the Church and of the world that it bas been so! i. The limitation set to this principle: " Even as I also am of Christ." This was an acknowledgment of the Lord's supremacy; in copying Paul, the Corinthians were ouly to be copying Christ, as it were, at one remove. 3. The extent to which this imitation was designed to go. Surely they might, and we may, be imitators of the apostle, in his love to Christ, in his devotion to Christ's cause, in his affliction for Christ's people, in bis obedience to Christ's laws, in his willingness to suffer for Christ's sake, in his wise forbearance with the infirmities of the brethren, and in his overflowing and very practical brotherly kindness and charity. In these respects it is not possible to follow Paul without at the same time following Christ.-'f.

entries.title: 1CO 11:2
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Apostolic authority a11d traditions. In using language so imperious to all seeming as this is, St. Paul spake as an apostle, i.e. as one sent and commissioned by the Divine Head and Ruler of the Church. That be should use such language at all is very instructive and significant to all who read the Epistles and desire to receive them in the appropriate and intended spirit. I. APOSTOLIC INDIVIDUALlTY AND AUTHORITY ASSEilTED. "That ye remember me." "What an assumption is here of importance and peculiar authority! It was Paul's great concern that bis couverts should remember Christ: does he here set himself up as a· rival of the Lord? By no means. But he claims to be the minister, the ambassador of Christ to the Churches, whose words are to be received as the words of one speaking by the Spirit of Christ. Readers of the New Testament are by such language reminded that the inspired writers, through their personal, intimate, official relation to Christ, have a claim upon the respectful attention and the cordial faith of those who profess to lie Christ's. II. 'l'Hl> ODBERVANCE OF INSPIRED TRADITIONS ENJOINED. In Christianity there is an 1lement of law and an element of liberty; and these two elements are in harmony each 1vith the other, the two being necessary in order to the completeness of the dispensation, In some passages even of this Epistle stress is laid upon freedom; whilst in this verse stress is laid upon subjection. Traditions, communications, of a religious kind had been committed by the apostle to these Corinthians. What were these? 1. Traditions or doctrine. It was from Paul's lips that many of them had first heard the gospel; to Lim all were indebted for the systematic exposition of its glorious truths. 2. 'l'raditions of precept and conduct. This letter is itself full of such; for Paul combined, in e. remarkable and admirable manner, the functions of the teacher of truth and those of -OH, :u. 1-34.] THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 375

the ethical instructor. 3. Traditions of discipline. As soon as societies were formecl, it became necessary to draw up and promulgate regulations for the internal government .and ordering of such societies. They naturally looked to insp;red apostles for direction, how to proceed, and they did not look in vain. The context shows us how dependent the first Churches were upon apostolic guidance for the maintenance of their order and. the administration of their offices and affairs. III. SUBJECTION TO APOS'l'OLICAL DIRECTIONS COMMENDED. We gain here an insight into the very mixed character of the members of the primitive Churches. Much in tbeiL· conduct is in this very Epistle censured with something like severity; yet praise is not withheld where praise is due. There is a kind of praise which is dangerous, which involves insincerity on the part of those who offer, and fosters pride on the part of those who receive it. Yet the general fault amongst men and amongst Christians is unduly to withhold praise. Such commendation as this of the apostle could not but encourage and stimulate to a cheerful and resolute obedience to the injunctions of apostolic and Divine authority.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 11:3
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The hierarchy. Before entering upon particular counsels with regard to the attire of the two sexes respectively in the Christian assemblies, St. Paul lays down a great general principle, from which, rather than from custom or from experience, he deduces the special duties devolving upon the members of Christ's Church. The case upon which he was consulted, and upo1L which he gave his advice, has lost all practical .interest, and is to us merely an antiquarian curiosity; but the great principle propounded in connection with it holds good for all time. I. THE APPOINTED SUBORDINATION OF WOMAN TO MAN. There is a. sense in which there is equality between the sexes. In Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female. The gospel is intended for and is offered to both men and women. Both are equally -dear to him who died for all. As in Jesus' earthly ministry he wrought cures ancl expelled demons for the relief of women, and as he chose certain women as his personal .friends, and as he willingly accepted the affectionate and generous ministration of other women; so in the dispensation of the Spirit he numbers women amongst his people, antl honours them by promoting them to his service. There is, so to speak, spiritual eq unlity. But domestic and social equality is quite another thing. In the household and in the -congregation there must be subjection and submission. "Order is Heaven's first law." "The head of the woman is the man." And this notwithstanding that many men arc base and unworthy of their position nnd calling; not withstnnding that many women file not only pure, but noble and well fitted for comman,l. ll. THE ARCHETYPE IN SPIRI'l'IJAL AND HEAVENLY llELATIONS TO WHICH THIS ORDER CONFORMS. 1. Man is not suprnme, though invested with u. limited authority. "The head of every man is Christ." He, the Son of man, has the prnnacy over this humanity. In wisdom nnd in righteousness, in power and in ~race, the Lord Jesus is superior an,l supreme. The law is revealed in him and admiuistered b_y him. Every man is morally bound to subjection and submission to the Divine Man. And he is Heatl over all things to his Church. 'J'his is the truth, the ideal, the purpose of eternal wisdom; though, alas I often misunderstood, or forgotten, or denied by men. 2. Even in the Godhead there iR an official subordination of the Son to the Fnther; "the head of Christ is God." This language takes us into the region of heavenly things, of Divine mysteries. But it reveals to us the fact that the universe is one great hier- archy, of which not every member is mentioned here, only certain leading dominant notes being successively sounded in the celestial scale. Men may suppose that onlcr nod subordination in human society, civil and ecclesiastical, are merely expedients fur pe,,ce and quietness. But it is not so; there is Divine archetype to which human relationships and affairs conform. Let there be non-conformity to this, ant.l there is ◄ iisconl breaking in upon the harmonious minstrelsy of the spiritual universe. Let there be conformity, and the sweet concert proves that earth is iu Luno with henven.-T.

Ver. 7,-.711an the image and glory of God. The Dible is tho book of pnrauoxcs; .and, if it were not, it would not correspond with the facts of human nature and history. Nowhere do we find such an exposure of human sin and such denunciations of human guilt ns in the Scriptures. And, on the other hand, nowhere do we meet with sucu 376 THE FIRST EPIS'l'LE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. x1. 1-34.

majestic representations of man's grandeur and dicmity. There is a depth in this simple but inspiring language which we cannot fathom; but we may remark some particulars in which it is verified by facts. I. MAN IS Goo's IMAGE AND GLORY IN HIS FORM AND FEATURES. 'rhis seems to be asserted in this passage. Why must not man's head be veiled when in the sacred assembly he draws near to tbe Father of spirits, the Lord of the universe? Because "he is the image and glory of God." This does not imply tlmt the Divine Bein" possesses a body as man does. No sue!~ anthropomorphism is suggested in the texi:. But so far as matter can be moulded mto a form which shadows forth the Divine majesty, it bas been so fashioned in the construction of the human frame and features. High thoughts, n?ble impulses, pure desires, tender sympathy, these-the glory of humamty-are written upon the countenance of man. II. IN HIS INTELLE~TU.~L AND ~ORAL ENDOWMENTS. This is probably what is meant by the declaration m Genesis that God made man in his own imaa-e. In his ca_pacity to apprehend . truth! in bis recogniti?n of moral excellence, in b~ power of will, man resembles his Maii:er. And there 1s no way by which we can arrive at a knowledge of God in bis higher attributes other than by the aid of the nature with which he has endowed us, and which he has declared to be akin to bis own. III. IN HIS POSITION OF SUBORDINATE RULE OVER THE CREATION. The psalmist asserts that God crowned man with glory and honour, and set him over the works of his han<ls, putting all things under his control. '!'bus did the Lord of all delea-ate to his vicegerent an authority resembling his own. IV. IN THE Bn0TIIERH00D OF JEsus CHRIST. The assumption of human nature by the eternal \Vord was only possible because man was originally made in the Divine image. It is wonderful to fiud language so similar used concerning man and concerning the Son of God, who is described as "the emanation from the Father's glory, and the very image of his substance." The Incarnation seems a necessity even to explain the nature of man; it casts a halo of glory and rndiance around the human form, the human destiny. For the Incarnation was the condition, not only of a Divine manifestation, but of the redemption of humanity; and Christ's purpose was to bring many sons unto glory. V. IN HTS FuTURE OF ETERNAL BLESSEDNESS. All things which show forth God':; glory are passing and perishing. Man alone of all that is earthly is appointed for immortality. 'l'he mirror that reflects so bright a light shall never be broken; tl10 glory which man receives from heaven and returns to heaven shall never fade.-'!'.

entries.title: 1CO 11:20
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-" The Lord's Supper." 'fhe abuses and disorders which prevailed in the Corinthian Church served as an occasion for an apostolic exhibition and inculcation of a more excellent way. Incidentally, we are indebted to them for the account given by the apostle of the original iastitutfon, and for instructions as to the proper observance of the ordinance. The designation here applied to the distinctive observance of the Christian Church is one of beauliful simplicity, and suggests an exposition of the acknowledged nature and benefit of the ordinance. I. THE DIVINE AUTHORITY OF THE LonD's SUPPER. 1. It is an ordinance of Christ, and its observance is consequently an act of obedience on the part of his people. It is not a service of man's device ; the Lord h~mself has said, " Do this." 2. It is :\ tradition of apostolic times. Paul professed to have "received from the Lord that which he delivered." The sacrament was accordingly celebrated within a generati01~ of Christ's own lifetime, and has been celebrated in unbrolrnn continuity from thai time to our own. 3. It was in the first century a regular observance of the Christian societies. 'l'hie is apparent from the way in which it is mentioned in this Epistle; it is treated as something actually existing, although in some cases misunderstood and abused. And as Paul writes, "As oft as ye," etc., it is presumed that the observance took place regularly and frequently. II. '.l.'HE D00TRlNAL SIGNIFICANCE OF THI!: LonD'B SUPPER. 1. It is a memorial of Christ, and especially of his death. He himself appoiut.ed that it should be observed "in remembrance of" himself and of his sufferings whose body was broken and whose blood was shed for his people. 2. It is a Eucharist, or service of thanksgiving. 'l'h19 Institutor of the ordinance "gave thanks," or "blessed," probably upon the suggestion of the cup of which the Jews partook durin.11; the Paschal meal. 'l'be sacrament is OH, xr. 1-34.] THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 377

a reminder of all the benefits which we have received from God, and especially of the "unspeakable gift." 3. It is a symbol and means of spiritual nourishment. Spiritually,. the communicants eat the body and drink the blood of their Saviour, partakina and, feeding upon Christ by faith. The real presence of the Redeemer is experi~nced in the heart of the faithful recipient. 4. It is a bond of fellowship and brotherhood. Hence called a communion, or the communion, as the appointed means and manifestation of a true spiritual unity. The brethren of the family are seated at one table, they join in one meal or sacred feast, they eat of one loaf and drink of one cup. III. 'l'HE SPIBITUAL PROFIT OF THE Loan's SUPPER. 1. It is a divinely appointed means of increased and more vivid fellowship with the uuseen Redeemer, who in this service draws near to those who draw near to him. 2. It is a profession of faith, attachment, and loyalty, the admitted and enjoined method or declaring Apon which side we stand in the moral conflict which rages, under whose banner we have enlisted, and whom we purpose loyally to serve. 3. lt is a testimony to the unbelieving world around. The death of Christ is proclaimed, not only to those within, but to thosewithout. More effectively than by words, men are reminded that the grace of God and. the salvation of Christ have come very nigh unto them.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 11:26
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Tlie Church's proclamation. What so fitted to rebuke those who profaned: the Supper of the Lord, what so fitted to arouse them to a s.ense of their high calling:, as a solemn declaration like this? 'fhe noisy, greedy, quarrelsome gatherings which. seem at Corinth to have been associated with the professed observance of one of the highest mysteries of the Christian faith, naturally awakened the indignation and the reproaches of the apostle. Recalling them to a sense of the dignity of their position aewitnesses to God in an ignorant and sinful world, the apostle summons the Corinthian Christians so to eat the bread and drink the cup of the Eucharist as to declare to all the sacred tidings of a Redeemer's death. I. THIS SACRAMENT IS A COMMEMORATION OF THE PAST. 'l'he Lord's death was Ill) admitted fact; and if anything was needed to establish the historical fact, the existenc" of this ordinance was sufficient and more than sufficient for the purpose. But men may forget and lose sight of an event which they do not dream of denying. An,! it seemed good to Divine wisdom that the crncifixion and sacritice of the Sun of G0<l should be held in everlasting memory by means of this simple but most si;ruilicant observance. It was not simply as an historical fact that tho death of Christ was; to be recorded, but as a Christian doctrine. Christ's was n redeeming, atoning, reconciling death ; nnd as such was cherished in el'erlasting memory by those who profited by it, who owed to it their eternal hopes. II. 'l'HIS SACRAMENT IS A PROCLAMATION TO 'l'HE PRESENT. "Yo set forth, or proclaim. the Lord's death," says tho apostle. And from his expression, "as often," it mny be inforred that periodically and frequently the primitivo Christians kept the feast, remem bcring aud declaring that "Christ our Passover is slain for us." '!'here is something very affecting and at the 8amo time very inspiring in this representation. From generation to generation and from age to age the sacrament of the Lord's body and blood publishes salvation to mankind, telling of him who tasted death for every mnn, and in his cross reconciled the world unto God. It is an aspect of the Holy Communion which should not bo left out of sight, upon which great stress should bo laid; for some, whom words may fail to reach, may havo their hearts openctl to the grace and love of Chri~t by witnessing tho silent yet eloquent declaration concerning the Saviour which is presented when the members of Christ's Church partake of the symbols of their redemption, ill. Tms SACRAMENT IS A Pl\EDICTION OF THE FUTUI\E. " Till he come! " Our Lord, in instituting the ordinance, had turned tho gaze of his disciples towards tbo future, speaking of drinking wine new in the kingdom of God. And here the eyo of faith is pointed on to the glory which shall be revealed when he who came to c\ie shall come to judge, shall come to reign 1 "And thus that dnrk betrayal night, With the Inst advent wo unito Dy ono bright chain of loving rite, Until he come I" T. S78 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORIN1'HIANS. [cH, xI. 1-84.

entries.title: 1CO 11:1–16
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Decency in pnblic worship. When we appear before God we should 0~1s,m·c the greatest pruprie~y.. Ei:--ternal_s should not be lost sight of, for they are s1g11ificant. Often they are rnd1cat1ve of mward condition. The apostle had occasion to blame the women of Corinth for laying aside the veil-the mark of mouesty and subjection-in public assemblies. On the ground of the abolition of distinction of sex in Christ, th~y claime_d equality in every respect ,vith men, >lnd the right to appear and act as men did. \Vhtlst women, they would be as men. Equality as believers they had a right to claim, but they forgot their "subjection in point of order, modesty, and seemliness." When women leave their proper sphere, it is never to rise, but to fall. Men-women are failures. In the apostle's argument valuable truths artl enunciated. . I. HE i_->EFIXES MAN'S 1:osrTION. 1. Man is the head of the woman. (Ver. 3.) \Voman 1s subordrnate to man, 1s largely dependent upon him. He is her natural guide defender, supporter. Authority lies with him, not with her. "I suffer not a woma~ to . . . usurp authority over the man . . . for Adam was first formed then Eve" (1 Tim. ii. 12, 13). w·oman is the" weaker vessel " (1 Pet. iii. 7). She is t~ be "in sub- jection" (eh. xiv. 34). This is after the Divine-order, and any subversal of it is sure to lead to injurious results. 2. The head of rnan is Christ. (Ver. 3.) Man is not a monarch; he is subordinate to the God-Man as his Head. Man can only act aright as head of the woman when he recognizes Christ as his Head. The apostle does not mean to intimate that Christ is not the Head of the woman as of the man. He is pointing out the order in the Divine economy, and "by the term 'head 'he expresses the next immediate relation sustained." Man is subordinate to Christ; woman is subordinate, though not in the same sense, to man as well as to Christ. To further illustrate the Divine order, the apostle states that: 3. Tile head of Christ is God. That is, of Christ the God-Man. There is nothiug here which conflicts with the doctrine of the divinity of Christ or of the equality of the Son with the Father. Rather is there here additional evidence of the former, since the distinction between the position of man and woman obtains where there is identity of nature. Christ is here spoken of as he assumerl "the form of a servant." Christ in his mediatorial capacity is lower th:i.n the Father (John xiv. 28). 4. Man is the Image and Glory of God. (Ver. 7.) Man was made in the likeness of God (Gen. i. 26). How great is the dignity of human nature! But how that dignity is lost when God is blotted out of a man! How eagerly should fallen creatures seek recovery, that the blurred image may he restored to its original beauty, and the impaired glory made once more lustrous! Through the Son of man, the ideal Man-declared to be " t.he brightness of his glory and the express image of his person "-this may be effected. '!'he apostle docs not intend to con"ey that woman is not in many respects the image and glory of God, but that man is this "first and directly, woman snbsequently and indirectly." Man represents the authority uf God; he is tile ruler, the head. II. HE DEFINES WOMAN'S POSITION. 1. She is snbject to man as her head. She spran~ from him (ver. 8). She was created for him (ver. 9). Still, there is mutual dependence: "Neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man" (ver. 11). "In the Lord "-this is of Divine appointment. And man and woman constitute complete humanity-one supplying what the other lacks; and thus forming in Christ "the Bride," the Church redeemed by his blood. And further, although at 1irst woman sprann from man, now the man is of the woman (vcr. 12). But "all things are of God "-mm7 and woman. Man has a real but qualified supremacy; so qualified as to save "·oman from any humiliation, and to allow her a position of peculiar dignity and beauty. 2. She is the glory of the man. (Ver. 7.) Woman is not directly the glory of God; she cioes not directly represent God as the head of creation-sl-.e rather 111 man's representative, as man is God'~. She is the glor_y of man directly, of Goll indirectly. Man is the sun, woman the moon (Gen. xxxvn. 9). III. HIS C0?-'CLU6IOKS AS TO PllOPllmTY OF DRESS IN PUBLIC WORSHIP. 1. That man shoul,d not have Ids head covered. The covering woi;ld indicate subjection, which, in relation to those joinirw with man in puulic worship, was not man's true condition. There he appeared as "file image and u\ory of God," representing the Divine headship, and to assume the badge of suhjcetion °;vould be to "dishonour his head." This may mean to dishonour bis own head by placing upon it something unsuitable, or to dishonour Christ, the Head of man, who has placed man in his position of honom. Wo ,cH. xr. 1-34.] THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 370

•should not usurp a higher position than Goel has appointed for us; we should not take a lower. Our best place is where God places us. :.:. That woman should have her head covered. The veil was a recognition of subordination and an indication of modesty. To discard it was to claim man's position and thus to dishonour man, her bead-or to dishonour her own head by depriving it of a mark of propriety and even of chastity. For by discarding the head-covering a woman put herself in the class of the disreputable. It was but a carrying out of the principle involved for a woman to have her head sbave,l (vers. 5, 6), which was sometimes done in the case of those who had forfeited their honour, and became thus a brand of infamy. Thus a woman snatching at the position of man would descend far below her own. An apparent rise is sometimes a very real fall. The apostle enforces his argument by : (1) An appeal to nature (vers. 14, 15). Paul evidently thinks that there is accord between the kingdom of naturo and of grace. Both are from one hand and one mind, and conflicts between the two may be very apparent, but can never be real. Nature gives the man short hair and the woman long; here i6 a natural distinction which should be observed, and which indi- cates that woman specially needs the bead-covering. Or by nature the apostle may mean "what obtains among men who are not instructed by revelation. Among many . of the heathen the wearing of the hair long by men was ridiculed, but long hair for women was generally recognized as appropriate. (2) The presence of angels in Christian assemblies (ver.16). Earth looks on, but heaven also. Woman should have the symbcl of power, of subjection to man, upon her head, because any usurpatiQn of improper position or flaunting boldness would be offensive to these heavenly visitors. (3) Apos- tolic authority (ver. 10). Where reasoning fails, authority must utter her voice. Paul always preferred to convince rather than to compel. But he possessed the right to determine when the contentious persevered in contention. The regulation was accord- ing to the mind of an inspired apostle, and was observed by Churches founded by him- self or other like-minded leaders. In estimating the teaching of the passage, we must discriminate between the necessary and the accidental. 'l'he principle is that women should be so attired as to indicate, or at all events so as not to conflict with, their right- ful position. Amongst those to whom the apostle wrote, the veil was the symbol of modesty and subordination. Because women in Western Churches are not so nttired, it does not follow that they are acting antagonistically to the apostle's precept, though it will be admitted by most that the preposterous head-genr of many female worshippers, in our own land calls loudly for reform, and is frequently an outrage upon all propriety and a sarcasm upon womanly modesty. I do not understand that the apostle has here specially in view the praying and preaching of women in public assemblies-this he deals with further on in the Eµistle (eh. xiv. 34, etc.); but he is now insisting upon what is approi:riate in the attire of woman (and incidentally of man) on public occasions. His primary reference is to public worship, and surely when we come to "appear before God," we ought to be most specially anxious that everything about us shall be decent and in order. Whilst nothing that is outward can compensate for absence of the inward, that which is external is often an index of the internal, and has its influence upo11 tho interno.1.-H . . Vers. 17-22.-Some hindrances to the right observance of the Lord's Supper. Holy institutions may become unholy by perversion. That which is bestowed upon us as a peculiar blessing may prove a very renl curse by misuse. The ordinance of the Lord's Supper is for our spiritual help and joy, but we may "come together not fur the better, but for the worse." This was so with many of the Corinthians. 'fhey had conjoined to the Lord's Supper the love-feast. To this feast each brought his provision, the rich bringing more, so ns to supply the deficiencies of the poor. From. this supply the bread and wine required for the Lord's Supper were taken. These feasts were the occasions at which the evils reprobated by the apostle occurred. Tho poor were despised and neglected, the congregation became divided into cliques, somo communicants were hungry, and others had drunk to excess. The apostle insists that, under such circumstances, it was impossible to observe aright the sacred feast .of the Lord's Supper. Noto some hindrances to right observance thus suggested. I. PnmE. At the Lord's table all are equal. Conventional distinctions disappear. There is one Lord, and "all ye arc brethren." Arrogance and conceit, always out of 880 'l'HE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [en. xr. 1-34-

pl11;ce and intol!'rable_, are most ~trikingly so where all should be humbled and subdued. It 1s 1;1ot for us to thmk there how excellent we are, but how vile, and to admire the amazmg grace which rescue~ us from the dominion of sin. Instrad of despising others there, we should rather despise ourselves for our sins which crucified Christ, and we should feel, like Paul, that we are "the chief of sinners." It is utterly impossible for a proud heart to rightly show forth the death of him who was meek and lowly. It is preposterous and absurd to attempt it. II. SELFISHNESS. How can the. selfish )iave corumu'!li.on with the infinitely unselfish One! If we have a self-seekmg, graspmg, greedy spmt what part can we have "·ith him who" gave h~rnse_lff~r us"? How alien \o the spirit .of Christ is the spil'it of selfishness! If we sit 'IVlth 1t at the table of the Lord, we sit tn,ere as Judas did. III.. EsTRANG~ME::--T. Christ calls us ever to union, and most specially and pathetically at his table, where we eat of the one bread (eh. x. 17). To cherish a spirit of disunion is to run directly counter to one of his commands at the moment when we profess to observe another. And the spectacle of estrangement at the Lord's Supper must be one of utmost offensiveness in the Divine sight, as it is one of greatest scandal in the eyes of men. If we seek to be one with Christ, we must also seek to be one with the brethren. He is the Head; we are the members of his body. How utterly incongruous to be disunit,ed at that feast which specially sets forth our union with Christ and with one another! IV. HATRED. This in some form generally accompanies division. But where is the place for hatred at the feast of dying love? God is love, Christ is love, and we are-hatred. How can two walk together unless they are agreed? What reason our Saviour had to hate us! "He was despised and rejected of men," crucified hymen; and yet he loved men, and at his table his love is specially set forth. How can we there cherish our animosities, for whieh we have such little cause! "We know that we have pas~ed from death into life, because we love the brethren. He that loveth 11ot his brother abideth in de,ath" (1 John iii. 14). 'l'he Lord's Supper is a song of love; hatred at it is a terrible discord. V. GLUTTONY. Some of the Corintliians loved their meat more than they loved their brethren. They ate greedily, not even tarrying for others to arrive. A singular carnality for so spiritual a season. Men with the manners and unrestrained appetites of beasts are scarcely fit for the table of Christ. Sensuality and spirituality are at opposite poles. Those who abandon themselves to gratify the lower nature sacrifice the higher. "Man shall not live by bread alone." VI. DRUNKENNESS. It seems scarcely credible that any should have drunk to the excess of intoxication at the love-feast so intimately associated with the Eucharist; but it is to be feared that this was so. And there are degrees of iutoxication, so that the dancrer of imitating the Corinthians in this matter may not be so remote from some as the/'imagine. There is a great deal of semi•intoxication. And if this sin be not committed immediately before the Lord's table is approached, undue indulgence at all is surely a fatal hindrance to right ob~ervancc. No dmnl_rnrd shal! inheri~ th_e kingdom of heaven. And no drunkard, whilst be cleaves to his degradmg ho.bit, 1s entitled to a place at the Lord's table. VII. !RnEVEnENCE. There must have been vast irreverence in the Corinthians rebuked by Paul, or such abuses could never have obtained amongst them. '!'here may be as much irreverence in us, thongh we do not commit the same sins. Anyway, to approach the Lord's table irreve.rent.ly is to instantly demonstrate our unfitness. There we should be filled with godly fear, and our hearts should bo subdued to greatest devoutness anrl awe as we marvel over the justice of Jehovah, the amazing sacrifice of Christ, and the tender ministry of the Divine Spirit, whereby we who weM once afar off are brought nigh.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 11:23–26
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The sacred feast. Paul's description ie singularly beautiful. His information apparently came directly from Christ (Gal. i. 12). Additional importance attaches to the observance of the Lord's Supper, since an express revelation was ma4e to the great apostle of the Gentiles. The supper was for the Gentile world as well as the ,Jewi8h. Jts institution was associated with the preaching of the gospel throughout the world. • • oH. xr. 1-34.] THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 381

I. l'l·s INB'l'ITUTION. By tho Lord Jesus (ver. 23). 1. Persrmally. Evidently important in his eyes. Specially precious to us because instituted personally by our Master. Appropriate; for he in his great redemptive work is set forth. Christ is" all in all" at his table. As Christ was present at the first celebration, he should be looked for at every celcbrntion. 2. Under most affecting circumslcmces. "The same night in :which he was bet-rayed;" whilst betrayal was proceeding-and this known to him. (1) He thought of others rather than of himself. Might have been expected to think of his sufferings; he thought of our needs. He had sorrow, but no selfish sorrow. 'l'he unselfishness of Christ is here shown in unrivalled beauty. (2) His love was not quenched by treachery. The betra_val by Judas did not dry up his fount of affection. When treachery was at its height, love was at its height also. ,vhen men are most anxious to injure us, we should be most anxious to do them good. (3) His sacrifice ·was not arrested by hate. 'l'he multitude were hotly against him when he prepared to give himself {or them. Outside the upper room and inside in th1; breast of Judas there was bitter hate, but Christ was not checked in his purpose for an instant. He resolved to go on and to fulfil all that had been foretohl respecting him, and so he quietly and calmiy instituted the supper which should in every after age testify to incomparable self-sacrifice under all-adverse conditions. If we would be like Christ, -hostility must not hin<ler sacrifice. II. lTs MODE. 1. Thanhgiving. Thanksgiving for the bread and wine. We should not "say grace" but really "give thanks." Perhaps to teach us that our ,thanksgivings should ascend for what the bread and wine typify. 2. Bread. (1) Symbolic of Christ's body. Not actually his body, seeing that that was intact and before tbe eyes of the <lisciples. If Rome's teaching were true, the disciples would have required a vet·y lengthy explanatiou to enable them to grasp the meaning. We have no such explanation recorded; we might have expected it in this place, H anywhere. (2) Broken. Many see in this a symbol of the violent death of Christ. But the better rendering of ver. 24 is, "'l'his is my body which is for you." Breaking the bread was, I rather think, the mere adoption of a custom suited to the kind -of bread used at that time iu Palestine. We read, "A bone of him shall not be broken." (3) Eaten. Indicatiug that we are to feed upon Christ spiritually, to appropriate, .to assimibte, him. 3. Wine. Symbolic of Christ's blood shed for the remission of sins. Partaken of to indicate the application of the blood of Christ to our hearts and -consciences. 'l'ho blood must not only be shed, it must be npplied. III. lTs SIGNIFICANCE. 1. Remembrance of Christ. Of his dying love specially; and of his life, lordship, etc. 2. Communion with Christ and with each other. (See eh. x. 16, 17.) 3. .A feast. We feed upon Christ spiritually. As bread and wine support the body, so he supports the soul. '!'here is a physical symbol and a spiritual reality. Joy should be one element in the obsen·ance; it is a feast, IJot a. funeral. 4. A covenant. Vve enter into coveuant with God for pardon, peace, service, nnd the covenant is ratified by the blood of Christ typified by wine: "'l'his ,cup is the new covenant in my blood." 'l'he Hebrews entered into covenant with God when the bloou of the heifer was sprinkled upon them; they bound themselves to obedience, nud God bound himself to bestow the promised blessings; so when we receive the cup, we commemorate the covenant which we have entered into with Gml .through the shed blood of Christ and the covenant which he has entered into with us. 5. Proclamation of Christ's death. Christ's death is the great central fact shrLllowed forth. The cross is exalted. Not a now sacrifice offered, but the old yet ever-new sacrifice of Calvary commemorated anu shown forth. 6. .A pledge of the Lord's second coming. "Till he come." He will come, and it is not for us to say, "My Loni -<lelayeth his coming." He will come not too soon and not too late. "'fill ho come " we must be watching. IV. ITS INCUMDENCY. "This do in remembrance of me." A dying command. .Some believers have many excuses for not coming to the Lor<l's table; they do not find one here: " This do." Last requests of loved ones are held precious: should not the request of this loved Oue be also? In this command our welfare is consultcu as in all Divine commands laid upon us. We lose much if we refrain from doing this in ,remembrance of our Master-much spiritual joy, enlightenment, strengthening, and. not a little usefulness. The Lord's table is the J<:lim of Ghristiaus; we act foolishly THE FIRST EPIS1'LE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [oH. x.1. 1-31►

if we fail to embrace opportunities of resting beneath its palm trees and drinkincr0 from its many wells of living water.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 11:24
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Remembering O!trist. The Lord's Supper is very specially a feast of remem- brance. Is there in it a suggestion that we are very prone to forget Christ? '!'his i$, alas! our tendency, and here we are in strange contrast to our Lord. He needs. notbing to keep us in his remembrance; he ever thinks of his people. In the institution of tbe Lord's Supper he thinks of our forgetfulness, of its perils, of its certain sorrows. He remembers that we are prone not to remember him. ,vhat should we remember concerning Christ? I. Hxs HOLY SPOTLESS LIFE. What a life that was! 'l'he greatest and best of human leaders have been marked by defects, but our Leader was "without blemish." In the lh·:s of heroe_s there. is alway_s something which we s~ould be glad to forget; but there 1s not!twg m the hfc of Chnst. Jealousy, hatred, malice, and all uncharitable- ness could _find in ~1im "no fault;'' Many great men have grown small, many holy men questwnable m character, many honoured men dishonourable, under the ruthless criticism of modern times; but not Jesus of Nazareth. The fiercest Jicrht has been focussed upon his earthly course; the brains of sceptic and of scoffer hav;been racked in prolonged endeavour to discover the flaw; but it has not been discovered yet I The Yoices of all the centuries cry, "Without fault! " "Holy and undefiled!" "Separate from sinners!" \Veil may we remember that life. II. Hrs TE.A.CHING. When compared with Christ, all the other teachers of the world seem to have nothing to teach upon matters of high moment. At best they guess, and often they guess folly. He teaches with the authority of knowledge; all other teachers seem hidden in the valley, imagining what the landscape may be. He alone has climbed the hill and beholds what be speaks about. We need to remember, more than we are accustomed to do, the utterances of the world's great Teacher. Seekers after knowledge should be careful lest after all they miss the richest mine of truth. Learned scoffings and atheistical ribaldries are naught but devil-blinds to hide from our view the beautiful form of truth as it is in Christ. In him "are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col. ii. 3). When God broke the dread silence upon the Mount of Transfiguration it was to exclaim, "This is my beloved Son: hear· him." The Holy Ghost was promised as One who would "bring to remembrance" what Christ had declared. Through the Lord's Supper, as a meaus, the Divine Spirit works now for this end. III. Hrs MIRACLES. These speak eloquently of his power. Nature bows before her God. How weak the mightiest of the earth are compared with this mighty One! ·when the kingdom of Christ is about to be overwhelmed and shattered and generally annihilated by blatant wiseacre warriors, with their sceptical pea-shooters and atheistical popguns, I laugh as I remember that it is the kingdom of Ghrist which is being assailed! We do well to bear in mind what Ghrist did when he was upon earth, and then to say quietly to ourselves, "'l'be same yesterday, to-day, and for ever." What he did, he can do; what he was, he is. His miracles illustrated his beneficence. They meant the supply of liv.man need, the binding up of wounds, the restoration of the outcast the arrest of sorrow, the wipin" away of tears, the cheer of lonely hearts. We must r;member his miracles; they sh~w so truly what the Christ was. With all his omnipotence, bow gentle and tender I IV. H1s DEATH. This was the grand culmination of his life; it gave to him the great title of Saviour; to it the Lord's Supper specially points. We must remember him as the One who laid down his life for us, who bore our griefs and carried ·our sorrows, who was wounded for our trangressions and bruised for our iniquities, who died the just for the unjust that he might bring us to God. '1'1e Lord's Supper leads us to Calvary-throu"h the motley crowd, past the wecpiug Marys, beyond the peniteut thief, to the central figure in the Judman tragedy, and there we see salvation I "Mercy and truth are met together: righteousness and peace have kissed each other" (P~- lxxxv. 10). Remembrance of Christ's death will mean remembrance of our sinfulness. And when we remember that "he endured tiw cross, despising the shnme," we may ask ourselves the suggestive question, "What would be our preseut condition and prospect if I.le bad not <lone so?" OH, XI, l-"---34,J '!'HE Fl){S'l' El'ISTLE 'l'O THE CORINTHIA~S. 383

V. His RESURRECTION AND ABCENs10:-i. The Lord's Supper was for the rcmembrancG of Christ both after he had died and after he had risen from the <lea,!. We must not forget tho dying Christ; but neither must we forget the· triump!,ing Christ. The resurrection of Christ is the counterpart of the cross; one is not without the other. The Lord died, but the Lord i8 risen indeed. He came to this world in abasement; he lived so, he died so, but be did not depart so. He rose from the dead, and ever liveth. We remember the dying Christ, but we remember also the living Christ, ··.xalted at God's :::ight hand, our Advocate, preparing our heavenly home, looking down upon us, present with us by his Spirit. "\Ve remember the reignin_~ Christ, the Onewho has completed his glorious redemptive work, who bas triumphed openly, and we remember him thus "till he come." VI. His MARVELLOUS LOVE. Shown in every incident and every instant of his course. In his coming; in his words, deeds, spirit; and pre-eminently in his sufferings and death. God is love; Christ is God; Christ is love. VII. His PERSONALITY. Not only what he said and what he did, but what he was. All his acts and words of beneficence and love were only expressions of himself. They were but manifestations of what dwells in perpetual fulness in his heart. Remember him. "This do in remembrance of me." '!'his is a dying request. Are we observing it P The dying request of him who" gave himself" for us.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 11:27–29
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Perils at the Lord's table. A frequent question, "Who should come to the Lord's table?" Many have come who ought not to have come as they were; not a few have been ,leterred from coming who were quite suitable. Many have not pondered sufficiently the duty of observing the Lord's Supper; many have been alarmed by certain expressions contained in this passage. I. GLANCE .c\T THE SCENE. It lies in gay, voluptuous, immoral Corinth. A city magnificent externally; abased and abandoned internally. A meeting of Christians in some private house, light amid darkness, truth surrounded by error, holiness in the centre of corruption. The gathering is for the love-feast and the Supper of the Lord. A love-feast, alas! in which love is largely absent; a i::,upper of the Lord in which the Lord is strangely dishonoured. The light is dimmed, the truth iE alloyed with error, the holiness is defiled by guilt. 'l.'here are divisions (eh. i. 11, 12); there_ are pride, selfishness, irreverence (vers. 21, 22); there is even drunkenness (ver. 21); yea, even further, the hideous head of immorality is raised in the midst of this little Christian society ( eh. v. 1). This Epistle arrives from the founder of the Church-a letter _smiting Corinthian transgression and transgressors hip and thigh. Picture the scene! JI. GLANCE A.T CERTAIN WORDS AND THEl!t MEANINGS. 1. Damnation. This won] has so terrified some that they have never been able to summon sufficient courage to obey the dying command of their Lord. 'l.'hey havo supposed that an unworthy participation in the sacred feast would seal their doom and consign them to perdition without remedy. Dut tho word does not justify such a view. Instead of "damnation," we should read, as in the Revised Version, "judgment." Aud ver. 32 explains what "judgment" means: "When we are judged, wo are chastened of tho Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world." J udgment here means "chastisement," and note particularly that this chastisement is sent to prevent us from being condcm11ecl w·ith unbelievers. ,vhat follows upon unworthy participation at tho Lord's table, if we are believers, is not something to destroy us, but somcthi11g tu prevent us f,·om being destroyed. If we will not benefit by the chastisement, if under it wo harden our hcr1rts like Israel of old, then wo shall be cast away. 'l.'ho sin of unworthy participatiOll is great, and the correction will be severe, but neither is what some sensitive natures have dreaded. 2. Unworthily. :Note that the apostle speaks of the 1111 worthiness of the act, not the unworthiness of the person. 'l.'o say, "I am unworthy," is doubtlc~s to speak tho truth, but it is irrelevant. Unworthy persons may participate worthily. Nay, further, only those who feel that they are unworthy aro in a right stato to sit at the table. The self-righteous are never "fit." The supper is for penitent sinntrs ; for such as Paul, "the chief of sinners." But the act may be unworthy, and thr1t from many causes. Anything that hinders us from "discerning the Lord's body" (ver. 20) will cause us to eat and drink unworthily. "\Ve have to recognize the bread and wino as emblems of that body, as set apart to show this forth, aud therefore to :384 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. xr. 1-34.

be dealt with solemnly, thoughtfully, reverently. We must enter into the meanin"' of the feast, and through the outward re11ch the inward and spiritual. At the supper we do not halt at the emblems; we have fellowship with Christ, we remember him we renew our vows, we profess to be his followers, we show forth his death "till he cor:ie." Now, many things may hinder us from doing this, and thus cause us to eat and drink -unworthily; such as: (1) Thoughtlessness, leading to irreverence. (2) Ignorance of the meaning of the ordinance. This may be very culpable ignorance. (3) Unconverted -con<litiou. Quite unfit for supper because have nut received what it sets forth. (4) \Vorldly spirit. " Ye cannot serve God and mammon." We may be trying, and thus be charging_Christ with falsehood, eve_u as w~ approa?h his table. (5) Unbrotherly feeling. That which separates us from believers 1s very likely to -separate us from Christ. (6) Immorality. If we hug sin, we cannot embrace the Saviour. Such unworthy participation involves: (1) Guilt. We become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord seeing that our sin is concentrated upon that observance which specially sets thes~ forth. (2) Punishment. "For this cause many are weak and sickly amonu you and many sleep" (ver. 30). Present chastisement, and, if this prove ineffic~cious' future ar.d final punishment. ' III. A REMEDY. This is not to see that " we are good," according to a very current expression aud impression. In one sense we can never be "fit." ]t is to examine or prove ourselves by (1) appeal to conscience, (2) God'~ Word, (3) God's Spirit. And what we have to ascertain is whether we (1) revent of sin, (2) believe on tbe Lord .Jesus Christ, and (3) are seeking to live in the fear and love of God. If we are right upon these points, Wfl need have no dread in approaching the Lord's table, but rather draw near in joy and confidence aud in anticipation of large spiritual blessing. IV. A WAR::,;-~G. Remark that none are here told to absent themselves from the Lord'~ table. Not even the Corinthians most blamed, an apparent exception being the immoral person (eh. v. 1), and he was excluded only until he had shown repentance for his sin (2 Cor. ii. 7, 8). The reason is that to abstain from the Lord's Supper is .to siu. We ought to be "fit," in the true sense oi the expression. There is only one place which is right for us, and that is at the table. We may be wrong in coming; we must be wrong in staying away. To refrain is to condemn ourselves at once. " This do in remembrance of me" is one of the most sacred of commands. If we are bound to break it because of our carnal and lost state, we do but multiply transgression. We are not bound, for we may escape from the condition which unfits us, and then draw near with boldness and with hope. 'fhere is a false humility restraining many from coming to the Lord's Supper; it is a very false humility and a very deceptive humility -it is the adding of another sin. Away from Christ we are altogether wrong, and in escapin~ from one sin (coming to the table whilst unconverted) we only fall into another (disobeying the dying command of Christ). There is every obligation resting upon us to repent, believe, and live to God; then we are fitted to discharge the other Db]iCTation, "This do in remembrance of me." Failure in the one involves failure in the other, and our condemnation is increased. There is no right place for the .unbeliever.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 11:31
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The clwstisement of believers. The apostle has been speaking or disorders at the Lord's table and of the Divine judgments which in Corinth had .followed upon the profanation of the sacred feast. He now pursues the latter theme and discourses upon the afflictions which sometimes fall upon the people of God. I. ITS lNFLICTOR, We may well ask," Where do our troubles come from?" 'l'he chastisement of bis people cumes from God. " Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth" {Heb. xii. 6). God is behind the sorrow. Reflect that: 1. lle sees sufficient cause for the chastisement. This shows that there is sufficient cause. He never sends a trouble without a cause, and never without a sufficierd cause. We may not see th~ cause, but he does. 2. He might destroy instead of chastising. '!'here is mercy in the visitation: had there been wrath only, there had been destruction, not chastisement. 3. He may destroy. If chastisement does not bear fruit unto repentance, \\'O shall be cut off as was Israel of old. Here is a solemn warnin" acrainst resisting and resenting Divine chastisement. If we Btiffen our neck and harden °onr heart, we shall be broken with a "rod of iron." We are in the hands of the Omnipotent; let us beware of folly and impiety. 4. Chastise- oH. XL 1-34.J 'l'HE FIRST EPISTLE 'l'O THE CORINTHIANS. 385

ment is a message from God. '\Ve should listen. '\Ve should learn what the Lord our God has to say to us. '\Ve shall find in the chastisement a command; it is for us to obey that command, We shall discover in it a promise; it is for us to embrace it. II. ITs CAUSE. Always sin in some form or other. Sin is the only possible cause. God does not affiict us "willingly" or for his "pleasure," but for our profit. We fall into sin and he whips us out. So when a believer transc,resses he cuts a rod for his own back. Is it God who chastises us? More truly, we ~hastise ourselves. Our sin puts the rod into God's hand. We cry out when we have hurt ourselves if we cry out when we are under the chastisement of God. III. ITS BENEVOLENCE. It is sent in love. It is a good gift, not an evil one. God has not changed in sending it; he is still love. Here the special object of Divine chastisement is beautifully conveyed : "'!'hat we should not be condemned with the world." Many think that their afflictions will destroy them ; the afflictions arc sent that they may not be destroyed. We feel that we shall sink under our troubles, but they are sent that we may notsinlc. We cry out" Poison!" but it is" medicine," sent to keep us from being poisoned. God troubles his people now, that he may not trouble them hereafter. He smites them gently now, that he may not smite them then with the arm of destruction. '!'hey stand near the precipice and the rod falls upon them to drive them back. In heaven, perhaps, we shall bless God more for our earthly chastisements than for our earthly joys. Chastisement is sour to take, but sweet when taken. It is a nut hard and rough of shell, but goodly in kernel. It is the love of God transfigured into darkness by the black shadow of our sin. IV. How WE MAY AVOID THE NECESSITY OF IT. "If we would judge [or, 'discern'] ourselves, we should not be judged." If we dealt with ourselves, there would be no need for God to deal with us. If we would avoid the chastisement, we must avoid the sin. If the cause be destroyed, we need not fear the effect. If the Corinthian» had examined themselves, they would have avoided the irregularities of which they became guilty. They were careless, unwatchful, o.nd so they fell, and when they fell th,y opened the door of chastisement. We may keep that door shut if we" walk with God," as Enoch did. The only way to escape the rod is to escape the necessity or it, and that is to escape the sin.-H.
