entries.title: 1CO 16:6–18
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-St. Paul and his purposes; his friends; earnest exhortation. If the apostle were before us in his Epistles as an inspired man of genius only, whose intellect teemed with great thoughts, and whose heart was absorbed in supplying fervency to· those thoughts, his hold upon us would be weakened. 'rho man has nolhing about him of the intellectualist. Among the varieties of mind and character that have 658 THE FIRST EPISTLE 'l'O THE COHINTHIA;'.\S. Leu. xvi. 1-24.

arisen from time to time in the development of humanity, turn for a moment to the ideal of an apostle, and tell us if the conceptio1, of such a person is not somethina- unprecrdentcd, an idea altogether original with Christianity. A new a·nd most maiTellous form of a public man-not a representative man, not a typical man in no sense either the one or the other, since the man antedated the Church and had no continnat.ion in the Church after its opening century. Take your ideals of philosopher poet, military chieftain, statesman, ruler, ancl tell us what resemblance these bea; to the character St. Paul sustained and the office he filled. Or take the worthiest dignitaries of the Church, and follow the procession as it moves, now in splendour and then in gloom, from the hills of Rome, over the Alps, through the forests of Germany, by the Hhine and the Rhone, over England, Scotland, and .America, and see how they compare with him who fought with beasts at Ephesus and died daily. Quite as remarkable as the conception of this ideal was its realization in St. Paul from his con,ersion to his death. Look at the matter in another connection. What -is the final test of greatness viewed in relation to society? Is it not the ease and freedom of access to the common heart of humar.iity, the magical power to create sympatl_iy and fellowship, the God-like capacity to pass through the shallow feelin"s of admiration and conventional honour--often more of a tribute to our own vanity th;n to the worth of others-and to gain entrance to the depths of truthful affection? Beyond doubt, this was St. Paul's greatness. Just from an argument, that must have put an extraordinary pressure even on his great abilities, and which was well calculated, as all intellectual men know, to make him insensible, or at least indifferent at the moment to the details of life, he is not forgetful of his brethren, but hope~ to pass the winter in their midst. ".A flying visit" (by the way) will not satisfy his love. But, for the present, he must "tarry at Ephesus." Why he would stay in this city, be states-" a great and effectual door is opened unto me;" the field of usefulness is lar~e and promises vast results. Stay he would, moreover, because "there are many adversaries." .Adversaries were the men to convert; if not that, to silence ; but, any way, he will not desert a post of duty to gratify bis desire to see the Corinthian brethren. If the Lord will permit, he will refresh himself among them, but, for a time, he will face the worshippers of Diana and bear the brunt of persecutiou. Then he thinks of the young Timotbeus. If he visit you according to his expectation. be thoughtful of his youth, be specially considerate of his modesty, and ·see that his ~tay among you is "without fear," disturbed by none of your rivalries and factions. Honour him for his work's sake, for "he worketh the work of the Lord, as I also do." "Let no man therefore despise him;" on the contrary, "-send him on without annoyance, with good understanding, and kindly affection','' that he :tnd bis travelling companions may come unto rue. .Again, some of the partisans at Corinth might suspect him of jealousy as to A polios. The name of the eloquent and holy man had become a watchword of strife. Lest they should do St. Paul this dishonour, he tells them of the affectionate relations between them ; nor will he say my brother, but " our brother .Apollos," whom he wishes "greatly" to visit the Church at Corinth. But see! One of those sudden changes which originate in the soul, which pass from the soul into the nerves, and from the nerves into the muscles-one of those quick escapes from memory and stored-up emotion-occurs, and what an intenser expression settles in the !s IDUscles about the eyes, and in the eyes themselves! There a break in the thought. 'l'wo verses intervene before the main idea is resumed. .And 1t could hardly have been otherwise. It is nature to the life; it is St. Paul in the very soul of bis temperament. It was scarcely possible for the apostle to mention .A.polios without being reminded of the unhappy divisions at Corinth, for we can neither think nor feel except, by means of association and suggestion. Each faculty, each sensibility, is an individual centre of 1hesc activities. No wonder, then, that there is an abrupt transition, all the more true tu the laws of mind because abrupt. "Watch ye." .Ah! if there had been Christian watchfulneRs in the Corinthian Church, what criminations, what reproaches, what humiliations, had been averted! To be a man, one must be apprehensive of the danger~ ever lurking in ambush; must have the sentinel spirit and habit, and must exert it every moment. "Stand fa6t in the faith." Occasional watching will not do; steadfastne,s must go along with watchfulness, and fortify you against the wiliest assault. "Quit you like men." No manhood can live without courage; be manful. .l!'ighting 1s ~11. X:VI. 1-24.] THE FIIlST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 559

your snfety, business, profession; fight like men, fight on, fight to the end. "De strong," or as it is in Eph. iii. 16, "Strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man." Bnt fight how? There are many sorts of fighting-business fightin" profes- sional fighting, legislative fighting, alas! even Church fighting. And there they arc, each class of fighters with his particular weapons and his code of warfare. Only in this are they all alike, viz. the fighter gets the help of the animal soul. Beastly fi"htin" he abhors; the fighting which b!"ings hot blood and excited nerves and quick bre~thin~ into service, he admires, encourages, and depends upon for victory. Not so is St. Paul~ view. "Let all your things be done with charity "-love, and, after his grand discourse on "love," an allusion is enough. To have a gentlemanly intellect in our fighting is a .rare thing and a great thing, but to have a loving intellect in fighting for what we believe to be truth is much rarer and infinitely greater. Christian fighting is a very unusual excellence. From this emotional digression, he returns to " the house of Stephanas." This family were "the firstfruits of Achaia." How he likes the figure! St. Paul had baptized this household. They have "addicted themselves to the ministry of the .aaints." What the precise ministry was, we know not, but we know that it was a kind, beautiful, noble service, for it was rendered to the "saints." Think of the manifold ministries that Christianity set a-going. It is Anno Domini, say, 57. Chris- tianity has in its Churches men of the generation that saw Christ die, that beheld him .risen, that witnessed Pentecost. ,Jerusalem, though approaching her overthrow, still shows the temple where he taught, the spot where he was crucified, aud the grave where he was buried. In this short space of time, what numerous workers have entered on careers of beneficence! From the apostles downward through all grades of kind an,\ loving agencies, mark the variety, the diffusion, the heterogeneous civilizations, the unity, the accordant response, the consecration, pervading these Christian ministries. Mark it, we say; for it is a solitary phenomenon, up to this time, in human annals. Mark it, we repeat; for all the antagonistic forces of the world are in league to crush it, nnd they are reinforced and augmented by Satanic power. 'l.'ake a single specimen, the household of Stephanas. No information is given as to his social position, no mention made or the sphere or spheres of usefulness filled. Enough to know, it was a" ministry" and a blessed one, since it was "a ministry to the saints." Yet we may picture that Corinthian home in the midst of a. mongrel aud licentious population, keeping alive the fervour of its love and the purity of its privnte heart, watching, standing fast in the faith, courageous and strong, and abounding in the work of the Lord. ,ve may be sure that the poor, the sick, the infirm, were duly cared for and helped, and that tbe home itselr was devoted to hospitality. Now, says the apostle, "submit yourselves unto such." '!'here are two kinds of submission-one to authority, the other to influence. We ucc,\ both. vVe need law, we need grace. Law and grace are coexisting constituents in modern civilization so far as Christianity has permeated, and, in our times, influence hns assumed a very significant relation to govemment and society. We are governetl much more by influence than authority. St. Paul urges that Stephanas and his housc- ·hold be respected and honoured, their wishes consulted, their ju<lgments followed. And not only they, but "every oue that helpeth with us and bbouretb." Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus had come from Corinth nnd visited St. Paul at Ephesus, am\ "they have refreshed my spirit and yours." 'l'hey had been sent as representatives or the Corinthian Church. The comfort and cheer were mutual; let them be acknowledged -(valued, recognized) for these good offices. Wise instruction this; to be influenced by excellence in others, and submit our minds to such a gracious power, is the strongest of all evidences that we are on the path of culture and piety. l!'or it has pleased Got! -0ur Father, not only to reveal himself in Jesus our Lord, but he manifests himself also in thoso who are Christ's. D:scipleship is a revelation nnd an inspiration. All the ministries are of God. 'l'hey are his presence, his helpfulness, his glory, among the habitations of men. And whether it be the "ministering spirits sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation,'' or the lowly ministrations that fall in the silent dew and breathe in the hidden violet, they are alike frolll him who "worketh J\ll in all."-L.

entries.title: 1CO 16:19–24
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-0losing wcrds. The salutations follow: first, from the Churches of Asia: then from Aquila and Pr:scilla, honoured names in the Churches; again from 6G0 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. XVI. l-2L

the Ephesian brethren. Let them renew their fellowship and pledp;e their love ouain "with a holy kiss.'' The work of the amanuensis over, St. Paul adds the salutation, from himself with his own hand, •• The salutation of me Paul." And the words follow "Ir any man love not the Loni Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema," let him becom~ nccursed ; "Maran-ntha," the Lord comes. Between the greeting "of me Paul" and " the gra~e of our Lord ,Je_sus Christ be wite yo_u," followed i~medi,\tely ~vith "my ]ol"e be with you all m Chnst Jesus. Amen, this utterance of mtense feehn<Y occurs. "'hnt his tone of mind was, we understand fully from the chapter, which ;.'i:presses confidenet>, hope, and brotherly affection. \Vhat his emotions were at the inst11nt we know from the salutation which precedes and the benediction which succeeds' the· Anathema Maran-atha. The warning is terrible, but it is one of love and tenderness. Had he been less conscious of the obligation to love the Lord Jesus Christ, less sensible of its immeasurable worth to the soul, less aware of the stupendous folly and guilt of rejecting it; or if the profound sense of that love had not been present in the full blaze of his own consciousness ;-then, peradventure, words less stern and denunciatory might have been used. As it is, he speaks from the same high level of love to God and man and the sentence of condemnation has its preface in a greeting and its sequel in; benediction. So closes this wonderful Epistle. Writing under the zenith of his years, if we rate those years by the chronology of his preaching and pen, St. Paul comes before us in its successive pages as one whose temperament, nervous vigour, observation, culture experience, had been so far co-ordinated and interblended as to fit him, in an eminent degree, to give birth to this production. Never did a human soul exhibit its individu- ality more perfectly through all its organs of expression. Those organs are varied in every man. They were singularly diversified in the apostle. He cannot reason long without waking other forces of utterance. Imagination, in its form of relativity rather than its creative quality, is stirred into activity. Most of all, impassioned emotion is quickly evoked. And, in this Epistle, the transitions from one topic to another, and from one aspect of a t,,pic to its contrast, are vivid tokens of his superabundant energy. Much is left without minute elaboration. Hints are given that might be expanded into essays and disquisitions. But he was not writing these; he was writin!{ apostolic letters, and " first and last and midst" he adhered to his plan and method. Judging from his recorded speeches, he is quite as much or more of a speaker when writing than whe-a addressing a multitude. The spirit in him is often impetuous and finds it easy work to loose itself from restraints. Keenly conscious of himself, still more keenly conscious of Divine truth in himself, his personality is as nearly merged in his apostleship as we can conceive possible, and hence it is Paul, the servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, who. has the pre-eminence in all the manifestations of his genius and character. This Epistle, a manual of Church order, an epitome of cardinal principles adapted to the ever-changing externality of Church life, presents many a germ-idea for future development. Not one of his Epistles bears so directly on certain questions of the day. If we study the human body from the Pauline point of view, we shall be rid. very soon of those dangerous teachin"s which some of our physiologists are pressing on popular acceptance. If we follow St. Paul, we shall know more of the human soul than most of our philosophical systems teach us. There are no "wandering mazes" here in which men are "lost," but over every realm he traverses, light gathers as he advances, and the splendour always bangs its noon where the radiance is most wanted. Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God. Christ is therefore bis Power and Wisdom, wherever the duties of the apostleship have to be discharged and its sorrows have t? be endu~ed. The day has not come for this Epistle to be fully understood and appreciated. Science has_many years -:,f apprenticeship to serve before it can reach the plane of thought on which ~t. Paul stood. And our Christian thinkers have much to learn before culture and piety can open to them the hidden treasures of this Epistle. As true Biblical criticism advances, the profundity of this letter to the Corinthians grows more apparent, and we feel in our day, as was never felt, ~fore the amazing compass of its power. Here are ideas which wait on time and have given as yet scarcely more than a fragment of themselves to our foremost scholars. Here artl latent inspirations that will one day astound the world. Nothin(7 that he wrote has a better-grounded assurance of a great future, and when that future :hall come, the world will have a far juster sense of its indebttdncss to St. Paul aa a grand tcacber.-L. cu. :xvi. 1-24.] THE FIRST EPISTL!!, TO THE CORINTHIA:N'S. 5131

entries.title: 1CO 16:1–4
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -0hurch gifts, There arc few interests in human life which can be separated from the consideration of money. Money is the first necessity of governments, and it is the sinews of war, In business, in professional life, in industrial pursuits, pecuniary considerations are prominent, perhaps paramount. It is no otherwise in religion; and, however some superfine Christians may object to associatincr anything so base as money with what is the loftiest of human interests, no way ha~ been found of excluding money matters from the Church of Christ. Indeed, as Christianity claims to affect and to control all that is human, there seems no possibility of excluding anything so important as money from its range. I THE PURPOSES TO WHICH CHURCH GIFTS SHOULD BE DEVOTED, The contributions gathered in Achaia, Macedonia, and other places, at the instance of the apostle, were for the poor Christians of Jewish race at Jerusalem. There is no reason to suppose that all the methods and practices of the primitive Churches were unexceptionable. We have to deal with aims, with impulses ancl principles, not with details of method and administration. And we cannot question that the relief of the poor, and especially of the Christian poor, is a lawful and becoming means of displaying practical brotherly love, Wisdom, discrimination, ought indeed to be exercised, but for the direction and not for the extinction of liberality. II. THE METHOD IN WHICH CHURCH CONTRIBUTIONS SHOULD BE MADE. From this passage, containing principles of apostolic authority, we learn that such setting apart of our substance to benevolent and ecclesiastical purposes should be: 1. Periodical. Some have, indeed, held that the words of the apostle especially sanction the devotion 0f money ns an observance peculiarly appropriate to the Lord's day, In any case, regularity is enjoined, 2. In proporticn to means, There is both common sense and Chtistian feeling in the apostle's direction as to the measure of liberality. The poor man gives of his poverty, and the rich man of his wealth; whatever is consecrated being regarded as an acknowledgment that all is from God. 3. In preparation and accumulation. 'l'o avoid a sudden levy or collection upon the apostle's arrival, he recommends that each shall lay by him in store, so that the product may be ready to hand when the day comes that it is wanted. III, THE WAY IN WHICH CHURCH GIFTS SHOULD BE APPROPRIATED AND ADMINISTERED, Paul· showed his wonted wisdom in the arrangements he suggested. 1. Personal ministration should be employed. Everything, especially everything connected with money, should be open and above-board, 'l'he givers choose the bearers of the gift. 2. 'l'he manner of apportionment should be altogether above any possibility or suspicion, Of such precautions Paul has set us an admirable and excellent exarnple.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:9
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The open door and many adversaries. Ephesus evidently had, as a scene of labour, many attractions for the ardent and fearless spirit of the Apo~tle Paul. Its vast population, its devotion to idolatry, the excitability of its inhabitants, all rendered it a congenial field for such a worker. And the opposition he encountered and the danger he braved, it is plain from the narrative, made him feel the city all the more to be an honourable and attractive post for a bold and faithful soldier of Jesus Christ. I, 'fHE OPP0nTUNITY OF SERVICE FOR CHRIST REPRESENTED IN THIS FIGURATIVE LANGUAGE. A door offerij the means of admittance to a house, and an open door invites approach and entrance. In Scripture a door is often used to express the opportunity t't> do God's will and advanca his cause. So here, the apostle represents by this figurative lauguage the summons which Providence addressed to him to evangelize this great city of Asia Minor. The citizens and visitors were numerous, the idolatry and vice which prevailed were flagrant, human sorrows and difficulties and temptations abounded; so that there was abundant room for evangelistic and pastoral labour. Further, there seems to have been in some quarters a remarkable and gratifying readiness. to hear the gospel of Christ, II. THE HINDRANCES TO SERVICE FOR CHRIST HERE ALLUDED TO. 1. Observe from what quarters it came, The narrative in the Book of the Acts makes it evident that opposition to Christian preaching arose from both Jews and Gentiles, On different grounds sinful men oppose the truth. It always has been so. It was so in the time of our Lord, and the disciple, the servant, must not expect or desire to be above his I. C0RINTHIA!II!, 20 5G2 TI-IE FIRST EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORIN'l'HIANS. [cu. XVI. 1-24~

llfaskr. 2. Observe what forms it took. Slander and secret misrepresentation was• one "·ay in which adversaries sought to hinder the truth. And another was open hostility and violence. This we know to have been put in motion at Ephesus ngainst the apostle. The ignorant and impassioned mob was stirred up to oppose tho work of Paul; in this sense, at all events, he fought with beasts at Ephesus. Ill, THE COMPAT!DILITY OF GREAT OPPORTUNITIES AND MANY ADVERSARIES, It is certainly a paradoxical statement. Yet reflection will show that there is no red inconsistency. 1. Hindrances, calumnies, serve to draw attention to any cause, and the gospel is sure to profit by anything which leads men to inquire into it.. 2. These obstacles serve to test the quality of the labourers, and to brina out couraae and resolution and patience where such qualities are required. 3, They always an~wer a valuable purpose in testing the sincerity of the converts. Times of persecution are times of testing. IV. THE ATTRACTION THIS COMDINATION BAD FOR THE APOSTLE. 1. It called forth and employed his many and remarkable powers. 2. It enabled him to realize his fellowship with his Master. 3. It promised great results of spiritual good. APPLICATIOK. 1. Enter in, Christian labourers, at every open door I 2. Be fearless of adversaries !-T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:13
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -The word of command to Christian soldiers. Now and again we meet with passages in the New Testament which remind us that Christianity does not lose sight of the sterner virtues. Certainly our religion has brought the softer and more imiable virtues into honour and prominence; but we should make a mistake did we suppose that for the severer excellences of character it finds no place. I. T!IE CHRISTIAN LIFE IS A SCENE OF WARFARE. It is an opportunity for bearing witness to the grace of God, an opportunity for faithful and diligent service. But this is not all. Who can, in any station of life, sincerely endeavour to live as a Christian, without finding out that life is a campaign, a scene of discipline, of conflict? Surely the lauguage of the New Testament in which we are addressed as soldiers of the cross, 's not mere poetry, the utterance of imagination! IJ. THE FOES WHOM THE CHRISTIAN IS CALLED TO ENCOUNTER ARE SPIRITUAL. As the apostle expresses it el~ewhere, "We wrestle not with flesh and blood, but with principalities and powers," etc. Whether at Corinth or at Ephesus, or in modern London, or far away beyond the seas, he who is bent upon doing the will of God must needs make up his mind to face the adversary. Many are the forms assumed by the foe of souls, many his devices, great his craft and power. In his temptation, our Divine Lord and Leader, the Captain of our salvation, himself faced the enemy, and withstood his repeated and various assaults. Ill. OUR POSITION OF DANGER CALLS FOR THE EXERCISE OF THE SOLDIER-LIKE VIRTUES oF COURAGE AND ENDURANCE. 1. Watchfulness; lest the soldier be surprised at his post, and fall a victim to his foe. What stress our Lord and his apostles have laid upon this attitude of vigilance! If we know ourselves, our weakness\ our liabilitf to sin ; if we know the resources of our enemies-we shall feel the necessity of watclung, lest we enter into temptation. 2. Steadfastness in the faith; lest we be tossed to and fro by our indecision and vacillation. Persecution and prosperity are alike in this, that they expose us to this danger. 3. Manliness is, no doubt, in contrast to the spirit of effeminacy and sloth. "Quit you like men!" is the ringing battle-cry of one whose own life illustrated the precept. 4. Strength is needed in such a combat, in which only the weapons of warfare which are not carnal are mighty through God to the pulling down of the strongholds. JV. DIVINE GRACE ALONE CAN EQUIP AND UPHOLD THE BOLDIEllS IN THIS HOLY WAR. This great truth is always, when Dot expressed, in the baclcground, when admonitions to vicrilance and courage are addressed to Christians. It is not to be supposed that in our o~vn strength we can comply with requirements_ so strin~ent and conduc_t a warfare IIO perilous. But "if God be for us, who c~n be aga_mst us?" Th? "'.arfare 1s not ours, but God's, and his are the weapons and his the might, even as his 1s the glory of the vietory.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:14
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Love a principle of action. We may regard love as a sentiment. It ls

~uch; ond yet Hs place in the economy of human nature and life is not fully described when thus much is said. For it is one of the most powerful practical principles of our being. Human love can effect great things. And Divine love is the motive which God himself has appointed for the renewal and salvation of our humanity. And this same emotion becomes in Christian society an -elevating, purifying, regulatin", 0 and transforming power. It is thus that it is regarded in the text. I. THE MODEL OF THE LIFE OF LOVE IS TO BE FOUND IN THE LIFE OF CHRIST. Who that reads the incomparable story of our Lord's earthly ministry can be insensible to _this fact, which distinguishes that ministry from, and raises it above, every other life and work this world bas witnessed? Love gleamed from his countenance, spoke in his tones, flowed from his presence, wrought by his hands. And love led him to his cross. JJ. THE AUTHORITY FOR THE LIFE OF LOVE IS TO BE FOUND lli" THE WORDS OF CHRIST. Again and again did the Saviour enjoin upon his disciples the virtue of brotherly love. It was his new commandment. It was his test of discipleship. Love to God and love to man constituted, according to him, the sum of obedience, righteousness, religion. III. THE UNIVERSAL APPLICATION OF THIS PRINCIPLE. It is too common to regard Christian charity as a grace to be displayed in certain relations and upon certain occasions. But this is not the New Testament idea. Love is to govern the whole life, and is to permeate the Christian society. There is no limitation in the language of the text:." Let all that ye do be done in love!" It is a lofty motive, a far-reaching principle. The precept is doubtless one not easy of application so general. Yet nothing less than its universal adoption and prevalence can satisfy the Lord of the kingdom. IV. THE ADVANTAGES ACCRUING TO THE CHURCH FROM THE ADOPTION OF THIS PRINCIPLE. How different is the selfish principle adopted by the unchristian world, is at once apparent. This is a new, an antagonistic principle, yet, in its proper influence, the principle which is to pacify strife, to harmonize conflicting interests, to breathe new life into human society. "All ye are brethren" was the Master's explicit declaration concerning the members of his Church. "See how these Christians love one another! " was the exclamation of a surprised and admiring world. V. THE IMPRESSION PRODUCED UPON THE WORLD BY m-,;; PRACTICAL EMBODIMEN'l' OF THIS PRINCIPLE. The world is doubtless impressed ~ ~he novelty, the beauty, the celestial dignity, of Christian doctrine. Yet the expression of that doctrine in the life of brotherly love is more effective ; and the realization of Christ's idea, the fulfilment of Christ's law, will do more than all preaching to convince the world of the Divine mission of the Christ.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:15
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Service and honour. As the family that had first in Achaia received the gospel, Stephanas and his household were regarded by the apostle with peculiar interest and affection. The manner in which they are introduced in this passage is highly instructive and suggestive. I. THE VOCATION TO SPJRI'l'UAL MINISTRY. 1. Its first condition is sincere personal adhesion to Christianity. Stephanas and his household were converted, baptize,l, and well instructed in the Christian faith. It was when they had become penetrated with the Spirit of Christ that they were impelled to holy and devoted service. Wo cannot expect men and women to become unselfish labourers for the welfare of their fellow-men, until they have come under the new and Divine motive and power. 2. Christian ministries are of many and very various kinds. These vary with the capacity and opportunity of the labourers, and the necessities of those whose welfare is sought. Too limited a view of ministry is frequently taken; the fact is, that what- ever service men render to their fellow-men, for the sake of Christ, is a Christian ministry. Not only the preaching of the gospel, but the instruction of tbe young, the nursing and healing of the sick, the showing of kindness and hospitality, the 8Upporting with generosity of benevolent undertakings, all fall into this cla8s. 3. Services of such kinds involve both labour and co-operation. His people find a pleasure in offering to Christ, their Lord, that which costs them something. And they delight to help one another; some leading and others following, but all setting before them 56! TIIE F.iRST EPISTLE TO TIIE COIUNTHIANS. [en. xvi. 1-21.

the same end, and toiling in the same spirit. 4. Ministerin<" "unto the saints" is an especial form of acceptable service. From the begiunin"° Churches have cared for their widows, and for their poor and aged members. Th~ household of faith has e. peculiar claim upon the sympathy and affection and liberal support of the Saviour's friends. II. THE HONOUR AND SUBJECTION DUE TO THOSE ENGAGED IN SPIRITUAL MINISTRY. 1. They should be treated with especial regard and gratitude. Paul himself honoured the good Stephanas and his like-minded wife and household, and he reminded the Corinthians that a family among themselves so distinguished in the annals of the Church, and so dear to the apostle's heart, should be esteemed hi()'hly in love for their wo:k's sake. 2. They had a claim upon such as were in a position to render them help in the good cause. Doubtless it was the case at Corinth, as elsewhere that the burden was too readily left upon the shoulders of those disposed to bear it.' But this ought not to be. "\Vben one man is seen working bard for Christ bis nei()'bbour should put t_o himself the question?" C~n I help my _br?thei:, r:Iieve him of some p~ssure, or render bis labour more effective? ' 3. Subm1ss1on 1s, m many cases a duty in Christian Churches. There are those whom we should be ready not only to work with but to work under.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:18
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Spiritual refreshment. The three honoured members of the Christian society at Corinth who came to Ephesus, came officially as a deputation to consult the inspired apostle upon matters of faith and practice. But their visit was not. simply official ; for all three were personally attached to Paul, and their sentiments of affection were reciprocated by the fervent nature of the apostle of the Gentiles, whose largeness of heart was even more conspicuous than his keenness of intellect. The grateful language in which Paul acknowledges the benefit he had received from intercourse with bis visitors, is suggestive of thought regarding the refreshment of spirit which is one happy result of Christian associations. L THE :NEED ALL SO]l(ETI]l(ES FEEL OF SPIRITUAL REFRESHMENT. 1. Work may be burdensome, and even oppressive, and may weigh down the soul as well as the body. 2. 'l'rials, desertion of friends, disappointment in fellow-labourers, etc., may distress the soul and dispose to melancholy. 3. Living much alone and in one's own occupations is wearisome to the spirit; the energies flag; the quality of work suffers; gloom tnkes possession of the life. 'l'bese and many other causes render it most desirable that the thirsting, fainting spirit should be reanimated by some suitable influences. II. THE APPOIKTED AGENTS OF SPIRITUAL REFRESHMENT. Letters and books are precious, but in the case before us they are inadequate. Living companionship, the society of those like-minded with ourselves, alone can meet the requirements of the case. Not only so; sympathizing friends have a peculiar power of restoring the equilibrium of the soul. Sympathy was what Paul sought and valued. It is hard to do even work for Christ without the smile and word of encouragement which our brethren in the Lord are able to give us. IIL THE ]l(EAKS OF SPIRITUAL REFRESH]l(ENT. The presence of Christian friends is much; but their conversation, the opening of their hearts, the inquiry concerning our labours, successes, and failures,-these are all much to be desired. .l\'ot only the ccmmunication of knowledge and advice from our superiors, but the friendly conversation of our equals, and even the sympathy and heart-revelation of those in some resrects beneath us, may prove truly recruiting to our energies and restorative to our sp:rits. l V. THE RESULTS OF SPIRITUAL REFRESHMENT. 1. Depression gives place to cheerfulness. 2. Weariness gives place to vigour. 3. Sluggishness gives place to vivacity. 4. Despondency gives place to hope. 5. Inefficiency gives place to successful labour. 6. Doubt gives place to living confidence. In all iB seen the operation of that Spirit of grace who does not disdain to work in and through the lowliest of Christ's sincere disciples and friends.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:19
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Christian greetings. In St. Paul's Epistles personal messages occur in juxtaposition with doctrinal statements and arguments and moral counsels. Their occurrence makes us feel the true humanity of thiB method of religious communication;

we gain an insight into the hP:i.rt, not or the apostle alone, but or his fellow-labourers nnd friends. And we cannot but admire the evident power of Christiar,ity to hallow nor! ennoble, to refine and bless, the relations subsisting among friends. I. FnoM WHOM, AND TO WHOM, ARE THESE GREETINGS? 1. Individuals are named. Of Aquila and Priscilla we know that they were regarded by Paul as his dear friends and trusty fellow-labourers. Wherever they went they carried the gospel, they formed a circle of Christian friends, they provided a home for workers and a gatheri na-place for worshippers. 2. Households join in the greetings. This is evidently th~ case, whether we regard the expression "Church in the house" as applying to the Christian family and their dependents and guests, or to a party wont to assemble in a certain house for mutual edification and common worship. 3. Churches send salutations. The Christian congregations of Asia Minor were linked together in bonds of mutual confidence and affection, and expressed their feelings by the medium of the apostolical letter. This practice authorizes communications between Churches and groups of Churches, as promotive of brotherly love. II. OF WHAT KIND? 1. 'l'hev are fraternal. In the salutation those who send the messages are termed brethren. Not as fellow-professors of one faith, but as members of one family, did these primitive Christians exchange their greetings and good wishes and prayers. 2. Cordial and affectionate. Salutations are often matters of form, and are then cold and all but meaningless. 'fhe holy kiss, which was the custom in those primitive communities, was a sign of the warmth and sincerity of the good feeling which prevailed. 3. Mutual; for they were admonished to greet one another. "All ye," Christ had said, "are brethren;" and we see how true an attempt was made to comply with his commands, and to realize his descriptions. IIL UPON WHAT BASIS? Not upon the basis of mere courtesy, or or common interests or expediency, but upon a specially Christian basis; the greeting was "in the Lord." By this we must understo.nd: 1. In fulfilment of the Lord's command, who had so often and emphatically enjoined the cherishing and m1nifestation of brotherly ;ove. 2. In imitation of the Lord's conduct, who himself, in o.11 his communications with his friends, bad been wont to display that love which he desired to witness among his followers. 3. Under the influence of his Spirit, whose presence and gracious operations make themselves felt by the diffusion of courtesy, good will, and kiudness.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:22
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The absence of love to Christ. There are t!1ose who, not having known Christ, have had no opportunity of loving him. But of all who have heartl and reacl of Christ, we may say that the one test of their charncter and their position lies in their feeling with regard to him, with all which that feeling invoh·es. The apostle"s warm heart could tolerate no indifference, no neutrality, here. The Lord Jesus must be not only respected, but loved. And not to love him proves that the nature is iusensible to all that is good and Divine-involves its own condemnation and cur~e and misery. I. TnE ADS ENCE OF LOVE TO CHlllST. Where there is no love to the Lord J esns there appears to be: 1. A want or appreciation of his perfect moral character. If Jesus be known by a holy and sympathetic nature, he will appear to such a nnture "the chit-f among ten thousand, the altogether lovely.'' Who can gaze upon the sinless and pure, the just and kin<l, the meek and patient Jesus, and be unaffected by the spectacle? Only those for whom moral excellence and beauty have no charms. 2. A deep sensibility to his infinite compassion. !<'or it must be borne in mind that the Saviour's disposition and ministry, and especially his sacrifice, have a personal relation to omselves. It was for us men and our salvation that he livt•d a life of poverty and contempt, that he deigned to die a death of agony and shame. 'l'o withhold the heart's best love from One who endured the cross for us argues n callousness of nature beneath the level of common humanity. 3. A base ingratitude for all he has ,lone and is doing on our behalf. Even those who are indifferent to the Lord Jesus owe him a vast debt for the benefits which, by his mediation, he has confcr!'ed upon the human race, and for the forbearance with which they have individually been treated. If ingratitude to earthly friends and benefactors be base, how shall the hdnousuess be described of ingratitude to the Son of man? 566 THE FIRST EPISTLE '1'0 THE CORINTHIANS. [cH. xvI. 1-2·i.

II, THE CURSE A~"D CONDEMNATION INVOLVED IN INDIFFERENCE TOWARDS CHRIST. 1. "' e can trace this in the moral degradation which such insensibility occasions. Not tu love the worthiest and the best is to debase our nature. Character is largely moulded by love ; and they who turn away from the love of Immanuel choose death. 2. The condemnation of concience is inevitable. Its voice may be stifled for a season, but it will be hea.rd, and that voice must needs utter a censure of no feeble or ambiguous kind. The judge is within, and chnot be escaped; that judge will charge the sinner with hating him who was and is supremely worthy to be loved, and the accusation is self-evidencing and brings its curse. 3. 'l'he judgment of the Lord may tarry, but it will surely come. 'l'he Lord himself is at hand, to deliver those who love him, but to execute a righteous sentence upon the unbelieving, the unloving, the unspiritual.-T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:1–4
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-0oncerning the collection. I. THE NECESSITY OF GIVING. 1. For maintenance of public worship in our own community. Churches should aim at self- support. .Assuredly there should be no unwillingness to give where we ourselves reap the advantage. .And often the return, being spiritual, infinitely exceeds all that we part with. 2. .For various works which have for their ob}ect the dissemination of the truth or the relief of the needy. Gospel at home is good, but we must see that the gospel is sent abroad. There are many societies aiming to reach the heathen in this land and in other lands; ready support should be rendered. "Go ye into all the world," etc. (Matt. xxviii. 19). Relief of the destitute is a bounden duty of the Christian. Here we have a beautiful example. The apostle is no doubt referring to the distressed believers in Jerusalem and Judrea (Rom. xv. 26). The largely Gentile Church is incited to aid the largely Jewish. This will form a new bond, and do the double work of relieving suffering and breaking down prejudice. Our charity should know no limits but the limits of need and ability. 3. For givers individually. Christians who do not give do not grow. The cultivation of charity is the cultivation, not of one grace, but of many. It is usual to plead the needs of others ; our personal need of giving is a strong argument. Parting with some ballast pro~pers our voyage, and, instead of imperilling our safety0 increases it. Right giving is great gaining. We cannot be like Christ unless we give. He "gave himself for us." 4. For the Church. That Church which is not a giving Church will not be a prospering Church. .A spirit of charity in a religious CQmmunity exercises a gracious influence upon everything that that community attempts, and is ever prompting fresh efforts. Church charity should be wide. There is such a thing as Church selfishness. A Church may bestow too much thought upon itself. High shutting-in walls are not good for gardens. 5. For the glory ef God. Giving manifests the power of the Christian faith. It is a very powerful testimony in the eyes of the world. The world is apt to scoff at profession, even at worship; but this practical outcome often startles, and bas sometimes staggered, the world. It is a great instrument of conversion. Moreover, every gift should be a direct offering to God. We must see in the band of the needy the treasury of the Lord. The Master often sits over against that treasury. II. THE APOSTOLIC SUGGESTIONS. 1. Setting apart eaql, week. This is very convenient for many. It also ensures frequent and regular giving. Further, and what is of far more importance than is :renerally thought, it faci!itates. our lcnow~ng how 'Tnuch we give. Those who do not know bow much they give thinlc they give three times as much as they really do. Perhaps the most certain way to increase our giving would be to keep a strict account of how little we give! Setting apart each week would provide us with a store from which we could draw as necessity arose. ~e a~·e ready for the collection in the sanctuary when we have first made the collect10n Ill the home. 2. On the first day of the week. How appropriate a time ! .Associated with so many hallowed memorits, and pre-eminently with the _con!pletion by his resurrection of Cl,rist's great gift to us. His charity should be the msp1rer of ours .. A beautiful act for a holv day. How could we refuse to give then, or how could we give grudgingly 1 3. 'l.'he umount of gift to be determined by the measure of prosperity• .All gifts are not expected to be of the same value. "8he bath done what she could" was the Mastees gracious expression of apprornl. Note: Our prospetity is ~f ~od. He gives that we may give. Ii we take all to ourselves, we are robber~, not Clmst1ans. -en. xvi. 1-24.] THE FIRST EPIS'l'LE TO 'rHE CORINTHIANS. 5G'j

And in so far as we do not give what we knc,w he would have us to, we are defrcmders ,of God. He trusts us with so much: let us see that we do not abuse the trust. Stewards are we, not proprietors. Christ's commendation of the widow's two mites is abused by some well-to-do folks; they always aim to give that amount. Alas! when the chill of adversity comes to many men it kills at once all offerings to the Lord- retrenchment "begins at the house of God "-aud when prosperity comes they give but the old sum, which in the altered circumstances is a beggarly and disgraceful offering. 4. All to give. All ltave received. 'l'he widow gave "all her living." None are too poor to give something. , Every Christian should be a giving Christian; it is a part cf his Christianity. The gift of a Church is specially valuable when it is a gift of all its members. And right giving is such a joy, that when the most destitute part with something for Christ's sake they do not lose now, but gain. When we give we get. ii. Giving is to be voluntary. It is to be giving. The apostle does not propose to make an assessment. The matter is left between the individual and his God. Giving is valuable only as it springs from the he;;.rt. Where compulsion (and there are many sorts) -begins, there charity ends. The beauty of Christ's offering was that it was voluntary. No man took his life from him; be laid it down of himself. III. GIFTS SHOULD DE CAREFULLY ADMINISTERED. Charity is greatly checked if 1;uspicion arises that gifts do not reach their intended destination. The apostle uses great care here. He arranges that those who give should elect custodians of their gifts, who might bear the offering to Judrea. 'l'be loose way in which some Churches manage their finances tends to lessen liberality. A Church should keep its accounts more carefully than a bank I The administration of a Church's gifts is no mean work. 'l'he apostle offers to take part in it, if this shall seem well. Not alone-lest 8ome should take opportunity to slander: ministers cannot be too carefal in money matters. But with others he is willing even to journey to Jerusalem.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 16:5–9
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Words to those who travel. I. WESHOULDAL\V.!.YS BE ON ou&l\fasTElt's BUSINESS. This we may be if we are engaged in " secular" affairs. Every part of life is to be consecrated to Go<l. A Christian is a Christian always, and a servant always. Everything may be consecrated. Whether we eat or drink, or whatever we do, wz may do all to the glory of God. Secular engagements become truly sacred if in them (1) we act justly; (2) seek to please God; (3) avoid injury to our fellows; (4) endeavour tu display a Christian spirit. To do this as we travel, we should (1) preserve a prayerfi1i frame of mind; (2) watch vigilantly for temptations. These are often very numerous and strong when we are away from our usual surroundings, and not amongst those who know us. We should embrace every opportunity of doing good. Not only to men in things temporal, but also in things spiritual. .At last it will seerr, marvellous to some that their "charity" and "love" extended only to men's lower needs. II. OUR MOVEMENTS SHOULD BE ORDERED OF THE LonD. 1. In secular affairs we should seek the mind of the Lord. He who can help us in the great can help us in the small. 'l'bere is nothing too insignificant to pray over. 2. Jn sacred a.ffairs we need ever say, "lf the Lord permit." " D. V." on a bill amounts to little; we need it engraved on the heart. 3. Those who, evangelizing, pass from pluce to place will do well to study the conduct of their apostolic protutype. (1) He did not think a difficult post meant a post·to be abandoned as speedily as possible. Some are all for running away. They are ever" seeking rest,'' but they are ever" finding none." '!'here is no" rest" out of the path of duty. (2) Ho was not overwhelmed by a little opposition, nor by much. Many adversaries being there was a reason why he should be there. Where the ene:nr i.s strongest, there the loyal soldiery should be strongest. (3) He read in an open door the mind of the Lord directing him to remain. He did not read this in (a) comfort, (b) applause, (c) remuneration, (d) predilection. Some communities have attempted to 1,tereotype the mind of the Lord in a three years' pastorate; this looks wore like the mind of man than the mind of the Lord. Some divines can only hear certain "calls' -0f the Lord; it is to be feared that these "calls" are, after all, nothing more than the ~choes of their own voices.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 16:13
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-A fivefold exhortation. This the Corinthians needed. It fitly comes ,near the conclusion of the Epistle, summurizing much that has g ue before. 'l'lu., 5GS 'l'HE FIRST EPJSTLE '1'0 'l'HE CORINTHIANS. [en. xv1. 1-21.

Corinthians tended towards false security, reliance upon gifts and teachers• so the aposlle says, "\Vatch ye." 'l'hey were wavering in arlhesion to the gosp;l which Paul preached; so he says, "Stand fast in the faith." 'l'hcy were but "babes" (eh. iii. 1); so the apostle incites them to seek more of the qualities of manhood: "Quit you like men." They were enfeebled by fal~e doctrine, Church .abuses, irre"ularity• of spiritual life; so he says, " Be strong." They were more remarkable rof jealousy . rivalry, contempt, pride, than for the pre-eminent Christian grace; so Paul says, "Let all that ye do be done in love." Corinthian perils are our perils. Corinthian failures may be our failures-perhaps arc. Let us heed the apostolic exhortation to- I. WATCHFULNESS. 1 . .Against dangers from without. False teachers, bad examples, unholy influences, Satanic attacks. We who arc of the day should be awake. 2. .Aga.inst dang,r from within. We often tempt ourselves, often deceive ourselves, often injure ourselves. Our greatest enemy is within, not without. It is the traitor in the camp who does the mischief. 3. For opportunities of usefulness. Our <lay is short. Soon the_ final account must be rendered. We have many opportunities, but they never wait for us. \Ve must watch for them, and catch them as they come. OJ'por- tunities have no resurrection. 4. For the coming of Christ. 'l'he Master himself enjoined this: "What I say unto you I say unto all, \Vatch" (Mark xiii. 37). II. STEADFASTXESS. ,ve have to abide in the faith. He that" endureth to the end" shall be saved. Lack of steadfastness (1) hinders our spiritual growth; (2) mars our usefulness; (3) imperils our salvation; (4) is a stumbling-block to others; (5) a grm:t offence to Christ; (6) spoils our spiritual joys. III. MAKLINESS. Christians should be robust. They are not always to be children in the faith. They need a manly temper, (l) to contend with difficulLies; (2) to bear up nn,ler opposition; (3) to endure temporary defeat. Christians should be bold and fearless. Every Christian should be a courageous Christian. 'l'he service in which we are en~aged is grand beyond conception-the issues how momentous I "Quit you like men!" IV. STRENGTH. Does it seem strange that we are commanded to be strong? Some will say we can only be what we are, and it is worse than futile to say to a weak man, " Be strong." But Paul said, "\Vhen I am weak then am I strong." 'When we are lidden to be strong, then we often feel most our weakness; but then we go to the Strong for strength. The Lion of the tribe of Judah can give to us a lionlike might. As to means: if we would be strong we must (1) abound in prayer (::l) and in work -using all the strength we have; (3) avoid evil influences-not be more than duty calls us in pestilential worldly atmospheres; (4) seek solid knowledge of things Divine; ( 5) strive against sin. V. LoVE. Love should rule aU our tliou_qht&, purposes, words, and acts. We am nothing if we are without love (eh. xiii.). This is the key to the preceding exhortations. If we have a real living love towards God and man, it will become easy to live in watchfulness; we shall not want to relinquish our faith; our Christian manliness will rapidly develop; and we shall be strong, for we shall be lilce God. "God is love." Love is salt; it will preserve from corruption our whole spiritual life.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 16:15
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Ministering to the saints. I. A VERY NEEDFUL WORK. Many of God•s children are poor children. The saints who presently shall inherit all things, at present often lack the necessaries of life. Not a few of God's choicest servants are afflicted, and need sympathy and aid. Persecution for the faith should be counteracted as far as possible by ca1eful ministration. In early days imprisoned saints were specially cared for by those at liberty. "Remember those who are in bonds." In modern forms of persecution aid is equally needful. Many need to bo "taken by the hand." "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do :;ood unto all men, especially unto them who are of the househokl of faith" (Gal. vi. 10). II. A VERY HONOURADJ.E AND DEA UTil'UL wonK. Angel-like : they are "ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for tht:m who shall be heirs of salvation" (Heh. i. 14). Obrist-like: "The Son of 01an came not to be mini~tered unto, but to minbter" (Matt. xx. 28). At last the Lord will say," Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of thl'se my brethren, ye have done it unto me" (Matt. xxv. 40). Many do not . on. XVI, 1-24.J 'l'HE FIRS'!' EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 5C!i

rightly estimate this" high calling." 'l'rue love for the brethren (a sign of our salvation, 1 John iii. 14) will make us diligent in this service. Ill. A wonK wmcn CAN DE EXERCISED IN MANY WAYS. Thus suited to the abilitirsnnd opportunities of a largo number. Many are idle in our Churches because they can find nothing to do. Let them look in this direction. Visiting the sick, condolino- witlt the bereaved, relieving the destitute, cheering the depressed, securing rest for th; overworked,. guiding the perplexed, encouraging despondent workers (ministers, sabbathschool teachers, etc.),-how many might find a suitable sphere in such holy ministries as these! IV. A WOBK WHICH MERITS RECOGNITION ON THE PART OF THE CHURCH. Those who engage actively in such service as this should be: I. Highly esteemed. Jt is no slight service which they render. They do much to elevate the tone of the Church; much to preserve it in peace and content; much to stimulate its zeal. 2. Encouraged. The work is trying. Those who seek to encourage others often need very much encouragement themselves, 3. Aided, 'l'his is probably what the apostle means by" Submit yourselves unto such." "As they serve you, do you serve them." Above all, no obstacles should be put in their way. V. A WORK VERY DENEFICIAL TO THOSE WHO ENGAGE IN IT. .. They who wnter others shall themselves be watered." Here when we give we take. We grow rich by bestowing. Christians stagnate because they think of themselves. Saints take S() much care of themselves that they become spiritual invalids. We may "sit under" our own ministry with great profit. A sure way of getting to heaven is resolving that some one else shall get there. Labours for others make us blic.d to our own troubles. If our ears are filled with the cries of the needy, we shall not be nble to hear the croakings of sceptics or the evil prognostications of Satan. 'l'rue ministering to the saints is truest ministry to ourselves.-H.

entries.title: 1CO 16:22
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -Those who do not love Oh1·ist. I. THERE ABE sucH. Alas! how ma-.:iy! Not those who have never heard of him, but those who have heard much of him-those before whom the great revelation of Christ has been spread out. Not those who have been brought up under sceptical influences, but those who have been trained in Christian homes. How many of those to whom Christ has been made kilown as fully as he ca:i be to any who have not received him, yet do not love him! This is (1) strauge, (2) saddening, (3) explicable ouly upon belief in the extreme virulence of sin. II. 'l'HE l;{EINOUSNESS OF THEIR srn. Cons:der: 1. Christ is altogether lovely ancl lovable. 'l'here is nothing in him to clleck Jove, but everything to encourage it. 2. He has never done the slightest evil to any man. 3. He has relinquished heaven for men. 4. He has humbled himself to assume human nature for men. 5. He hns lived for men, 6. He has died for men. 7. He is willing to redeem men from all things evil, and to ensure to them all things good. Not to love such a Being as this is the chief of crlmes. No tale of guilt could bo sterner. It is a fearful revelation of the "carnal heart," which is enmity against God and Christ, instead of lo'l'e. III. Timm DOOM. They aro "anathema "-accursed, 'l'hcir crime merits completest condemnation. if they can be guilty of this, they can be guilty of anything. Their sentence is" everiasting destruction from the presence of the Lord;" their home, with "the devil and his angels." Their choice is to be accursed. 'l'hey choose the curse rather than the blessing which Christ waits to bestow. 'l'hey choose tho curso rather than the One who nlone can deliver them from it. '!'hey a~e now accursed; their present condition is this condition, and their future condition will be this unless they " turn to the Lord." IV. A SOLEMN QUESTION-Do WE LOVE CHRIST? 1. Not-Do we admire him? He is admired even by atheists. 2. Not-Do we abstain from hostility towards him? 3. Not-Do we t:J,ke his n:J,me upon our lips, observe his day, meet with his people? 4. Not even-Do we work for him? 5. llut-Has he touched our heart? Do we love him? Christ is the 9reat test applied to human he:J,rts. The issua reveals conditiun, character, prospect.-H,

entries.title: 1CO 16:1
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The law of Christian giving. It is interesting to note that one of tho first and most natural expressions of the Christian spirit was a consideration of .1370 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. [cu. xvI. 1-24.

the needs of the poorer members of the Church, and a readiness to share what crood thin~s were possessed with them. Of this spirit Barnabas is presented to u~ as offering the highest example (Acts iv. 36). His thought and feeling in this matter had very probably influenced his companion St. Paul. We can well understand that th4l Jewish Christians, dwelling in the holy city, would be placed under great disabilities. Many of them were very poor; their opinions would prevent their obtaining the ordinary charities; perhaps they found it even difficult to secure remunerative labour; and, when times of famine and distress came, they would be the first to suffer. When Christianity was proclaimed freely to the Gentiles, there was this grave danger to face; the separation between Jew and Gentile miaht be kept up within Christianity, and the conception of one Church--one floclt under one Shepherd-might fail to be realized. 'l'o correct this tendency, St. Paul sought to keep up the sympathy of the newer Gentile with the ol<ler Jewish Church, and guided the expression of such sympathy, letting it take the form of collections and money gifts. In the passage now before us the principles upon which Christian givin"0 should be regulated are indicated. They concern- I. THE CL~IM OF ALL TO A SHARE IN CHRISTIAN GIFTS. Nothino- that a man possesses is his own. Money, talents, position, influence,-all are Divine gifts and trusts; none are sent for the man's sake alone who receives them. He is only made an agent for ministering God's good gifts· to others. The whole Church has its claim to share in whatever good things any of its members possesses. It should be impossible to find, among Christians, an unrelieved sufferer, or a helpless, poverty-stricken beggar. We must distinguish between charity and the meeting of the family claims of our brethren in the Lord. It is not charity, it is duty, it is faithfulness, that leads us to share what is entrusted to us with those who share in the same salvation, and who have the same "good hope through grace." We do not speak of charity among brothers and sisters of the same family, and the right view of Christian giving is taken only when the Christian Church is regarded as a family. . II. THE l>"EED FOR PREPARATION BY PREVIOUS STORING. The claims upon us only come at times, but they do come at times in forms quite beyond our meeting, if we have made no preparations. And there is the further danger that when, through circumstances of distress, our feelings arc unusually moved, we act from impulse, not from principle. So St. Paul urges that the separation of shares for the needy brethren be made regularly, as a matter of duty; that a proportion of all our acquisitions be regniarly set aside and stored up for due occasions, and that so we keep our brethren and their needs constantly in mind. III. 'l'HE TIME MOST SUITABLE FOR BUCH STORING. "First day of the week." The Lord's day. The memorial day of the Lord's resurrection; which, we cannot doubt, bad become the Christian day for worship. When minds were directed more especially to Christian privileges and duties, the separations and storings would be more liberally clone, and would be made acts of worship. It seems probable that the amounts thus regularly laid by were not stored privately, but made offerings at public worship, and stored by the treasurers. IV. THE UULE THAT REGULATES THE AMOUNT STORED. Many have argued for a tenth, but it was not in St. Paul's way to fix any limitations upon the free expression of Christian feelinu. He does r.ot mean to suggest any proportion by his law, "As God hath prosper~d him." Really he means, "Let your separation for others be accordin.,. to your sense of God's goodness to you." And this he suggests because, while th; due provibion for the poor is of grave importance, it is even more important that our storing and giving should be a means of grace to ourselves, an agency of spiritual culture. Practically it is found that brotherly and generous regard for our needy fellow-Christians bears most directly on the• efficiency of our own graces and the culture of the true Christian spirit. "The liberal soul is made fat."-R. 'l'.

entries.title: 1CO 16:3
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-Tlie relatwns of Gentile to Jewish Churches. Apart from the historical interest of this subject, which was one of the chief causes of anxiety to the apostle, it may be studied as illustrating for every age the principles on which older and younger Chnrcbes, richer and poorer Churches, can be brought into practical union and follow- .ship. Then the topic for consideration becomes this-How can the idea of the -011. xiv. 1-24.] THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 5il

·Christian brotherhood be applied to Churches? As introdnctory it may be well to show, concerning the duty of brotherliness, (1) its ground; (2) its character; (3) its -examples; (4) its natural forms of expre8sion. These may be treated in connection with the personal and individual relationships of life, and also in connection with the social and Church relationships. 'l'hen in practical detail, varying accordincr to the sent!ments and associations of the Christian bodies to which we may belong, ~ve may -cons1der- J; BROTHERLINESS AS EXPRESSED TO EQUAL CHURCHES. In this case the brotherliness will take such forms as: 1. Fellowship in worship. 2. Mutual aid in enterprise and work. 3. _Due watchfulness of each other's honour and spiritual health. 4. Anxious repression of all jealousies of each other's successes. G. Manifestations of sympathy in -times of Church depression or sorrow. Among equal Churches there is little oppor- tunity for the charity of material help. II. BROTHERLINESS EXPRESSED TO INFERIOR OR DEPEllDEllT CHURCHES. Besides those already dealt with, there should be these further expressions. 1. Careful con- servation of the rights of the dependent Church. 2. Readiness to give material and moral help, as occasion demands. 3. Avoidance of superior airs or assuJ]lptions of .authority. 4. Use of all opportunities that may be offered for the manifestation of .sympathy. While it is true that times of calamity find special occasions for brother- liness, it is also true that those in any way dependent on us would not have us wait for the trial-times. True Christian brotherhood wants to find utterance for itself every .day, and to fill all the ordinary associations of life with its helpful spirit.-R. T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:9
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content: -The mission of our hindrances. "There are many adversaries." In life we always find that the "open door" and the "many hinderers" go together. Very seldom can we have the one without the other. For the use of the tet·m "doer" as a figure for "opportunity," see Acts xiv. 2i; 2 Cor. ii. 12; Col. iv. 3. For the narrative which illustrates the expression here used, see Acts xix. 19, 20. Of hindrances affecting St. Paul, we may think of (1) bis own frail health ; (2) the diflicuities and dangers of travelling; (3) the wilfulness sometimes showu by his trnvelling companions; (-!) the sudden and unexpected claims of the Churches altering his plans; (5) the persistent .and watchful opposition of his Jewish enemies; and we may even add (6) the some- t-imes strange and trying limitations put by the guiding Spirit, as in Acts xvi. 6, 7. "That which was so eviJently true of St. Paul is the common experience of God's servants ; and we must accept the conditicns, and win virtue out of the very limitations. I. Goo's PROVIDENCE IS EVER MAKING OPEN DOORS F0R us. '!'his is true in educational life, and in business life, Every man sooner or later gets his turn and opportunity. But we observe how true it is both of personal Christian life and of Church life. Goel sets before us open doors, shows us spheres of service which we may occupy. .Antl such we enter upon with great hopes and expectations, assuming that if Providence has so manifestly opened the door, the path within must be straight and plain and easy. This we find is not always true; for- 11. Goo's PROVIDENCE IS ALSO EVER MAKING HINDRANCES. 1. Often health fails at the moment of opportunity. 2. Sometimes the will to do it fades when the opportt1nity for doing appears. 3. Events as providential seem to block the path ju-st inside the open door. 4. 'l'he work involves labour which seriously taxes energy and faiLh. 5. Too often we faint and fail, and prove the greatest hinJerers of our work. \Ve must fully .accept the fact that, here on earth, Got! has put open doors and hindrances together, that the combination might nurture and develop the noblest qualities in his servants. -R. T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:14
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-The limitation of the robuster virtues. "Let all your things be done with ,charity." The connection in which this sentence stands suggests the topic. The apostle had been calling the Christians at Corinth to manlinc~s, strong anJ vigorous action, watchfulness, and firm holding of the foith. He kuew well how readily firmness ,could become stubbornness, anci strength roughness. The strong may forget the rights of the weaker brethren, and the manly may fail to realize that full manlit1css which focludes womanly tenderness and gentleness. Therefore, in an all-suggestive sentence, be says," Temper the whole of your relations wiU charity, heavenly Divine charity," 5i2 THE FIRST EPISTLE TO 'l'HE CORINTHIANS. [CH, XIV, 1-24-,

which "hopeth all things, endureth all things, and thinketh no evil." Chrysostom•~ note on tliese 'l'erses brings out a somewhat different association. It is as follows:- " Now in saying these things, he seems, indeed, to advise; but be is reprimanding them as iudolen_t. Wherefore he ~aith, ~atch, as though they slept; stand, as though they were rock mg to and fro; qmt you like men, as though they were playinCT the coward, let all your things be done with charity, as thou~h they were in dissensi;ns. And th~ firs! caution ~efers t~ the deceivers,. viz. watch, stand; the next to those who plo11 agamst us, quit you like men; the third to those who make parties and endeavour to distract, let all youi· things be done with charity, which thinCT is the bond of perfect,.. ness, and the root and fountain of all blessings." In the teachinCT both of our Lord and of his apostles, the passive and gentle graces were so constantly commended that the enemies of Christianity might Pasily, and with some show of reason, say that it was ~ wea~,, unmanly thing, ,~ith_yielding; .and patiently enduring and quietly waiting, as its chief _an_d characteristic virtues. J herefore 8t.. Paul makes so much of his point, that Christianity was the only force that could really and harmoniously culture the full ~nanhood. Only this i_s true-t~e supreme grace of Christianity is love, charity, and 1t must tone and qualify and direct all other graces, all expressions of character in action. Consider- I. THE TENDENCY OF RUMAN NATURE TO CORRUPT EVERY1'HlNG. .A.II the good thin"S men may possess or attain are in constant peril of running over into extremes a;d exaggerations. Observe two points. 1. A man's strong side becomes inspired by selfwill, and spoiled. 2. Some tiides are unduly cultured by expression, and th,i whole character is put out of harmony and fair balance. Self-reliance, which has a small place in every good charact,er, becomes corrupted into self-conceit; and so of other features of character. II. How FAR IS THIS HUMAN-NATURE FORCE KEPT IN THE REGENERATE? It mil!ht seem that St. Paul's counsel only suited the worldly, and was hardly needed by the Christian. But we have to accept the fact, which both observation and experience attest, that the renewal of the principle on which our life is conducted does not involve an immediate deliverance from the ordinary deteriorating influences which affect men. Christian men's very graces ruay become so exaggerated as to be really vices. Strongwilled men may "love to have the pre-eminence,'' and be masterful and inconsiderate. The Christian life in a man ought to hold the evil tendency in strong bonds, but we cannot get free from the evil influence while we dwell in a body aud are surrounded by earthly scenes. III. How DOES THE CHRISTIAN SPIRIT AFFECT THIS EVIL? Apply especially to the robuster virtues. Manliness is liable to become rnasterrulness. Those who can watch come to despise the weak ones who must sleep. The strong try to force the frail to go at their pace, and easily quarrel with them when they cannot. Now, the Christian spirit proposes one effective triumph over all these evils. 'J'one all your life and relations with charity, which is, as treated in the New Testament, precisely this-consideration for others rather than self. All the evil comes out of thinking of and glorifying self, and the conquest surely comes by thinking of and glorifying others: getting the mind of Christ, who "pleased not himself."-R. T.

entries.title: 1CO 16:15
entries.author: Frederic William Farrar
entries.content:
-'l'he natural right of priority. "The firstfrnits of Achaia." We need not think of the household of Stephanas as being actually the first converts St. P,1ul made in the Peloponnesus, as apparently another person is spoken of in the same terms in Hom. xvi. 5 : "Salute my well-beloved Eprenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ." The meaning need only be that the household of Stephnnas was among those brought to Christ at St.. Paul's first missionary visit. The apostle had an affectionate regard for his first converts in new spheres, as may be illustrated in the case of Lydia at Philippi. The intrrest we always feel in first things can be illustrnted by wny of introduction. 1. Firstborn children. 2. First forms of enterprise. 3. Firstfru:ts of onr Jabour, etc. Natural feeling gives all first things prominence; and the Old Testament history and religion rested on the recognition of the rights of the firstborn and the interest or first thing~. They are the key to the life; the strong impress of the character. They are like the first proofs of an l·ngrav,ng; every lrno is shnrply defined in them. They may become the reproach of our weaker after-doings, for tht·J cu. xvr. 1-24.] THE FinST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. 573

show what we did actually attain once, and prove that we coulcl, throu"'h life have clone better. It is, however, the hope and promise of first things on which 1;e now propose to dwell. I: F!RST Tl!INGS _ARE DONE WITH I_NTENSE FEELING. Il!ustrate from the youth bcgmmng ~usrness hfe; the man entenng on a new underta~mg; the ~issionary goiug i~rth to !us new sphere, etc. Men brace themselves up to deal with new things. 'lhey have no experience to tell them what amount of strength the new work will ,lemand, so they are likely to put too much Into it. A vague but arousing wonder clings all about new things, and imagination makes them bigger and better than they .are. At first we fail to estimate difficulties, qualifications, hindrances; we start out dike Israel, and expect to reach our Canaan quickly: so all our hearts go out into our first things. And happily life is full of them, especially early life, and they exert a most gracious influence on us, for they again and again lift us out of ourselves and above ourselves. II. FIRST THINGS HAYE A NATURAL PRE-EMINENCE. Of this the position and rights -of the firstborn sons are but the illustration. First things are felt to have a representative character; they are the natural leaders of all that come after them-the specimens and examples of their sort. In all the spheres of life we give prominence to beginnings. When a servant comes to a new situation, the master or mistress watch the first actions t-0 see "how they will frame." vVhen a convert joins a Church, the pastor give prominence to the first forms in which Church responsibilities are met. 'l'urning their thoughts back to their hopeful "first things," the apostle reproaches his converts thus: "Ye did run well; who did hinder you?" III. FIRST THINGS HAVE PROMISE FOR THE FOLLOWING TFrums. As firstfruits have for harvest. The harvest need not be worse than the specimen firstfruits, but it may be much better. A man's first work need not be his maximum standard., but it ought to be his minimum standard. A first result may tell of power, and power al ways holds the promise of what culture can make it. Or, applying the point in relation to our text, one convert made in a new sphere of Christian labour holds the promise of a great ingathering; as we find at first one star in the darkening evening sky, which is the "glorious prospect of millions more." IV. Fll!ST THINGS KEEP PROMINENT PLACE IN OUR MEMORY. Illustrate our first school; first steps in business life; first love; first communion; first convert to Christ by our influence; first sickness; first success in life, etc. 'l'he most treasured things in our memory are these first things of life; and, as such, their moral mission is (1) to aid us in the review of life, by fixing attention upon points; (2) to remind us that the ipirit of energy in which we take things up is the spirit in which we should carry them through; and (3) to show us that we need the Divine help for " patient continuance in well-doing," as much as we remember we needed it for our anxious beginnings.-R. T.
